line: e4
en: Ponomariov plays 1. e4 in much the same way as any of the other top-level GMs.

line: d4
en: A difficult choice. From a computer's point of view 1 e4 is the most likely choice to be played, but I like surprises and I had something in mind.

line: e4 e5
en: The events where the younger generation play with Karpov are fewer these days, but it's interesting to see Karpov show his best form and teach the young "kids" a lesson.

line: e4 c5
en: Already in the last century Anderssen was confident to experiment with the Sicilian Defence Bereits im vorigen Jahrhundert genoss die Sizilianische Verteidigung das volle Vertrauen von Anderssen, der gern damit experimentierte.

line: e4 e5 Nf3
en: Developing a piece and attacking the pawn on e5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6
en: No more Petrov's Defense, as he played against Kasparov!

line: d4 Nf6
en: Although this game is interesting in every part, its main feature is in the exceptional conclusion, where three consecutive sacrifices for Black can be considered as the solution of a chess problem (Tartakower).

line: d4 Nf6 c4
en: The normal follow-up to 1. d4. White puts pressure on d5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5
en: The choice of openings is a little surprising. The Ruy Lopez is well known for its closed positions and extreme complexity.

line: d4 d5
en: Despite Shirov's reputation he doesn't always play the most blood-thirsty unbalanced defenses. 1...d5 weakens e5, but directly aims to prevent White from gaining too much ground with c2-c4 and e2-e4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6
en: Prevents intrusion on e5.

line: d4 d5 c4
en: The Queen's Gambit, offering a pawn to deflect Black's central d-pawn from its solid post. This has been one of the most common opening systems at every level of the game.

line: c4
en: This is called the English Opening. It usually leads to a postional struggle.

line: Nf3
en: Kasparov continues his testy strategy, avoiding main lines and waiting to see what Deep Blue offers before committing his pawns.

line: e4 e6
en: No surprise here. The wonderful veteran playing the black pieces is the French extraordinair of the 20th and perhaps the 21st century! :) I know Sofi, and this was the first line she prepared extensively for!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6
en: This gives Black the freedom to play b5 when needed. White cannot now win a pawn with 4. Bxc6 d7xc6 5. Nxe5 because of 5... Qd4 attacking the knight and e pawn.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5
en: Black gets the initiative.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
en: The Najdorf Sicilian has been the main opening of choice for decades.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6
en: Black could use ...b7-b5 to get rid of the Bxc6 "threat", but so long as that doesn't hurt Black he'll ignore it.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6
en: Whoops, didn't count on that one. In the specially prepared openingbook I counted on the Grunfeld, the Queen's Gambit Accepted and the Slav. Also the Queen's Indian was prepared, but less thoroughly than the other openings.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6
en: In some cases this restrains Pe4 sufficient to allow ...Ng8-f6, but in some other cases Black needs more control of e5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O
en: 5... Nxe5 is a playable move, but Black should not strive to hold on to the pawn. After 6. d4 b5 7. Bb3 Black should play 7... d5 giving back the pawn rather than 7... exd4 which is refuted by 8. Re1.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3
en: I've had doubts about this move for a long time. It's not so easy to prove it's wrong, but by blocking Pc2 it makes d3 less hospitable for a bishop and it makes Pd4 a little weaker.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4
en: I suppose the first curiousity is that Karpov isn't playing 1. d4, his standard opening.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7
en: With the e file blocked, Nxe4 is now a threat.

line: e4 c6
en: The Caro-Kann Defense. Kasparov used to play this right at the start of his career.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3
en: Now Black has to decide how to prevent Nxc6 and e4-e5. To that end Black has played ...d6 (Scheveningen) , ...e5 (Sveshnikov) and ...Qb6 (Benko) . All have good qualities.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1
en: Guards the pawn. Now White threatens to win a pawn with 7. Bxc6 d7xc6 8. Nxe5.

line: e4 c6 d4
en: Controlling the center with pawns.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5
en: This time we have a Caro-Kann proper.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4
en: The bishop is more aggressively placed on c4 than on b5. However, 3. Bb5 leads to longer-lasting pressure.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6
en: French Defense, Classical Variation, He's hoping for e4-e5 to create a fixed blocked pawn structure where Black has ...c7-c5 to create queen-side play.

line: e4 e5 f4
en: The King's Gambit. White sacrifices a pawn for control of the center square d4 and the possibility of his King's rook becoming active on the f file.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6
en: The classical way to decline the gambit.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3
en: White is threatening 4. e4.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3
en: Developing and putting pressure on d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3
en: Again the English Attack.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6
en: Following Kramnik's strategy? Kasparov goes for the Berlin Defence.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6
en: Fritz decides on the Queen's Indian Defence.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4
en: Stopping 4. e4. This variation is called the Nimzo-Indian.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4
en: Computers like to open files but this is an opening that Vlad really has had great success with.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4
en: Eliminating part of White's pawn center.

line: Nf3 d5
en: Black's response indicates no desire to copy white's actions.

line: c4 e5
en: Staking a claim to the center.

line: c4 Nf6
en: Developing and attacking the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6
en: Odd, from someone who generally plays the Black side of a Spanish, hoping for a Marshall Gambit.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3
en: Developing a piece and protecting the pawn on e4.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6
en: Developing and defending d5.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5
en: Sofi's pet variation against the French from the white side. She never opted (at least not that I remember) for 4. e5 Nfd7 5. f4 c5 etc. with slower spatial play. She's more of a tactician hoping for the open game.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3
en: One of the most solid systems in the very solid by nature Nimzo Indian Defence. It has been played many times in World Chess Championship matches - it's a sign of quality by itself.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4
en: The Open Variation, a long-time favourite. In most lines, Black gets active piece play.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O
en: Considering his need to win this is a good choice.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6
en: Now we are in basic position of the open variation.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7
en: I have no idea if he plays both lines regularly or if these considerations actually came into play, since I had to leave immediately after the game.

line: d4 d5 Nf3
en: This is a flexible move which might still be followed by c2-c4, but could also lead to a Torre System (Bc1-g5) or London System (Bc1-f4) or Colle depending upon Black's response.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4
en: Winawer Variation -- by pinning Nc3 Black keeps Nc3 awkward. It does, however, give White time for e4-e5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5
en: Welcome to game 13 and the GI---that's Grunfeld-Indian. Fight from the start.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5
en: It was Pillsbury who first demonstrated the strength of the this move, which today is routine.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4
en: The Evans Gambit. White gives up a pawn in order to gain time to play c3 attacking the bishop and then d4 forming a strong pawn center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O
en: White offers Pe4 as a way of forcing open the e-file when White has castled and Black hasn't.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7
en: This line is actually the favorite of Anatoly Karpov. In fact the two have done battle from this exact position - but with Kasparov on the white side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4
en: Bb6 declining the pawn is also perfectly playable.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5
en: Lasker-Pilnik or Sveshnikov Variation.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5
en: If White doesn't try to exploit the weakness at d6 then his pieces become too passive.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6
en: Now that Black has secured square d6, White can switch to taking aim at c7 and f6 by using Bc1-g5xf6 and Nc3-d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6
en: This is necessary to prevent White's threat.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5
en: This has become the most common move. Black takes away Na3-c4 or Bf1-c4 and threatens ...b5-b4.

line: c4 e6
en: One of many possible replies. Black prepares for ... d5.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2
en: The French Tarrasch, a favourite of Anatoly Karpov, and the subject of a new book by John Emms published after the start of this game.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6
en: By defending Pe5 Black is free, if he were to choose, to play ...Nc6-a5xb3, so one often sees White move either his c- or a-file pawns to make room for the Bishop to retreat.

line: e4 c5 Nc3
en: Certainly an annoying move order against Najdorf junkies.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5
en: Kasparov has played the King's Indian Defense extensively, but not recently. He's also played the Gruenfeld Defense, but 2...d5 isn't considered all that good, so he finds another choice.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4
en: This is known as the Scotch Game.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5
en: Also playable is 3... b6 leading to the Queen's Indian Defense. The current position is a Queen's Gambit Declined by transpostion of moves. It could have occurred by 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3 Nf6.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3
en: Developing and putting pressure on the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4
en: Adams wasn't able to break through this defense in round four, so why not try it again.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6
en: One of Nimzovich's original ideas, which, has now been widely analyzed.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5
en: Black counterattacks the white center immediately.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6
en: Forcing a resolution of the pressure this way is considered safest.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6
en: Threatening to play 7...b5 and 8...c4 with a pawn advantage on the queenside.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4
en: Adams does play the Marshall Gambit and many people don't like to play against it, so they play such moves as 8. a4 to avoid it. Still, that doesn't end Black's attempts to play actively.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+
en: This is the main advantage of 7. dxe5. It isn't so easy to clobber Ke8 with queens off the board, but White has an easier time developing and has a five to four king-side pawn majority. Black, on the other hand, has the two bishops.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6
en: This is a little unusual. Black isn't forced to recapture with a pawn, so there's no major cost. And, after Black recaptures at f6 there's still the threat of ...b5-b4, so Nc3-d5 seems quite likely. I wonder what he had in mind?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6
en: It seems odd that Black would allow such a pawn structure, but he can't easily be prevented from ...f6-f5xe4 to give him an advantage in central pawns. That the position has many weaknesses gives White room to develop and fight for a win.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7
en: I've never felt comfortable playing against the Modern Defense, so I was not happy to see this in an important last round game!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3
en: It seemed to me the variation used to play by my opponent against system with g3 is rather doubious. That's why I chose this move. Nevertheless it was not so easy way indeed.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6
en: Black hasn't yet moved Pe7, so there's no pin after Bc1-g5. That makes Black's army more mobile. And, the more developed he becomes the more likely ...dxc4 will succeed.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5
en: The "spanish" variation of the Four Knights.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7
en: Nimzowitsch developed this whole system.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4
en: Reestablishing material equality.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4
en: Before Steinitz there was a belief that the only way to fight for advantage was to keep the pawn structure in the centre intact:.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3
en: Also possible is 5)Qa4 when Black can play 5)...Be7 6. Bg2 O-O 7. O-O c6 8)Nc3 d5 9. Ne5 Qe8! 10. cxd5 exd5 11. Bg5 h6 12. Bxf6 Bxf6 13. Ng4 Bd8 14)Rfe1 with interesting play.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5
en: This somewhat original move (the knight makes the second move in a row in the opening) is GM Igor Zaitsev's idea.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6
en: Ukrainian chessplayers always like the Sicilian Dragon. I believe GM Mikhail Golubev, one of the main experts of this sharp system, can confirm this.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4
en: This, however, wasn't played back in Najdorf's day.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6
en: A blast from the past - You need to go as far back as the Yerevan Olympiad 1996 for Garry's last Scheveningen, when he faced Topalov. Kasparov has never really been one to play the Najdorf with ..e5, and usually always falls back on ..e6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6
en: There are at least five good moves on Black's sixth turn. This is the most common these days. It controls square e5 and perhaps prepares ...Bc8-g4 and in some cases aims at Bd3 (via ...Nb4) to fight for control of light squares.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7
en: This is perhaps the most popular move at this point. It prepares ...O-O and blocks the e-file, but isn't very aggressively placed.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4
en: White tries to undermine Ne4 or force it to retreat, opening the d3-h7 diagonal and making it easier for White to develop without simplifying piece exchanges.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3
en: Pe4 needs defense to avoid ...Nc6-a5xb3 when Pe5 and Pe4 would just be traded. With Pd3 White might also consider the maneuver Nb1-d2-f1-g3, avoiding simplifying exchanges and aiming to attack on the king-side.

line: d4 f5
en: The Dutch Defense. Black accepts a somewhat weakened pawn position for kingside attacking chances.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5
en: I've suffered against this move in the past in OTB games and so felt it was time to change sides!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5
en: Topalov is an excellent tactician and prefers the unbalanced fight this could produce.

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5
en: Let's cite Savely Tartakover here: "old nad bad" is his short comment in the classic "Die hypermoderne Schachpartie" (1925).

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4
en: Trying to control the center and planning 4. Bxc4. Nowadays 3. Nf6 is preferred to prevent Black's next move.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5
en: While it was odd for Kasparov to use this against Shirov it makes more sense for Adams. Still, it's odd that two players would choose this when facing Shirov.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6
en: This is called the Steinitz defense. It is sound but leads to a cramped position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3
en: This is one of many possible moves for White including 4. Qc2, 4. Nf3, 4. a3, and 4. Qb3.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4
en: This position can also arise from the Queen's gambit as follows: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5
en: A small surprise, as Anand preferred 4 ... Nd7 earlier this year.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 c6
en: Entering the Slav Defence, only to be transposed into something else in a few moves.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5
en: Black attacks in a most natural way, though he does leave Pg7 exposed for the moment.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5
en: One can hardly believe that this modern opening was already played in 1858! Es ist kaum zu glauben, dass diese moderne Eroeffnung schon 1858 gespielt wurde!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5
en: 6...e6 is also quite common.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6
en: Black's pawns limit White's knights and Be2. Black seeks to keep open options while discouraging White from any active operations.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3
en: Now there are a couple of weaknesses in Black's pawn structure, so White will have a clear idea of where to play (d5, d6, b6) . However, Pe5 controls d4 and with ...Bc8-e6 Black controls d5 pretty well too. Only Bf8 will be noticably bad.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6
en: Black doesn't fear the backward Pd6 and the weak square at d5 if his pieces coordinate to control d-file squares. The dark-square pawns restrain Nb3 and Be3 pretty well and the Nf6 & Be6 contest White's control of e4 & d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3
en: There's no immediate need for this. He wants to play g2-g4-g5 to gain better control of d5. Playing Qd1-d2 is mainly to prepare O-O-O and I guess he doesn't want to commit to that yet.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3
en: Ponomariov takes on the bigger challenge.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2
en: Up to here, I'd been following Karpov-Korchnoi 1974. Douglas now surprises me with his reply - I'd expected 0-0 or Bd7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O
en: The center appears to be opening quickly, so it's only safe to move the king away from the e-file. Neither White nor Black was threatening anything significant just yet, so this was a good moment to ensure the king's safety.

line: f4
en: Bird's opening. White plays for control of e5 and a kingside attack.

line: b3
en: A01: Nimzowitsch-Larsen Opening.

line: d4 d6
en: Wow! The basic opening of Grandmaster A.Vaulin is accepted queen's gambit, but it when he plays for a draw. By the first move, that day the contender had an aggressive mood.

line: e4 d5
en: The Center Counter. Black frees his game quickly but loses a tempo because his queen is exposed.

line: Nf3 d5 g3
en: Anand avoids the main theoretical variations.

line: c4 e5 g3
en: Planning to place the bishop on the diagonal.

line: e4 d5 exd5
en: Any other move would be very passive. The modern way to play this for Black is to play 2... Nf6 since after 3. c4 c6 4. dxc6 Nxc6 Black has a good game. Instead of 3. c4 White normally plays either 3. Nf3 or 3. d4.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4
en: Black's idea is to counteract the power of the white bishop, by building a pawn fortress on the squares c6, d5, and e6. But before doing that, he makes sure that the his bishop isn't caught inside.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6
en: [2...Nc6 is the original symmetrical reply, whereas 2... Nf6 is Falkbeer's recommendation. Tseitlin and Glazkov favour Nf6 for Black. ].

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4
en: The game has now transposed into a Queen's Gambit Declined. This position could have been arrived at by 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5
en: After 4. dxe5 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 Be6 the position is even.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5
en: This often leads to Black playing a Tarrasch Defense with ...d7-d5 or perhaps a Hedgehog formation after d2-d4 and ...cxd4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3
en: Kasparov had a fondness for this system of Petrosian's in the 1980s.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4
en: Seizing the center and threatening to win a pawn by 5. Bxc6+ bxc6 7. dxe5 dxe5 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 9. Nxe5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4
en: A continuation which is believed less strong that the theoretical 4.O-O but, however, must be treated with respect.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7
en: Now if White plays 5. Bxc6 Black answers with 5... Bxc6 and the bishop is attacking the pawn on e4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5
en: This is less common than 4...Nf6 5. Nc3 e5, but it has it's own interesting character. Black avoids an early ...Ng8-f6 to prevent White from developing Bc1-g5 with a pin.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4 Bb4
en: Kasparov keeps the pressure on. This is usually intended to get rid of Nc3, so Black won't have to worry about Nc3-d5. However, in this position it threatens to undermine Pe4. That causes White to postpone d2-d4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4
en: (4... Nd4 used to be Rubinstein's pet line afterwards. ).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7
en: Apparently, this hadn't gone unnoticed by the veteran. This forces white to play e5 and close up the game. 4...dxe4 was undoubtedly what Sofi was hoping for, however I'm sure she prepared for this.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3
en: This is a saving grace which helps White straighten-out his queen-side a bit.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5
en: One of the key-positions of underdeveloped chess theory.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3
en: Najdorf, imperturbably confident in his slight spatial and developmental edge, continues to bring out his pieces.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nf6 Be2
en: (Be3 is a good alternative.).

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O
en: Getting the king out of the center.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6
en: Neo-Sveshnikov or Kalashnikov Variation.

line: Nf3 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 a3
en: Speelman's move, popular for a while but now out of fashion.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3
en: After this it's clear White has to attack at the base of Black's pawn chain (Pf7, g7, h7) and Black can attack Pc2, Pc3 & Pd4; but both will also be keeping their eyes on the opponent's king, hoping to ensnare him in an attack.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O
en: White could play e4-e5 next.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3
en: A Grischuk pet-line. The young Muscovite wants to play the English Attack without having to worry about the crucial, crunch-line, 6 ..Ng4 - the Kasparov Variation.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4
en: White immediately goes after the exposed Bg6. This has been a normal move for many years now. The main alternative is to first play 6. Nf3, threatening Nf3-e5xg6.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1
en: White anticipates that the c file will be open.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1
en: This idea was introduced by American GM Walter Browne in the US championship several years ago. The idea is to play e2-e4-e5 without having to move Qd1 off the d-file. It's important for the queen to support d2-d4.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6
en: One of the central positions in the modern development of the Caro-Kann Defense. The rarer continuation 7...Qc7 was covered in the previous game. Currently, the moves 7...h6 and 7...Be7 are also popular.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6
en: Solidifying the defense of the center.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O O-O d5
en: This is old classical method of occupying the centre with a Pawn. 7...Ne4 is also possible.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O h6
en: Black sometime s uses ...g7-g5 to help fight for control of the dark squares, in lieu of having a Pe5 to do that.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 Be3
en: I like this rather unusual move and play it myself too. It's idea - to prevent the quite unpleasant move Bf8-c5 with pressure on f2.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Ne7
en: I suppose he is clearing the way for ...Bc8-f5, but those squares on the king-side in front are risky to occupy. White's pawns might race forward.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8
en: Adams keeps hoping he'll find a way for ...d7-d5.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4
en: If 10.Bxe4 0-0, black later pushes through c6-c5 or e6-e5 with good play.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O Nc3 Bf5
en: After this Black might retreat ...Ne4-f6 and play ...Nb4-c2 to gain a quick draw by repetition by threatening White's Ra1. White has to do more to challenge the light squares, so cxd5 or a2-a3 are candidate moves.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Be2 Be7 a4 Nc6 O-O O-O f4 Qc7 Kh1 Re8
en: While this move has the virtue of clearing for ...Be7-f8 and ...e6-e5 with some chance of play on the e-file, it also neglects the queen-side Bc8 & Ra8.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7 Qf3 Qc7 O-O-O Nbd7 g4 b5 Bxf6 Nxf6
en: #(In my postal games against Humans recently, I have preferred 11...Bxf6 here. However, with myself owning a Saphire I knew the machine's opening repertoire so I played the main line.).

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 O-O Kh1 Qc7 a4 Nc6 Be3 Re8 Bf3
en: I usually don't care for the bishop here because Black can often play ...e6-e5 to block Pe4 and Bf3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 Be3 Nc5 Nc3 Nxb3 cxb3 Be7 Rc1 Qd7 h3
en: In the near future White's knight will be better than Black's e6 bishop, so it's useful to prevent a possible exchange.

line: d3
en: This move is never seen at Grandmaster level, for the simple reason that it hands over the advantage of the first move to Black.

line: Nf3 c5
en: Kasparov offers a transposition to a Sicilian Defense by 2. e4. But, Kasparov can also play many kinds of openings, so this might remain a closed position.

line: d4 f5 e4
en: The Staunton Gambit. White gives up a pawn for strong attacking possibilities.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3
en: Indirection already. Nimzowitsch avoid the natural and good e7-e5. (K) 2...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6
en: Philidor's defense. Black will have to contend with a cramped position.

line: d4 d5 c4 e5
en: The present game seems to have been the earliest occasion on which this opening appeared in master play.

line: e4 e5 f4 d5
en: Falkbeer's Countergambit, the most vigorous reply to King's Gambit.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6
en: This move is more popular than avoiding the pin by ...Nf6-e4.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2
en: In game one Kasparov played 3. b3.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4
en: This variation is called the Bishop's Gambit. White should not play 3. d4 because then 3... Qh4+ is good for Black since White would have to play 4. Ke2. A common move for White is 3. Nf3.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3
en: White plans to position his bishops on b2 and d3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4
en: White now has an advantage in the center.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3
en: A natural move. White develops a knight and gains time attacking the queen.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 g3
en: Since Pd5 will oppose White's Bf1 White will probably try c2-c4, but Black could still support Pd5 with ...c7-c6 (and Anand has played the Semi-Slav Defense) .

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5
en: The Nimzowitsch variation, wherein White drives a wedge into the opponent's position. 3...

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4
en: The obvious way to exploit the pin on Nf6, though other development moves should also be fine.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+
en: This looks threatening but actually is not the best move. Better are 3... d5 giving back the pawn and 3... Nf6.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6
en: To develop the bishop and castle.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6
en: Black plans to develop the bishop on g7.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4
en: Before this tournament I'd have said this was a pretty good way to aim for a draw. But, the Adams-Anand game showed a new plan which should be studied closely.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5
en: The proper response, an attack on the center.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6
en: (Page 54 Winning with the Modern, Norwood. So now its time to learn about the Pirc/Modern.).

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4
en: IMO this agressive continuation is best for a chess program.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1
en: The king is more securely placed here than it appears, and White can gain an important tempo by attacking the Black queen with Nf3.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5
en: The exchange variation. White's goal is now to move up his two queenside pawns and exchange them leaving Black with a weak pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3
en: This solid variation was a favorite of Steinitz.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5
en: Black does not want to give up the center to White.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5
en: This variation is called the Semi-Tarrasch Defense.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5
en: Black refuses to allow White to control d5, holding back Black's pieces in the center.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5
en: This opening (Fianchetto Variation of the Gruenfeld Defense) has been successful for Black over the years, despite the fact that Bg2 isn't terribly blocked by a strong Black pawn center (such as Pe6, Pd5, Pc6) .

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5
en: Having faced accusations of playing too many Kasparov openings, Deep Fritz adopts a Karpov favourite today.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5
en: Pinning the knight and therefore threatening the pawn on d5. The usual move for Black here is 5... Be7 breaking the pin.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5
en: Pinning the knight and threatening 6. Bxf6 and Black would have to recapture with the pawn because 6... Qxf6 loses to 7. Nxd5.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3
en: It is unusual to block the d pawn. The move works out well in this position, however.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3
en: White plans to play 6. d4 with a strong center.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3
en: A natural developing move.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3
en: Developing and protecting the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3
en: Guards his d4 against a knight invasion prepares for d4 if convenient and secures a retreat for the king bishop at c2 so that Black can not exchange it for his queen knight or queen bishop.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3
en: This has recently been a Shirov specialty.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5
en: Makes easier the defense for Black. Better was 5.Nf3.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4
en: This is the very aggressive attempt to refute the early ...Bc8-f5. It's played before Black can use ...h7-h5 to secure the light squares even further.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5
en: If black play s the immediate 5... Nxd5?, then white can crush black's position with 6. Nxf7! Typical play might look like this: 6... Kxf7 7. Qf3+ Ke6 8. Nc3 Ncb4 9. Qe4 c6 10. a3 Na6 11. f4! Nac7 12. fxe5 Ke7 13. d4 Ke8 14. O-O.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2
en: This line is known as Kramer's Variation though the Hungarian GM Szabo did work this line.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5
en: Not having faced this opening for about 15 years I show my ignorance. Better is Nf3, Be2 and 0-0 which gives White a clear edge.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6
en: This very principled (but highly dubious) move is the novelty compared to the 2nd game.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7
en: It is important not to block the c pawn by 5... Nc6.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6
en: Black would probably have been better off castling followed by ... c5 and ... Nc6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6
en: The fianchetto of the king bishop is a sound procedure. Also good was 5...a6 (to be able to drive the bishop away with b5 when desirable.) 6. Ba4 Be7 followed by 0-0.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7
en: Developing the bishop and preparing to castle. 5.. Nxe5 would lead to a disadvantage after 6. Re1, d5 7. Nxd4.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 e3 Nc6 d4 d5
en: The Tarrasch (or Semi-Tarrasch, which Bobby Fischer occasionally played) isn't considered to be fully equalizing, but it's not as bad against e2-e3 as against g2-g3.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6
en: This move is a prelude to the developement of the Bishop in b7 or a6 and a plan for a contrast at the center with d7-d5 or a besiege to the c4 pawn using the maneuver Nb8-c6-a5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6
en: Black offers this pawn to open the queen-side further, expecting his improved piece activity to compensate for the pawn.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 a6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Qc7
en: Black can choose this variation without fear White could set up a Maroczy Bind (c2-c4 & e2-e4 together) because of 3. Nc3. It gives Black the flexibility to develop his other pieces after seeing where White's are.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Bg5 dxc4
en: (This is without doubt the sharpest responce.).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6
en: Black intends Be7, Nh7 and Bg5 eliminating his bad Bishop.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5
en: Kasparov closes the position immediately and emphasises the weakness of b6 and the dark squares on the queenside.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3
en: A normal developing move.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4
en: Attacking the pawn again.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3
en: But, Anand varies; not repeating 6. c4 from the earlier game. White threatens Nc3-d5, Nb5-c7+.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3
en: White, instead, is preparing a better control of the center with his pawns.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5
en: Here it is! With this move White begins to maintain a stronghold on d4. Nowadays we prefer to refrain from the immediate exchange on c5, starting with.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5
en: Trying to put pressure on White's center which is, however, pretty solidly defended.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5
en: Now the d pawn is backwards: it will have trouble advancing to d5.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6
en: The bishop will be developed on b7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7
en: Developing and preparing to castle.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6
en: Guarding his f7 and developing his knight. Later 6...Nc6 was shown to refute the Salvio. A long analysis begins with 7. Nxf7 Bc5 8. Qe1 g3 9. Nxh8 Bf2.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4
en: There is no other square on the which this knight could find security. At e5, it can be protected by d4, and if White takes it e.p. d6, the knight can recapture.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7
en: Karpov would rather prepare O-O than try to develop Bc8 and Nb8. His Be7 isn't very good, but once developed his two bishops should blossom.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 e3 Nc6 d4 d5 cxd5 exd5
en: This standard Tarrasch should favor the younger and presumably more nimble player, though Karpov shouldn't be counted out too quickly.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6
en: Shirov has been playing this move (Panno) against the Saemisch Variation too (with mixed results) .

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7
en: See the Kasparov-Vallejo Pons game for notes to the opening.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3 O-O Be3 Nbd7
en: Not the standard move here. Most common is 6... e5 fighting for the center. Black could also play 6... c5. The move played allows white to develop his g1 Knight safely to f2 via h3.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2 O-O Ng3 c5
en: I had lost a previous game to John where I had played the Averbakh variation (5.Be2, 6.Bg5). This move was expected.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 e4 Nc6 Nf3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3 dxc3 d6
en: Maybe Black could have safely taken the pawn on e4 though this would cost him two tempi in retreating the piece hence my reason for playing d6.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3
en: White's pieces are actively placed.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1
en: Now if 7... 0-0 then 8. Bxc6 Bxc6 9. dxe5 dxe5 10. Qxd8+ Raxd8 11. Nxe5 Bxe4 12. Nxe4 Nxe4 13. Nd3 (If 13. Rxe4 then 13... Rd8+ and mate next move) 13... f5 14. f3 and White wins a piece.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4
en: Taking possession of d4 protecting his knight thus making it more secure and opening the line of his queen bishop.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4
en: It's odd to develop the bishop to this square, where it has no immediate prospects. White is aiming to O-O-O.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3
en: I'm not sure why he'd give up on O-O-O so quickly. What's Black's threat? Yes, Pd4 needs defense, but even after Bf1-d3 it's fine.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5
en: There's a pleasing symmetry to the struggles over e4. Black, on move 3, asserted control by pinning White's Knight. Now White returns the compliment on the other side of the board.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6 Be3 Be7 f3
en: To obtain any advantage it is important to avoid the Bishop exchange. My plan is to meet a Bg5 with Bf2 and h4.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5
en: A strategical mistake. May be even the losing move in a higher sense as the position is now closed and Fritz does not understand it at all.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5
en: Modern theory prefers 7...Nxe4 with a sound game for Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O
en: Continuing his developement. 7..Nxe5?? would lose a piece after 8. Re1, f5 9. f3.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5
en: As in a Sveshnikov Black threatens ...b5-b4 and uses Pb5 to prevent Na3-c4-e3.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6
en: The general idea appears to be to expand on the queen-side to pressure the weak Pc4, though at this early point Black might even have in mind ...e5 and ...Nd4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5
en: It took over 100 years to prove that after Ueber hundert Jahre hat es gedauert, bis bewiesen wurde, dass Schwarznach.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6
en: This was unnecessary. I would consider.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 b5
en: This early ...b7-b5 is a trademark of the Polgar family. They've played it a long time. Judit has played it infrequently in recent years, having switched to the Najdorf-like move-order which Kasparov uses.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6 Be3 Be7 f3 O-O
en: Now I want to castle queenside and use a pawn storm against the Black King. Unfortunately I can't play Qd2 because after Black plays Bg5 I could no longer play the necessary Bf2.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5
en: Black's pawn a5 is now very weak.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3
en: This is White's active bishop. The other bishop is blocked by its own pawns.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5
en: To exchange this knight for Black's king bishop, which would give White the two bishops and leave Black slightly vulnerable on the dark squares.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5
en: After this White might intend Bc1-e3-b6 followed by Nd5-c7+. But, Black won't leave Nd5 unchallenged.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3
en: White realizes Black might play ...g7-g5-g4, so he begins his own threat of b2-b4-b5 to counter it. They're fighting over control of e5 and d4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Nb3
en: The cautious approach. This just leads to a sort of main line Najdorf.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 b5 Nxc6
en: White trades knights before ...Bc8-b7 to prevent Black her ideal coordination.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 a3 Be7 e4 O-O Nf3
en: Korchnoi's patent - this way he played with Akesson in Antwerpen 1995.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5
en: This developing move protects his knight on e5, and opens the diagonal of his queen bishop, which now threatens White's knight.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7
en: What is White's plan? Often it's to play a "normal" way and to let Pc4 participate incidentally. The costs of having Pc4 is that it's impossible to pressure Pa6 with the Bd3 and Qd1-e2 and Bd3 is undefended.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3 O-O
en: White's quick queen-side threat (b2-b4-b5) prevented Black from getting to play his own ...g7-g5-g4, so Black simply castles and continues normally.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5
en: Although such a reply was generally thought as the best one, Lasker thought more than half an hour before playing it. Half an hour to evaluate the other two possibilities: 8... Bxd5 and 8...Nxd5.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4
en: Given an exclamation point by Gligoric and Wade in their book "The World Chess Championship" (1972). This move was apparently not in X3D Fritz's opening book so it was now on its own.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2
en: Better than 9. Nf3 that allows the annoying pin 9... Bg4.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2
en: Repositioning the knight and unleashing the bishop on b2.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5
en: This move would not have been possible with the Knight in d7.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4
en: A Pawn sacrifice already done by Alekhine against Eliskases, which, very wisely, declined it (as did Capablanca in this game).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6 d5 Ne7 b4
en: This is the first time I have had the white side of this position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O O-O d5 Ne5 c6 cxd5
en: Much more vigorous is 9.e4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6
en: After 9...Nxc3 10.bxc3 Bxc3 11.Qb3 Bxa1 12.Bxf7+, White's attack is irresistible, while after 9...Bxc3 10.bxc3 Nxc3 11.Qe1+, Black loses a piece.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6
en: Black plans to move the bishop to a6 and trade it for White's powerful bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3
en: Already there is no way back. Einen Weg zurueck gibt es schon nicht mehr.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Qe2 Nb4
en: This move defines Black's plan a bit prematurely. 9...b5 was more appropriate.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Be7 O-O Nc6 Re1 Bg4 c3 f5
en: Trying to put a pin in the enemy's territory.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4
en: This does not really win a pawn: the idea is to simplify rather than to grab material.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Bg5 dxc4 e4 b5 e5 h6 Bh4 g5 Nxg5 hxg5
en: (The alternative for Black is Nd5 inviting White to play Nf7 with fantastic complications.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Bd7
en: Everyone wants to play like a champion! Only one year has passed since the London-2000 battle between Kasparov and Kramnik, but the Berlin wall has acquired many admirers.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Bg5
en: This move is preliminary to a series of exchanges. Favorable to whom? 10...

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nc3 O-O Be2 d6 O-O Bd7 Nc2
en: Short prefers to avoid a knight trade (based on his earlier experience in this tournament) and to gradually build up pressure on Black's slightly cramped position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6 Be3 Be7 f3 O-O Bd3 Nc5 Bc2 c6 Nge2
en: I was tempted by b4 but was unsure what to do with my King after it.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Bd7 b3
en: White has tried a lot of ways here:.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4 Qc7 Ba3 e4
en: Fritz closes the centre. Not a good idea for a computer.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7
en: Planning 12... c4 chasing the bishop from its powerful position.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7
en: White could now play 11. Nxa8 exf2+ 12. Kxf2 Qh4+ 13. g3 Qxe4 14. Bg2 with an advantage in material.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Be7 O-O Nc6 Re1 Bg4 c3 f5 Qb3 O-O
en: "So what? I give you a Pawn, and you, in exchange, how many developing tempi do you give to me?" Indeed the attacks looks premature, and the american ignores it.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Be2 Be7 a4 Nc6 O-O O-O f4 Qc7
en: Black prepares ...Nxd4 and ...e6-e5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Be3 Qd7
en: The main line is 0-0, also playable is 10.. .Nc5 (Khalifman - Korchnoi, Ubeda1997), but Korchnoi, as an expert of open variation, minds something new.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 e4 Nc6 Nf3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3 dxc3 d6 Bg5 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 h3 Be6 Qd3 O-O-O
en: Risky but worthwhile as Black has a lead in development.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+
en: Instead White prefers a line with incredible complications. Morphy loved to take risks, and was leading in the match 5.5 to 1.5 (draws count .5).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O d3 Qb3 Qf6 e5 Qg6 Re1 Nge7 Ba3
en: The developement achieved largely compensates for the two pawns. The queenside, with the Bishop in c8 still blind, is the main drawback of Black's position.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bd3
en: White can defend Pe4, but he would be better off to capture Pf5 and not have a Bd3 which might soon be chased away by ...e5-e4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nc3 O-O Be2 d6 O-O Bd7 Nc2 a6 f3
en: Securing Pe4 allows Nc3-d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3
en: 11.exf5 first is also possible, but this move sets a trap. Already I had played the white side of this position three times, and no-one had taken on e4. My opponent was thinking. Dared I hope he might not know the trap?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Be2 h5 Bxg4
en: Instead of trying to detonate the position, white has found an efficient way to deploy his pieces based on challenging the a1-h8 diagonal with a gain of time.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+
en: This check gets back the pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2 O-O Ng3 c5 d5 e6 Be2 exd5 exd5 Re8 O-O Nbd7 Bf4
en: The major alternative is f4 which can allow Black to sacrifice a pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O d3 Qb3 Qf6 e5 Qg6 Re1 Nge7 Ba3 b5
en: A pawn sacrifice in order to give some fresh air. Un pedone sacrificato per poter "arieggiare" l'ambiente.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Na5 Bc2 c5 d4 Nd7
en: Keres made this move popular. Black prepares an opening of the Closed Ruy Lopez.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Be3 Qd7 Nbd2 Nxd2
en: Not so good 11. ... Bg4 12.Ne4 de 13.Qd5 Qd5 14.Bd5 O-O 15.Bc6 fe 16.gf Lautier-Korchnoi Ubeda 1997, but deserves attention 11. ...Rd8!? as Victor Lvovich played twice with Timman in 1987 and with B.Anand in Monte-Carlo 1993 blindfold.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6 O-O Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Bb2
en: The bishop has little mobility.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4
en: Threatening 13. Nxf6 checking with the bishop. Black appears to have no defense.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5 Bxc6 bxc6 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Re1 Qh4 Be3
en: Guarding his threatened f2. If 12. f3 at once was probably also good.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3 Bg7 Bd3
en: Now that Black has blocked the g-file Anand doesn't fear ...f5-f4 (generally cramping White's king-side) .

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Qe2 Nb4 Bd2 b5 Nd1 Nxd3+ cxd3
en: It's always strange for me to give an exclamation mark to a move that any professional player today would make automatically. But in 1885 it wasn't that easy to foresee all the consequences of this decision.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O O-O d5 Ne5 c6 cxd5 cxd5 Bf4 a6 Rc1 b5 Qb3
en: This is an odd and ineffective placement of the Queen. It bites on steel and blocks the progress of Queenside development.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6 O-O Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Bb2 Qd7
en: Black plans ... Qa4 if White moves his queen away.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6
en: Indirectly threatening the square g2 and once again threatening c4.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4
en: A clever resource, attacking the queen and the pawn on c2.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6 O-O Nf6 Be3 Bb4 Na4 Be7 Nxc6 bxc6 Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Qxc8
en: With this short flurry White has the two bishops and a simpler pawn formation. It's the next phase of the game which will resolve whether those two bishops are powerful.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Qe2 Nb4 Bd2 b5 Nd1 Nxd3+ cxd3 Qb6
en: 12...b4! was a must in this position, stopping White's plan, conquering space on the queenside and preparing a proper development of the light-squared bishop after a6-a5 and Ba6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O Nc3 Bf5 a3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nc6
en: This is the best retreat White could force. Pd4 opposes Nc6, restraining it.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+ Qd7 Qxc4 Qc6
en: Here is Black's idea. White has a large center, but provided Black can maintain control over key breakthrough points, the center will not be too important -- the more so because Black has managed to exchange off half of the minor pieces.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2 O-O Ng3 c5 d5 e6 Be2 exd5 exd5 Re8 O-O Nbd7 Bf4 Ne5 Qd2 Bd7
en: Now I'm out of the theory available to me.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6 Be3 Be7 f3 O-O Bd3 Nc5 Bc2 c6 Nge2 cxd5 cxd5 Qb6 Qd2 Nh5
en: This wastes two tempi. Better is Bd7.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4 Qc7 Ba3 e4 Nd2 Be7 b6 Qd8 h3
en: A dream position! Completely closed and a safe prey on a5.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6 Qe2
en: Preventing 13... c4. If 13... Rac8 then 14. Bb5 trapping the queen.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+
en: If now 13... Ke7 14. Nfd5+ Kd7 15. Qf7+ and 16. Nxa8 wins easily.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5 Bxc6 bxc6 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Re1 Qh4 Be3 f6 f3
en: To drive the knight away from the attack.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+ Qd7 Qxc4 Qc6 Qd3
en: Of course Lilienthal declines the Queen exchange and prefers to use his Queen to help pushing the central pawns.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O O-O d5 Ne5 c6 cxd5 cxd5 Bf4 a6 Rc1 b5 Qb3 Nc6 Nxc6
en: If 13. Rfd1, then comes...Na5 -...Nc4 with a good game.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Bg5 Be7 Bxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Bxe7 Nxe7
en: Now it is sufficient for Black to remove his king to safety, and he will have the better endgame because of the isolated White d-pawn, but he does not succeed in implementing this important objective.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5 Bxc6 bxc6 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Re1 Qh4 Be3 f6 f3 fxe5
en: An elegant and most surprising sacrifice.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5
en: It is unlikely that Anderssen has calculated all variations after Es ist unwahrscheinlich, dass Anderssen saemtliche Variantennach.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nf3 Bb7 Nc3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6 Qe2 a6
en: # After very passive Black play in the opening White's army is ready for action, and Lasker begins the final storm.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Qe2 Nb4 Bd2 b5 Nd1 Nxd3+ cxd3 Qb6 b4 Be7
en: If 13. ... Bd4, 14. Rb1 Qa7 (To provide a flight-square for the Bishop.) 15. Nxd4 Qxd4 16. Be3 and black loses his Queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Be3 Qd7 Nbd2 Nxd2 Qxd2 Na5 Bg5 Nc4
en: Before this game black played 13. ...c5 with a terrible statistics.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2 O-O Ng3 c5 d5 e6 Be2 exd5 exd5 Re8 O-O Nbd7 Bf4 Ne5 Qd2 Bd7 Bg5 Qb6
en: This move for Black is wrong as I felt that the Queen is better placed on a5 and on b6 it hampers any Queenside counterplay with b5.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6 Qe2 a6 Nh5
en: Threatening 15. Nxf6+ Bxf6 16. Bxf6 gxf6 17. Bxh7+ Kxh7 18. Qh5+ Kg7 19. Qg4+ Kh2 20. Rf3 and 21. Rh3 Mate cannot be prevented.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5 Bxd5+
en: Here Black should play 14... Ke7 leading to an extremely complicated position after either 15. Ng8+ or 15. Qh5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 h3 Nf6 Qe2 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 dxe5 Bxe5
en: White is in good control of the diagonal, but can't O-O-O. Black has plenty of open lines for development.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O Nc3 Bf5 a3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nc6 cxd5 Qxd5 Re1
en: I don't see that this move makes much sense until he's prepared another place for Be2. As things stand Be2 can hardly move, so Re1 is pretty well blocked.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Bg5 Be7 Bxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Bxe7 Nxe7 Re1
en: Can you see that Black would have had better castle at 9th move? Now Fonbarda must waste few tempi to castle "artificially". White also threatens 15.Re5. How to solve the problem? 14...

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+ Qd7 Qxc4 Qc6 Qd3 Nbd7 Ne2
en: Lilienthal continues his development behind the powerful center, not rushing to attack until he is sure that his pieces will coordinate well.

line: Nf3 Nf6 g3 d5 Bg2 c6 O-O Bg4 d3 Nbd7 Bf4 Nh5 Bc1 Nhf6 h3 Bh5 Bf4 e6 c4 Be7 cxd5 cxd5 Nc3 O-O g4 Bg6 Nh4
en: A horrible mistake, but Korchnoi was not the only one.(!).

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4 Qc7 Ba3 e4 Nd2 Be7 b6 Qd8 h3 O-O Nb3 Bd6
en: A little trick - the bishop can't be taken. But the trap is much too obvious for Kasparov and only valueable time is lost.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6 O-O Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Bb2 Qd7 a4 Rfe8 Qd3 c4
en: This move takes the pressure off the center, which is usually bad. Here, Black calculates that he will have a strong queenside attack after moving his knight to b3 via b8, c6, and a5.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6 Qe2 a6 Nh5 Nxh5
en: Black undoubtedly expected 15. Qxh5 f5 where White has a powerful attack, but the game still has a lot of play in it.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5 Bxd5+ Kg6
en: # Now the previou s line doesn't work: Moeglicherweise war Anderssen hier der Meinung, sein junger Gegner haette in diesem taktischen Variantendschungel die Orientierung verloren. Doch Morphy behaelt wie gewohnt die Uebersicht.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5 Bxc6 bxc6 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Re1 Qh4 Be3 f6 f3 fxe5 fxe4 d4
en: I wonder whether Lasker calculated all the lines, but his intuition hasn't betrayed him. Black was not in danger of losing. Ich frage mich, ob Lasker alle Varianten berechnet hat, aber seine Intuition hat ihn nicht im Stich gelassen.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Nf3 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Qe2 Nb4 Bd2 b5 Nd1 Nxd3+ cxd3 Qb6 b4 Be7 a3 f5
en: The decisive mistake - Black himself kills any potential of counterplay with this move. Worthy of attention was.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4 Qc7 Ba3 e4 Nd2 Be7 b6 Qd8 h3 O-O Nb3 Bd6 Rb1
en: Kasparov ignores X3D Fritz's provocative play and continues to develop his pieces. Black isn't threatening anything.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6 O-O Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Bb2 Qd7 a4 Rfe8 Qd3 c4 Qc2
en: White's next several moves are in preparation for e4.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3 Nbd7 O-O O-O Ne2 c5 Ng3 Qc7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Qc6 Qe2 a6 Nh5 Nxh5 Bxh7+
en: The first of two bishop sacrifices.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3 Re4
en: Rather than develop pieces White immediately threatens Re4-h4 to eject Qh3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 O-O Be7 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 O-O Nf5 d5 Bxc6 bxc6 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Re1 Qh4 Be3 f6 f3 fxe5 fxe4 d4 g3
en: A bishop retreat loses instantly.

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nc6 Bb5 Bg4 d3 Ne7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 O-O f5 Nd4 Qg3 Nxb5 Nxb5 f6 Be3 Bxe3 Qxe3 d5 O-O c6 Na3
en: This is a very ugly knight. Besides that, the crux of black's advantage is that he has the lever to open the d-file WHEN HE IS READY TO DO SO, by way of which he takes over the game.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nge2 O-O Ng3 c5 d5 e6 Be2 exd5 exd5 Re8 O-O Nbd7 Bf4 Ne5 Qd2 Bd7 Bg5 Qb6 f4 Neg4 f5
en: Necessary to try and deny the e3 square for Black.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 e5 d5 h6 Be3 Be7 f3 O-O Bd3 Nc5 Bc2 c6 Nge2 cxd5 cxd5 Qb6 Qd2 Nh5 O-O-O Nf6 g4 Bd7 Ng3
en: I was tempted to play the immediate h4 but became confused by Black's h5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 dxc4 e4 Bb4 Bg5 c5 Bxc4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bxc3+ bxc3 Qa5 Bb5+ Nbd7 Bxf6 Qxc3+ Kf1 gxf6 h4 a6 Rh3 Qa5 Be2
en: After my 15th move the position was the same as the previous game.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 O-O Ne2 b6 O-O Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Bb2 Qd7 a4 Rfe8 Qd3 c4 Qc2 Nb8
en: The idea is Na6-b8-c6-a5-b3.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5 Bxd5+ Kg6 Qh5+ Kxf6
en: White cannot play 16. Ne8+ because of 16... Qxe8 17. Qxe8 Bb4+ 18. c3 Rxe8. After the obvious attacking move 16. Qf7+ Black plays 16... Kg5 and it is not easy to get at the Black king.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3 Re4 g5
en: Because of this Black's king shouldn't be quite as safe and that gives White some counter-attacking possibilities.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+ Qd7 Qxc4 Qc6 Qd3 Nbd7 Ne2 Rd8 O-O a5
en: This prevents the a-pawn from being a target on a7, where it might be vulnerable to a later Qa6, for example. Yet the move loses time: Capablanca may have underestimated the force of Lilienthal's coming central play.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Bg5 Be7 Bxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Bxe7 Nxe7 Re1 f6 Qe2 Qd7 Rac1
en: At the present time 16.d5! is considered to be the strongest method, for example: 16...Kf7 17.Rad1 Nxd5 18.Ng5+! fxg5 19.Qf3+ Kg8 20.Rxd5, and White should be winning.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5 Bxd5+ Kg6 Qh5+ Kxf6 fxe3
en: Now Anderssen's illusions are over - the open f file ends the life of the black king not only in the King's Gambit. Nun zerplatzten saemtliche Illusionen bei Anderssen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3 Re4 g5 Qe2
en: This indicates an intention to give back some material (as Re4 is pretty well stuck in the middle of the board) and not to spend time chasing Qh3 back. He's only committed to this after Black weakened his king's position with 15...g5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 f3 d5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Ba6 e4 Bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Qa4+ Qd7 Qxc4 Qc6 Qd3 Nbd7 Ne2 Rd8 O-O a5 Qc2
en: Lilienthal patiently removes his Queen from the d-file, pre-empting any tricky ideas involving ...Nc5 or ...Ne5.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 a6 c5 Nbd7 b4 a5 b5 e5 Qa4 Qc7 Ba3 e4 Nd2 Be7 b6 Qd8 h3 O-O Nb3 Bd6 Rb1 Be7 Nxa5 Nb8
en: Probably to protect c6 and to blockade on a6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Bg5 Be7 Bxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Bxe7 Nxe7 Re1 f6 Qe2 Qd7 Rac1 c6
en: By evacuating his king from the e-file, and then playing 17...Nd5, Black could have successfully defended his position and assumed the initiative, although a knight check, 17.Ne5+ or 17.Ng5+, would have led to complications.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O a3 Nc6 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 Bf5 Re1 Rfe8 Bf4 Rac8 c4 Qe4
en: The queen seems very strong, but is in fact quite exposed so all of White's smaller forces.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 Nb5 d6 Bf4 e5 Be3 f5 N1c3 f4 Nd5 fxe3 Nbc7+ Kf7 Qf3+ Nf6 Bc4 Nd4 Nxf6+ d5 Bxd5+ Kg6 Qh5+ Kxf6 fxe3 Nxc2+
en: Loses instantly, but Verliert sofort, aber auch.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O d3 Qb3 Qf6 e5 Qg6 Re1 Nge7 Ba3 b5 Qxb5 Rb8 Qa4 Bb6 Nbd2 Bb7 Ne4 Qf5 Bxd3 Qh5
en: White has a huge advantage and it is time for desicive action. In accordance with his own romantic style and public demand Anderssen played.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O O-O d5 Ne5 c6 cxd5 cxd5 Bf4 a6 Rc1 b5 Qb3 Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 h3 Qd7 Kh2 Nh5 Bd2 f5
en: Operating on both the wings.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Ndb5 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ Nxc3 d5 Bd3 d4 Ne2 e5 O-O O-O h3 Re8 Ng3 Nd7 f4 exf4 Bxf4 Nde5 Qh5 f6
en: Third time with black pieces Korchnoi played f7-f6, but now this move is absolutely correct.

line: f4 e6
en: Opeining lines for the bishop and controlling d5.

line: e4 c5 d4
en: Morphy preferred this move order to 2. Nf3 and 3. d4.

line: Nf3 c5 g3
en: With Pc5 White won't get d2-d4 without having to consider ...cxd4. But, it could become an English Opening with c2-c4 or a King's Indian Attack with d2-d3 and e2-e4.

line: e4 c5 Ne2
en: An unusual Sicilian. 2...

line: d4 g6 g3
en: This is usually followed by c2-c4 to make a King's Indian Defense, Fianchetto Variation or, after ...d7-d5, a Gruenfeld Defense.

line: Nc3 d5 e4
en: I realized the problem, but the only other move is 2. d4 which I didn't like either...

line: e4 e6 b3
en: [This move is much better than its reputation, for the reasons I have already given above.].

line: e4 c6 d4 d6
en: This was the idea. Instead of a Caro proper, Kasparov is continuing his anti-computer strategy, attempting to take it out of its opening database. With this rare move, he might have succeeded.

line: d4 Nf6 Nd2 e5
en: This frees Black's game.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4
en: Otherwise White has control of the center.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6
en: Preparing to play 3... d5. Also playable is 2... e5.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6
en: If 3. Nc3 then 3... Nxe4 4. Nxe4 d5 and Black has an equal game or better.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6
en: Though a popular set-up (nowadays) I usually avoid developing a piece where it will be blocked (as Bg7 is blocked by Pe5) .

line: Nf3 Nc6 d4 d5
en: Janowsky would not have disliked (in case of 3.c4) the Chigorin Defense even if such a defense was already at that time partially condemned by the theory.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5
en: Well my opponent might be playing a Caro-Kann, but I have news for him...B.D.G.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 b3
en: One of the most memorable games in Kasparov's career was the last game of his 1987 world championship match against Anatoly Karpov. Despite the fact the he needed a win to preserve his title, he chose the rather passive double fianchetto.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3
en: Rather passive and probably chosen to get Rebel out of its book as quickly as possible.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3
en: A small success: Anand avoids the main theoretical lines, starting with 3 cxd5, 3 Nc3 or 3 Nf3.

line: d4 d6 Nf3 Bg4 e4
en: While there is an opportunity, it is meaningful to grasp the centre by the pawn. Alternative The continuation 3. c4 Nd7 etc. repeatedly met in practice of the contender.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4
en: The opening is now a Queen's Gambit Declined by transposition of moves. This position could have arisen from 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3
en: More usual is 3. d4. White's move leads to a closed game called the King's Indian Reversed.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 Nf3
en: Black can protect the pawn with 3... e5 since 4. Nxe5 would lose the knight to 4... Qa5+. However, White gets definite compensation after 4. c3 dxc3 5. Nxc3. Morphy's opponents rarely cared to risk this line.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3
en: The bishop is going to move to g2.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Nc3
en: Black isn't threatening ...e5 to block the center and 3...d7-d5 4. exd5 exd5 5. d4 favors White because Pd5 is already targeted by Nc3.

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4
en: If black declines the pawn offer, we get into French lines i.e.3...e6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 c4
en: Trying to set up a Marcozy Bind.

line: c4 e5 g3 c6 d4
en: Now we have a reversed Sicilian 2.c3 where White has the extra move 2.g3 I've long held the view that 2...Nf6 is Black's best against 2.c3 so maybe I should have played 3.Nf3here.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Bd3
en: Kopec variation which i am not familiar with.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c5
en: Dr. Siegbert Tarrasch's answer to the Queen's Gambit. Once again today, Fritz chooses an opening line which allows for piece activity.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7
en: Not 3... Nc6 blocking the c pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 Nd2 e5 dxe5 Ng4
en: If 4. Ngf3 then 4... Nc6 will win back the pawn. Not 4. f4 Ne3 trapping the queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4
en: White's pawn on e4 controls more space than Black's pawn on d6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4
en: Indirectly protecting the pawn. However, Black will be forced to trade this powerful bishop for the knight and give White a lead in development.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6
en: A logical developing move.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6
en: Also good is 3... c6 preparing for ... d5.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8
en: 3... Qa5 is considered somewhat better.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6
en: Shirov must suspect Adams has some improvement over the Kasparov-Shirov game or else he just wants to test Adams a bit by forcing him to find his own way.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5
en: This forces the game off into another direction. It's thematic for Black to fight on the dark squares, but White's setup is a little unusual. If White plays d4-d5 Black might play ...b7-b5; something he wouldn't ordinarily be able to do.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6
en: This is unusual, but not necessarily bad. If White captures Nc6 Black can recapture ...b7xc6 and have better central control. Perhaps Polgar is trying to take Kasparov out of familiar territory.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 c5 d5 b5
en: Bravo! This is the "I'm not going to let you get back into a normal opening" move.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 c5
en: This move-order is used almost exclusively today to avoid the variations with f2-f4. In Portisch's case it would have been a stylistic preference, but one which demonstrated admirable prescience.

line: e4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Nf6
en: This is what I wanted, and now I can go back into d4 lines.

line: Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 c6
en: He makes no attempt to punish me and so we have a Caro after all.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4
en: The main line of the Portuguese Variation of the Scandinavian or Center Counter Opening.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5
en: Marshall plays a weak move that will ultimately allow white to shred black's center. Perhaps black was hoping for tactical chances in the resulting complex position.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7
en: George and I have played many times. He usually plays a Colle or Torre System of some kind so I play a line that has brought me success against him in the past.

line: e4 e6 d3 d5 Nd2 e5
en: A move designed to take advantage of White's passive opening.

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4
en: [Black is better to take the pawn because 3. ...Nf6 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+!? Be6 6. Nf3 Be7 7.Ng5 is promising for White.].

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 c4 h6
en: I've never sen this move so early. Is it the latest theory?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 g3 b6
en: Played in the "spirit of the hedgehog" according to my book "Sizilianisch im Geiste des Igels". played in the "spirit of the hedgehog" according to my book.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4
en: As opening theory (even in the commonly played Open Games) was not well developed in the late nineteenth century, a critical analysis of the opening phase is redundant.

line: d4 d6 Nf3 Bg4 e4 Nf6 h3
en: It is useful to find out intentions of the black bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3
en: To place the bishop on g2 where it will reinforce the pawn on e4 and put pressure on d5.

line: d4 Nf6 Nd2 e5 dxe5 Ng4 h3
en: An innocent looking move. White expects 4... Nxe5 5. Ngf3.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3
en: The main idea of the gambit: If 4... exf3 5. Nxf3 White has strong pressure on the center and a lead in development while Black has weaknesses due to the missing f pawn. Nonetheless, it is sound to accept the gambit.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4
en: The queen is well-placed here. White has two pieces developed to Black's none.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5
en: If 4... dxe5 then 5. Qxd8+ Kxd8 6. Nxe5 wins a pawn.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3
en: Developing and keeping open the option of 5. f4 which would be impossible after 4. Nf3.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4
en: Taking possession of the central square d4 and opening lines for the bishop on c1.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4
en: This certainly weakens the c5-f2 diagonal and makes it less possible to utilize Bf1 offensively, unless he can also achieve d2-d4 without his position falling apart.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Qc2
en: This is a poor place for the queen. It weakens Pd4 and could easily become aligned with a ...Bc8-f5.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3
en: After this it's quite possible Black will aim for ...Bh3 to trade-off Bg2, thereby weakening all the light squares on the king-side. Opening the center with ...d7-d5 would be unwise because it opens the diagonal for Bg2, making it stronger.

line: Nf3 c5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O
en: White waits to see how Black is organized before committing any pawns. But, does that gives Black time to make any White pawn move a bad one? With ...Nb8-c6 he makes d2-d4 impossible and c2-c4 weakens d4.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+
en: Ivanchuk avoids complications stemming from 4. Nc3 a6 and just regains the pawn. He's also left Nb1, so as to not get in the way of his queen. If there's a Nc3 and Qc4 (after regaining the pawn) it can be awkward.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nbd2
en: Such a move, which rarely appears in grandmasters games, was played by Opocensky against Steiner in Brno, 1928.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3
en: At that time 4.Qd3 was thought to be some sort of confutation for this kind of opening. Nowadays it is rarely played in tournament practice because the theory has shown that Black can come out with a good position with no difficulty.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e5 dxe5 Ng4 Nf3
en: Capablanca goes his own way, avoiding book lines in so far as they existed. 4...

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3
en: White chooses to support his central pawn and to block Bg7, but at the cost of not having c3 available for a knight. Incidentally, Pc5 is now threatened.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2
en: Milos avoid s the usual 4. O-O to avoid whatever opening preparations Kasparov has made. Was this a prepared idea or a "spur of the moment" choice? Qe2 aligns with Ke8 and defends Pe4, so it should be alright.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3
en: As an interesting aside, White often reaches this position via the Bishop's Opening without giving Black the opportunity to take on e4, thus: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nf6 3.d3 Nc6 4.Nc3, etc.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4 Nf3
en: Other alternatives are 4. Be2 and 4. f3. For example 4. f3 Bf5 5. Bb5+ Nbd7 6. c4 e6 7. dxe6 Bxe6 8. c5! c6 9. Bd3 b6 10. cxb6 Qxb6 11. Ne2 c5 12. O-O! and white stands slightly better.

line: Nf3 d6 d4 Nf6 c4 Bf5 Nc3
en: (The traditional plan is 4...Nbd7 and 5.. .e5. The critical test of the move played is probably 5.Bg5 Be7 6.Qb3).

line: e4 e6 d3 d5 Nd2 e5 exd5
en: After this exchange it is difficult for White to "harass" the Queen on d5.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5
en: According to the December 1999 edition of the British Chess Magazine, this variation is known as the 'Frankenstein-Dracula' variation. This gamecertainly finished in a gruesome fashion!

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3
en: This is called the Modern Variation.

line: e4 c6 d4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Bg4
en: Now we have returned to something 'known', though rather unusual, the Prybl opening.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6
en: Out of book Rebel produces this slightly inferior move. The knight shouldn't block the c-pawn.

line: d4 d6 Nf3 Bg4 e4 Nf6 h3 Bh5
en: Obviously, that the exchange in f3 gave for White small, but proof advantage.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6
en: More usual and better is 4... g5 or 4...d5 5. bxd5 bd6.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6
en: The Queen's Indian Defense. Black moves the bishop to b7 to put pressure on the center.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5
en: A counter sacrifice to gain time and development. This move is not looked upon favorably nowadays.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6
en: Defending the pawn on d5.

line: d4 Nf6 Nd2 e5 dxe5 Ng4 h3 Ne3
en: White resigns. If 5. fxe3 then 5. ...Qh4+ 6. g3 Qxg3#.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5
en: Attacking the base of the pawn chain. A side pawn is usually less important than a center pawn.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6
en: Black prefers to give back the pawn to playing a defensive game.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6
en: Developing a piece and attacking White's queen.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6
en: By unprotecting the pawn on b7, this move makes it easier for White to play b4. First, however, White must guard his c pawn.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6
en: This may be a little too aggressive. 4... Be7 is better.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6
en: Developing and attacking the knight on e4.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5
en: A good developing move. Also playable was 4... Bb4.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6
en: It is very passive to shut in the bishop this way. It would have been better to play 4... Bf5 or wait until White played Nf3 and play ... Bg4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6
en: With this move, Black is able to keep the position closed.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4
en: There's no pin on Nc3, but he might remove it to prevent White from keeping control of d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7
en: I like this move because it makes Bb5 less effective. It can't force doubled pawns by capturing Nc6.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 e6
en: Shirov aims to blunt the bishop and prepares ...d6-d5. He might also use ...a7-a6 and ...b7-b5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8
en: Protects the Bishop in b7 and prepares the possible push c7-c5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 Bc5
en: Accepting the Gambit 4... dxc3, after 5. Bc4 Nf6 6. Nxc3 Bb4 7. O-O O-O Black keeps his extra pawn in a comfortable position.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7
en: Today playing 4.Bc1 before Ng1-f3 is considered an inaccuracy, because of 4... c5!

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5 Bd3 Nc6
en: Just to let White understand that he can suddenly lose the first move advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 f4 d5 d3 Bb4
en: This rarely adopted variation transfers to the second player the attack, which is, however, a short-lived one if properly defended.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 Nf3 Nf6
en: Safe enough. If White now takes the e-pawn, the game might go on thus: 5.fxe5 dxe5 6.Nxe5 Qd4 7.Nd3 Bb6, etc.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5
en: Black thre atens ...cxd4 to remove the central pawn. For White to simply defend it with Ng1-f3 is possible, but ...cxd4 cannot be replied to with c3xd4 (it's pinned) , so the central pawn is removed.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6
en: I was unfamiliar with this move, so from here on I was on my own.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5
en: This completes the Stonewall pawn formation.

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3
en: (Early departure from the usual. what's he up to.).

line: e4 Nc6 d4 d5 Nc3 e5 exd5 Nxd4
en: No pawn centres in this game. Who heens them?

line: d3 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5
en: [A Slav Exchange variation with colours reversed. According to BCO2, this takes the fun out of playing the Slav. Does it....?!].

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 c3 f5
en: A rare continuation. The usual moves order here is:.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3
en: Anand doesn't try to take advantage of Black's last move. 5 d4 was possible, after which the knight on c6 looks a bit silly.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3
en: Rebel had 5 Qb3 and 5 dxe5 in its book. Now it had to think for the first time.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 Nf6 b3
en: Bareev wants to play a closed position against the computer.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c5 cxd5 exd5 g3
en: The legendary Akiba Rubinstein found this most effective move against the Tarrasch Defence in the early 20th century. The fianchettoed bishop is to exploit the potentially-isolated d5-pawn.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4
en: If only because the game becomes so sharp.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4
en: Never before seen in such a high-level event.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3
en: The usual counter to the bishop on b7.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3
en: If now 5... fxe4? then 6. Qh5+ and after either 6... g6 or 6... Ke7 White plays Qxe5+ with a winning position.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4
en: White is controlling the center. Black must find a way to contest it.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5
en: Developing a piece and pinning the knight to the king.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4
en: Better is Qxd4 and the queen would dominate the center. If Black then tries 5... c5, he would have a hole on d5 and a backwards d pawn.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5
en: If 5... exd5 then Black will end up with an isolated queen pawn.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3
en: Both sides now develop their pieces and castle.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4
en: Occupying the center. Black should not now play 5... d6 because after 6. dxe5 Nxe5 7. Nxe5 dxe5 8. Bxf7+ Black cannot play Kxf7 because of Qxd8. If 6... dxe5 then 7. Qxd8+ Kxd8 8. Bxf7.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e3 e5 Bxc4 exd4 exd4
en: White has an isolated queen pawn but dynamic attacking possibilities as compensation. The position is equal.
