line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4
en: It's interesting that this position for White can just as easily be played against a Tarrasch Defense or a Queen's Indian Defense or a Benko Gambit.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5
en: White would rather trade for Nf6 and leave Bb4 to look for something to do.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3
en: This move co ntraddicts the strategical principles indicated by the theory. Since Turn knew that Mikenas had a deep theoretical preparation, he decided this line of play in order to surprise the opponent.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5
en: The best. The developement 5.Nf3 is less promising.

line: Nf3 Nc6 d4 d5 e3 Bg4 Be2 e6 c3
en: A bit too shy. Wasn't it better to castle and then attack the center with c2-c4?

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 exd5 exd5 Nf3
en: This form of the exchange variation is now considered harmless.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4
en: Logical play, for oly in the end-game can White turn his extra pawn on the King side to account.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3
en: A teporary loan of a pawn in the spirit of the gambit. 5...

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 a3
en: Not bad, but White could play Nc1-d2 at once, followed by the fianchetto of the KB with a definitely superior game. 5...

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2
en: White uses a small tactic to get rid of Qa5, so Pc3 can truly support Pd4.

line: Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 c6 d4 Nd7 Bc4
en: I was still trying to diverge from some earlier games with 5. Ng5, in which I got nothing from the opening. However the problem is that I hardly knew anything about this move.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3
en: Charousek offers Black one more chance to take a pawn, any pawn!

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5
en: Mieses, not to be outdone, counters by reducing Black's own control over d5.

line: b3 g6 Bb2 Nf6 e4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3
en: (Tactics already, keep your eyes open at all times!).

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 e3 Nbd7 f3
en: (This was a surprise to me as I had only started playing the Semi-Slav.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 d5
en: At this point I got the idea referred to in my introductory remarks that my opponent was going to play a cautious and defensive game. This made me feel pretty good, as I said.

line: d3 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e4
en: [Thanks to Black having played Nc6 before Nf6, it is possible to play this gambit].

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 Ne5
en: I had played this before in OTB games, but this was my first CC opportunity.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4
en: [The Hamppe-Allgaier Gambit.].

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 Nbd2
en: #Normal here is 5 g3,but the game soon transposes.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3 e5
en: Now we have a kind of Pirc-Ufimzev, with reversed colours.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 c6 Bg5 Be7
en: Black avoids the nebulous strategic realms of the Slav, in which Kramnik happens to be a leading expert. Instead the Fritzer transposes back into the Queen's Gambit Declined.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4
en: This method of seeking early exchanges is distinctly dubious.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4
en: 5...exd4?! 6.Nxd5 Nc6 7.Bb5 Bc5 8.Nf3 and White has an edge.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7
en: I think, this is a more flexible continuation compared to the classical 5...Qb6, for Black keeps a possibility to develop his queen on the square c7, intending to play against the pawn e5 by f7-f6.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6
en: Developing and attacking the pawn on e4.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4
en: This is an aggressive way to protect the pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7
en: Now Black threatens to take the queen.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5
en: To prevent 6. d4 5... d6 would have been better.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6
en: In positions with the d pawns advanced, the Black c pawn should be used to counterattack in the center. This move blocks the c pawn.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5
en: The usual next move for White when this game was played was 6. e3.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6
en: Opening lines for the bishop on f8. 5... h5 may have been better.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7
en: This would be a poor move in an open postion; here it is effective.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6
en: Developing and attacking White's center.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6
en: This is a typical, and necessary, response to White's effort to get the central pawn duo (Pe4 & Pd4) . Black continues developing, castles and hits Pe4 to force a resolution of the central pawns.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 Nc3 Nd5
en: This is sort of nifty. He's trying to get rid of a pair of minor pieces before White can utilize his extra central pawn to cramp him.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 c4 O-O
en: After this Black is conceivably threatening to take Pc4 and hold onto it.

line: c4 c5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nc7
en: The exchange in c3 and then g7-g6 was preferable.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7
en: Steinitz, always faithful to his favoured defense, this time has improved it with the move a7-a6.

line: c4 e6 e3 Nf6 Nf3 b6 Be2 Bb7 O-O d5
en: With 5...c5 followed by 6... Nc6 Black could have kept the center under control without compromise himself. (Tartakower).

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 d4 Qh4+ Ke2 d6
en: Some players tried the sharper 5...d5 against Steinitz, but without success. In the final game of his match against Zukertort he celebrated a victory and the attainment of the first official title of World Champion against this variation!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4 exd4
en: Accepting the challenge of "having it out in the centre".

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 f4 d5 d3 Bb4 fxe5 Nxe4
en: This sacrifice of the knight is a novel introduction. 5...d4 is generally preferred at this point, and is usually continued thus: 5...d4 6.exf6 dxc3 7.b3 Qxf6 8.Nf3 Bg4 9.Be2 Nc6 etc., and most practitioners pronounce the game even.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O
en: After this White would be wise to not capture Pe5 because ...Rf8-e8 would give Black's pieces open lines and targets.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O e5
en: This makes Bf8 bad and doesn't prevent White from playing c2-c3, d2-d4 to open the center.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 e5 h6 Bc1 Nd5
en: The pin is broken, but White's pawns remain. Can Black play around them or force them to be exchanged off?

line: d4 e6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 Nf6 f3 d5 a3 Be7
en: Very ambitious. On the one hand 5.a3 is a free move for white, but black is going to sack a pawn and try to demonstrate that 4.f3 weakened white's king.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6
en: This is the Modern Benoni Defence. Here Black develops his Bishop on g7 by playing... g6 and the move... c5 gives Black control of the dark squares in the centre.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5
en: Wollner is admirably "modern" in his lack of greed, and insists on completing his development.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 Nc3 Nf6 Nd5 Nxe4
en: (The only analysis of this line was by I Glaskov in the 1970s in the Soviet weekly "64". his analysis showed that the alternative) (The text move, however gets black into terrible trouble.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nd4
en: Way back in 1983 the moves 5...Nd4 and 5...b5 looked worthwhile. I wonder what current theory says.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 d4 g3 c5 b4 cxb4 a3 e6
en: [A reversed Benko. Personally I wouldn't dream of letting my opponent play such a critical variation with an extra tempo, but Bernard's play is nothing if not optimistic!].

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4
en: [If 5. ... Be7 6.Nxe4 Nxe4 7.Qxe4 Bf6 8.d4 Qd5 9.Qe3 0-0 10.0-0-0 Nc6 11.Nf3 is good for White. Totsky-Rapport, Minsk, 1996, saw White winning in 16 moves!].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6
en: The Euwe Defence, here white can play the line 6.Bg5 Be7 7. Bd3 Nbd7, but I like 6.Bc4 with idea's on e6, & f7.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5
en: This seemed a good idea at the time, aiming to immobolise White's pawn centre. White's alternative of 6.exd6 en passaunt has the same effect.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Bc2 d5
en: ...Ng4 not good because of doubled h pawns after Qd4 & ...f6 dubious, allowing scope for WBs.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 d5 Qb6 Nc3 Qxb2
en: The Trompovsky "Poisoned Pawn" ?!

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 Bf5 f3 Nd6
en: A rare continuation, which was played in the 1986 Soviet Union Ch. between Efimov - Kuzmin. White continued with 6.g4 Bg6 7.Nc3 e6 8.Qd2 h5 9.g5 Nd7 10. 0-0-0 and had the edge.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7
en: Larsen chose 5...e6 for the sixth match game because after the fourth, he was of the opinion that Black should not allow White the following sacrifice. Another common option is 5... g6.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3
en: End of Rebel's book, that expected 6 Be2.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+
en: 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ is duck soup for Tal.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O
en: 6. Qxf3, as also played by McDonnell, would lead to more independent positions. Note it is as if White played a Muzio and followed it up with Nc3 instead of the usual Qxf3.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3
en: The knight is not particularly effective here, but it will move to e2, g3 and eventually h5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6
en: So that the queen can remain in a dominating position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4
en: Threatening 7. Qxf7#. Black's best here is 6... Qe7 although since Qe7 blocks the bishop on f8, White would have a huge positional advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3
en: After 6...dxc3 7. Nxc3 White has a lead in development as compensation for his pawn.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4
en: White's queenside attack is off to a fast start. The threat is b5 winnng the pawn on b7. After 6... Nxb4 7. Qb3 Black is in trouble.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4
en: The pawn sacrifice is justified on the basis of White's lead in development and Black's weaknesses on the dark squares.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5
en: A nicely posted piece. Black cannot play 6... Nxe5 because 7. dxe5 would fork the Black bishop and knight. If 7... Bb4+ then 8. c3 and Black still loses a piece.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4
en: Spassky will demonstrate the strength of the pawn center.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3
en: A natural developing move.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+
en: Better to exchange than retreat.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O
en: White does not worry about 6... exd4 7. cxd4 Qxe4 because of 8. Re1 pinning and winning the queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O
en: Moving the king to safety and bringing the rook into the game.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3
en: By defending Pe4 White is now free to play Nc3-a4xc5. This would get rid of the bishop, but at the cost of opening the d-file for Black. Still it might be good.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4
en: Pc4 and Pe4 seem perfect for securing d5 and keeping Pd6 backward, but those pawns also get in the way of Be2 and Qd1, so it's not an advantage without a downside.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4
en: Refusing to capture Nc6 leaves Ne7 awkwardly placed.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3
en: A bit inaccurate. The following continuation would have lead to interesting complications: 6. Bd2 Bb7 7. Qg3 O-O 8. d5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5 Nc6 Nf3
en: Less convi ncing are the alternatives 6. Bd2 6... Bxc5 7. e3 O-O 8. Nf3 d5 and 6.Bg5 Bxc5 7. Nf3 Be7 8. e3 O-O 9. Rd1 Qa5 10. Be2 d5 and Black's play is acceptable.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 h4
en: The Chatard-Alekhine attack: a sharp weapon against the French Defense.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3
en: An interesting Bishop move.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7 e3 O-O c5
en: Even the great Lasker underestimated the danger of White's clamp on the queenside. Only 90 years later Black found the right way to create counterchances, in the game Lerner-Geller: 6...b6 7.b4...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5
en: Better than 6.Bc4 as played by Lasker in the first match with Steinitz. 6...

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Qe2
en: Threatening 7.fe de 8.Bxf7 Kxf7 9.Qc4+. 6...

line: c4 e5 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 g6 a3 a5 Nf3
en: The knight intends Ng1-f3-d2-f1-e3-d5.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2 cxd4 Nb3
en: Black's queen is chased off the a5-e1 diagonal!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6 b6
en: White refuses to cooperate and leaves Pa6 to block Bc8. Of course, he doesn't win a pawn this way either.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O e5 c3
en: Already Black faces a crisis since White is better developed and Ke8 might soon be exposed.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 a6 Be2
en: White simply ignores the possibility of ...Bf8-b4xc3, knowing Black's dark squares would be weakened significantly while White could then play c3-c4 to control both b5 & d5. This gives White the better coordination.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4
en: Whichever way White chases Nd5 it will retreat to expose Pd4 to an attack. Black also hopes/plans to utilize queen-side light squares which Bg2 can't contest.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3
en: Charousek follows suit, and the next few moves for each side are rather natural.

line: d4 h6 e4 d6 Nc3 a6 f4 b5 Nf3 Bb7 Bd3
en: (Mabe 6.a3 is more circumspect.).

line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3
en: [6.d5 is an alternative.].

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4
en: So much for theory, as far as my limited resources go. Though our wise database checkers may be able to point out precedents..

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3
en: After this move Black can opt to play the Bishop back, instead he decides to swop off the pieces.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7 Nxf7
en: Many American GM's, including Joel Benjamin and Patrick Wolff, have examined this line in quite some detail.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7
en: More usual is 6 ... Qb6.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7
en: 6...Nd7? 7.dxe5 is better for White as as e5-e6 is in the air and Black's e-pawn is weak.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7
en: Nevertheless, this is quite a "modern "idea as Black refrains from blocking the field of action from his Bg7, with for example 6...d6, followed by 7...Nf6.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6
en: The queen would have been better placed on h5, but Black plans to move his knight to h5.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7
en: It is important not to play ... Nc6 blocking the c pawn.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5
en: The bishop is more aggressively placed here than on d6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6
en: This looks like a logical move; however, it quickly leads to a losing position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7
en: Black should either take the pawn or develop his knight.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7
en: Now the c pawn is unblocked, but the knight is in the way of Black's queen and bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6
en: It would have been better to castle first.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5
en: Planning to exchange White's remainnig center pawn. Perhaps it would have been more prudent to make a developing move.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4
en: Black prepares his counterattack which consists of ...c6, ...b5, and ... a5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6
en: Black intends to maintain his pawn on e5. If Black were to play 6... exd4 then after 6. cxd4 White's center would be overwhelming.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6
en: Ivanchuk clearly wants to keep Bc5 to keep control of d4 and perhaps to have a piece which reaches all the way to f2 (or g1) to threaten White's king. This extra pawn move seems justified.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 Nc3 Nd5 Qxc4 Nb6
en: I don't understand. How could the knight be better on b6 than f6? Why not trade at c3?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 Bb7
en: Taking aim at Pe4 isn't going to succeed the way it would in many other variations. Here White has taken extra precaution to keep Pe4 safe and left Nd4 a little weaker. Black should adjust his play in recognition of this.

line: e4 e6 d4 g6 Bd3 Bg7 Be3 c5 c3 cxd4 cxd4 Qb6
en: (?!) Winning a pawn, but loosing time.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7
en: A developing move but...not very aggressive.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7 e3 O-O c5 Ne4
en: Of course Lasker doesn't wait for the realisation of White's plan. But his attempt to organize counterplay in the centre plays directly into Steinitz' hand.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6
en: Unclear. The Bishop had to be developed first in e7. Now White has the possibility to take the advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 Be7
en: Against Anderssen's form of attack in this debut it is more usual to open an outlet for the bishop by 6...g6. Black prefers to get his king into safety as soon as possible, and therefore at once makes room to enable him to castle.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 a6
en: This move was played by Anderssen against Blackburne in the Vienna tourney, whereupon the latter also replied 7.a3.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 O-O gxf3 Qxf3 Qf6
en: Believed to be the best reply.

line: e4 e5 f4 d5 exd5 e4 Nc3 Nf6 d3 Bb4 Bd2 e3
en: An ingenious and daring developing sacrifice, killing two birds with one stone: White's development is hindered, and the K-file is opened for direct attack on the White King.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7
en: Allowing Black to oppose both Ne4 and Bg5 seems to assure he will be able to trade several minor pieces to achieve the simplification he desires.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6
en: Black has little to worry about. He's going to have a convenient way to develop all his pieces and without having created any major weakness (es) .

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 Bb7 Bg2 Bb4+
en: Black has forced a slight weakening of White's queen-side and now he tries to discoordinate White's pieces.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 e5 h6 Bc1 Nd5 c4 Nb4
en: Black threatens ...c5xd4 when the "natural" response Qd1xd4 fails to Nb4-c2+.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5
en: Bengston mentioned after the game that this line is out of fashion, but it was the only one I (sort of) knew.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7
en: Shapiro decides to defer the exchanges and concentrate on getting his Queenside untangled. To that end, he fianchettoes the B/c8.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Qc7
en: This move is designed to discourage 7. Qg4 when black would play 7... f5. However, a more modern idea is simply 6... Ne7. Then if 7. Qg4, then 7... cxd4 is complicated, but OK for black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4
en: A new move ! The book line is 6... Qxd5 Nc3 7. Qd6 (7. Qc5?! leaves the Queen too exposed). Black can also play 6... h6 which drops a pawn for active play. 6... h6 7. Nxf7 Kxf7 8. dxc6 Bc5 (Kirilov - Shebenyuk, coor. 1985.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 Nc3 Nf6 Nd5 Nxe4 Qe2 Bxf2+
en: (The alternatives at move 6 are no better.).

line: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 c4 Bc2 b5
en: This is quite common in the Stonewall Attack. White castles short and Black Long and once the centre battle has been resolved a pawn race follows.

line: d3 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e4 dxe4 d5 Ne5
en: [Although at the time of the game I thought 6... Qa5+ would lose to 7.b4! I am not so sure now, and think this may win for Black].

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3
en: [Here 6. ... Qe7 is playable but 7.Nxe4 or 7.Kb1 both give White excellent chances.].

line: c4 e5 g3 c6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 d5 cxd5 cxd5 Bg2 Be6
en: Kosten gives only 6.... Nf6.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ng5 d6
en: [6...h6 or 6...f6 are more usual.].

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5
en: The sharpest continuation.

line: d3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c4 Nf6 a3 d6 Nc3 Be7 g3 O-O Bg2
en: Activating the bishop on the long diagonal, and building a solid home for White's king.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3 e5 h3 Be6 a3
en: White prefers a kind of Modern Defence setup, by means of a3 and b4.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5
en: As played with success against Kasparov.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2
en: From a strategical standpoint, this move refutes Black's opening. Now Black can retreat with 7...Bb7 but after 8.e4, White has a distinct positional advantage.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5
en: Another sharp alternative is 7.Qb3!? for example: 7...exd4 8.Bc4!? dxc3 9.Bxf7+ Ke7 10.Bxg8.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4
en: More aggressive is 7.Qd2 0-0 8.0-0-0. The text has the idea of hindering d7-d5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 O-O d4 Bb6 Qd3
en: At first a strange looking move but as the game goes, White has easier development, the option to play Qd3-g3, and in some lines f2 is covered.

line: d4 d5 c4 c5 cxd5 Nf6 Nf3 cxd4 Qxd4 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 b4
en: Suddenly it turns out that black queen feels itself uncomfortably. Here my partner spent much time again and took an unhappy decision.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3
en: Guarding the pawn and opening lines for the bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2
en: This is better than Nc3 which would prevent White from moving a pawn to c3.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3
en: White is continuing normal development.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3
en: Developing the knight and threatening the e pawn.

line: f4 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 e6 Bb2 Be7 Bd3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 Nf3
en: Attacking the key square e5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7 O-O
en: If Black plays 7... Qxe4 then 8. Re1 pins and wins the queen.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5
en: If now 7... exd5 then 8. Bb5 Bb7 9. Ne5 (Threatening 10. Bxf6 Bxf6 11. Bxd7+) 0-0 10. Bc6 Bxc6 11.Nxc6 and White has a strong postion.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3
en: The best place for the bishop. 7. Be2 would be passive and 7. Bb5+ 7... Bd7 would lead to nothing. If Black tries 7... cxd4 8. Nxd4 Qxd4 then 9. Bb5+ wins the queen.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5
en: Pinning the knight and threatening to break up Black's kingside pawn formation with 8. Nd5 and 9. Nxf6+.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4
en: The bishop is placed in an aggressive position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3
en: To prevent Bg5 putting indirect pressure on d4.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4
en: Now it's just transposed to a King's Indian Defense, Fianchetto Variation which is still considered good for White, though the players involved make the difference. In this case Shirov as Black should be up to the task.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5
en: This is a little different. More common is Bf1-e2. After the game move Nd4 remains weak for a move or two longer.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3
en: White clearly has an idea of how to coordinate his king-side, to avoid damage. But, such a passive position might still allow Black chances.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Bxc4 Nb6 Bd3 Nc6 Be3
en: White's early pawn advances and Bishop developments creates a curious appearance and flaunts the classical rule of developing knights before bishops.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4
en: A mistake. Even losing a tempo by retreating the Bishop in e3 was more convenient. (Chigorin).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3 Na5 d4
en: What is that? Some strange impulse or a new idea? Janowsky seems ready to give his lightsquare Bishop for the sake of attack. Is that too much? Pillsbury, categorically, commented: "Such a move should cost the game to White.".

line: d4 d5 Nf3 c5 e3 Nc6 b3 e6 Bb2 Nf6 Nbd2 cxd4 exd4
en: From "My Chess Career", I report Capablanca's comment: << ... I remember I played 1.d4 because that way Corzo could not take too much advantage from my weakness in the opening.>>.

line: e4 c5 Ne2 Nf6 Nbc3 Nc6 g3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nxc3 bxc3
en: Opening the "b" column, where a Rook, helping the action of the Bishop in g2 on the big diagonal, can increase the pressure on the opponent's field. 7...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Bd6 Nf3 Nge7 Qc2
en: According to Tartakower this move is a waste of time. Indeed, he says, the loss of the game is because of such a waste of time. Difficult to believe? Here one could play:.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4
en: Possibility not exploited!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5 dxe5 Bg5
en: An excellent move which completely refutes Black's opening strategy; either he remains with a weak, doubled and isolated "c" pawn or else he must weaken his King side with 7...f6. 7...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 Be7 h3
en: Not so much for defensive purposes as with the view of subsequently fortifying an attack by pawn to g4 against the opponent's kingside, after the latter has castled.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 a6 f5
en: Stronger than 7.a3, and it seems, from the progress of the present game, that the array of White's pawns on the kingside cannot be broken through.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e5 Nfd7 f4 e6 Nf3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2
en: L'ala del Re del Nero sembra essere immobilizzata, ma in compenso il suo centro e piu mobile. (Nimzowitsch) 7...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3
en: This seems slow, for gambit play. White should develop (and over-protect) by 7.Bf4. 7...

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 O-O gxf3 Qxf3 Qf6 e5
en: Typical pawn sacrifice, aiming to open the "e"-file.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2 cxd4 Nb3 Qb6 cxd4
en: O.K. White has the central pawn, but Nb3 isn't terribly well placed. Black could go after it with ...a7-a5-a4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6 Rd1
en: I don't see Rd1 being very useful since Black hasn't played one of the variations with Be7 and his Qd8 isn't quite so cramped. It can easily sidestep the alignment with Rd1.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O e5 c3 g5 d4
en: Opening the center is more important than the pawn he appears to be gambitting.

line: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 d5 exd6
en: Well, that changes it back to an open (or semi-open) center, where the better piece activity will generally be of primary importance. Just straight-forward counting of development moves would seem to indicate Black is o.k.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 d5 Bg2 Bb4+ Nfd2
en: (7. Bd2 Be7!(A common idea in such positions. The Bishop on d2 is misplaced.. 8. Nc3 O-O 9. cxd5 exd5 10. Ne5 Bb7 =.).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2
en: Not the best square for the Bishop. Better would have been 7. Nf3, 8.h3 and then placing the Bishop to d3 as per the latest theory.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4 Nf3 Qxd5 Be2 Nc6 c4 Qh5 d5
en: Not a good move, because of dark squares and pressure of white's kingside, better would be something like 7. O-O O-O-O 8. Be3 and so on.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nf6 Be2 O-O O-O c6 Re1
en: (I didn't really know how to deal with this at first so I did what I thought was in keeping with hypermodern chess and played.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 d4 exd4 cxd4
en: 7.0-0 was the main line, but the text immediately creates a strong pawn centre and steers the game away from better known lines.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 c4 h6 Nc3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nxc6
en: I prefer to exchange on c6 rather than go to b3.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O
en: This position can be reached from many move orders, including 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c6 4.g3 f5 5.Bg2 Nf6 6. 0-0 Bd6 7.Nbd2.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3
en: I was in no mood for quiet play with 7.d3.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Bxf3 c6 d3 e6 e4 Ne5
en: Gaining the bishop pair counts in Kasparov's favor, but in doing so he has lost time.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6
en: The fatal error....he should have played 7...Bd6, which leads to standard and frequently played positions.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nxc6 Qf6 Qd2 dxc6 Nc3 Ne7
en: Oddly enough, Kramnik has adopted Short's favoured reply to the Scotch, according to Mig Greengard.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nc3 Ne4
en: Common theme in the Nimzo/Queen's Indian complex; Black aims to give White doubled pawns on the c-file.

line: e4 c6 c4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 cxd5 cxd5 Nxd5 d4 Nc6 Nf3 Bg4
en: By transposition we have arrived at one of the best-known positions of the Panov Attack. The traditional move order is 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 7.cxd5 Nxd5.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 Kf8
en: This alternative to 7...g6 seems to be more reliable for Black, despite the unavailability of castling.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6
en: Black can try and make use of the omission of h2-h3 by White and play 7...Bg4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 Bg5 Be7 Qa4+ Bc6
en: This is a sharp method of fighting for the initiative for Black. Allowing the endgame after 7...Qd7 8.Qxd7+ Nbxd7 is also possible although Black will be on the defensive for quite a while.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5 a4 Rb8
en: Played without hesitation, as I and Nigel correctly guessed he wouldx his 7...Bb7 was not broken, but quite bent in the game vs Vishy, and also I probably don't give the impression of a man capable to prepare anything at all.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2
en: This is a questionable move since the bishop was more powerful than the knight. The key to White's attack in this game is the power of his dark-squared bishop.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5
en: Threatening 8... Ng3+ 9. hxg3 Qxh1+.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8
en: This allows the b pawn to move forward without fear that White's bishop on g2 will threaten the rook. Black is planning a queenside counterattack to White's coming kingside attack.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6
en: It is very unusual to block the d pawn in this way. However, it is the only active move in this position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6
en: This weakens Black's position. White will eventually post a knight at e6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7
en: White could win a rook for a knight with 8. Bxf7+ Qxf7 9. Qxb7. An immediate 8. Qxb7 does not win the rook because of 8... Qb4+ exchanging queens.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7 O-O Qe5
en: Black should pay more attention to development.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8
en: Guarding the pawn on b7.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6
en: Developing the knight and attacking the pawn on d4.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6
en: Preparing for the queenside attack and preventing 8. Nd5. Black threatens 8... b5 9. Bb3 a5 (Threatening 9... a4 trapping the biship) 10. a3 Nxb3 and White has a weakend pawn position and has exchanged his powerful bishop for a knight.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5
en: Developing the bishop before it is blocked by a pawn on e6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4
en: An alternative was 7... exd4 Black's move results in the exchange of pieces, which is good for the defending side. On the other hand, White ends up with a powerfully placed queen on d4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6
en: Developing with a tempo.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e3 e5 Bxc4 exd4 exd4 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 Nf3 O-O
en: Both sides have been developing.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 O-O
en: For a time this was considered bad, but has recently made a come-back. The king seems a little out of place (unlike after ...O-O-O) , but with ...f7-f5 he's been able to slow White's attacks.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4 Bb4 d3 d6 h3 O-O Be2 Ne7
en: He's apparently decided he can't play on the wing and must fight in the center with ...c7-c6, ...d6-d5, but to do that he has to reorganize a bit.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O
en: The king-side seems the natural place for active play (for both White or Black) , so removing the king to the queen-side, where it's adequately defended by Bc5 and Nc6, should be safer and enables freer offensive actions on the king-side.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 e5 Bc4 d6 d3 Be7 Nd2 Bg5 h4 Bxd2+
en: He is trading his "bad bishop" (the one which clashes with his central pawns) for a White knight which might maneuver Nd2-f1-e3-d5. Whether this is necessary isn't clear, but it is consistent positional play.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 Nc3 Nd5 Qxc4 Nb6 Qb3 e5
en: Black isn't going to delay the development of his pieces! This takes unreal confidence or large doses of courage.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4 b5 Bc2 Bb7
en: This approach leaves the question of how Black will play Pd7 for later, but it also leaves Pe4 in place and gives White time for d2-d4, if he should so choose.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1 Ne4
en: This is a nice response. Just get rid of the knight. White can't utilize the diagonal because ...Ne4xc3 hits White's queen. So, White would have to move Nc3 to avoid the trade and then try to exploit the exposed Ne4.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 Qb6 Nf3 e6 Be2 Ne7 O-O Bg4
en: More often seen is 7 ..Nd7, but there is no real difference here as the line tends to go 7 .. Nd7 8 b3 Bg4.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Qc2 c6
en: According to Flohr the following continuation is stronger: 7... c5 8. Rd1 Qa5 9. Bd3 h6 10. Bh4 cxd4 11.exd4dxc4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6
en: White hoped in the reply 7. .. 0-0 8.Ne2 with initiative on the kingside after 9.e4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5 Nc6 Nf3 Ne4 Bd2 Nxd2
en: Very good. It was tried 7... Nxc5 8. Qc2 f5 9. a3 Bxc3 10. Bxc3 O-O 11. b4 Ne4 12.Bb2 but such a variation hardly allows Black to keep equality.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8 Bg2 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6
en: Both the players keep a prudent attitude.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 exd5 exd5 Nf3 Bd6 Bd3 O-O O-O h6
en: 7...c6 would have been wiser. Black is overly concerned with the g5-square.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 d4 Qh4+ Ke2 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Bxf4 O-O-O
en: Here 7...f5! would underline the uncomfortable position of the White king.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Nf3 b6 Bg5 Bxc3+ bxc3 Bb7 e3 d6
en: With a right decision, Black withhold himself from castling too quickly, since this would favor the possibility of an attack for White, who has already his forces towards the kingside. (Tartakower).

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6
en: Black tries to keep control of e5 to prevent White from playing g2-g4 followed by Nf3-e5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6 Rd1 Re8
en: Black supports his central position and begins to aim for ...d5. He clearly doesn't fear White's approach.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 Bb7 Bg2 Bb4+ Bd2 c5
en: It seems a little unusual to allow Bxb4 cxb4 when Black gives up on some central control. What he gains is control of c3, so White can't play Nb1-c3 to control both e4 and d5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6 b6 d6 Nc3 Nbd7
en: Black might plan ...Nxb6 to pressure Pd5, perhaps with ...Bb7.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5
en: I think this is a little unusual, despite the move being common in most all other Gruenfeld Defense variations.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 e5 h6 Bc1 Nd5 c4 Nb4 d5 d6
en: Black meets White's pawns and forces exchanges before White can bring other pieces up to support them.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5
en: Though a typical move in the Sicilian Defense, it proves to be very premature at this stage. This is because Black is expanding on the Queenside at the cost of the development of his pieces.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 d5 Bg2 Bb4+ Nfd2 c5
en: Energetic play by Smyslov casts doubts on White's previous extravagant move. Otherwise White would have played a3 followed by e4.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6
en: What square does this move weaken? c6! Najdorf seizes the opportunity to take a peek at that square.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 N1e2 Nf6 Nf4 Nd5
en: The players leave the theory fast.

line: b3 g6 Bb2 Nf6 e4 Bg7 e5 Ne4 d3 Ng5 h4 Ne6 h5 d6
en: (A little prod at the centre.).

line: d4 d5 Nf3 f5 c4 Nf6 g3 e6 Bg2 Bb4+ Nc3 Nc6 O-O Bxc3
en: (Black will soon regret this as my Bishop on C! becomes all powerfull.).

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nf6 Be2 O-O O-O c6 Re1 d5
en: (David Norwood's book TEACHES!! White can either IGNORE/CAPTURE or ADVANCE, calculate each before moving.) I hoped he would advance. I had ideas on the f-file.).

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7 Nbd2 g6 Bd3 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 d6
en: It is a matter of "taste" whether Blacks pawn goes to d6 or d5. I prefer d6 when the centre can be contested with either e5 or c5.

line: Nf3 Nf6 g3 b5 Bg2 Bb7 O-O e6 b3 Bd6 d4 O-O Na3 a6
en: Prevents any ideas White may have about b5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+
en: 7...Bb6 was the alternative.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5 g6 Qf3 f5
en: In return for the exchange Black expands in the centre and White's position becomes cramped.

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O
en: Now that David has castled, white can concentrate on attacking the King-side position.

line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 d6 Qd3 c6
en: [The book line, but I prefer d5!?].

line: d4 b5 e4 Bb7 e5 e6 Nf3 a6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 bxc4 Bxc4 d6
en: Black wishes to test the soundness of my opening system.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6
en: I'm not sure whether this is the right time for Black to play this, limiting the c8 Bishop.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bd3 O-O
en: This move looks illogical. With hind sight why not leave the King behind a blocked pawn centre?

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 b3 Nf6 g3 Bf5 Bg2 Nbd7 cxd5 cxd5 Bb2 e6
en: Nh4 (move 11) can be played anytime now.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4
en: Black is now up by 2 pawns, can White recover, yes by developing and attacking at the same time.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7
en: Black usually plays ...Nbd7, to prevent White from occupying e5 with a knght.

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 c3 f5 fxe5 dxe5 d4 exd4 Bc4 fxe4
en: 7... Nc6 is the more usual continuation here but it does not equalize the black game at all as the following gem of a game demonstrates:.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ndf6 Bc4 e6 N1f3 h6
en: This move is a bit provocative. Black invites his opponent to sacrifice a piece.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6
en: Kasparov shook his head in disbelief. He had made a finger slip allowing a known sacrifice which, of course, was all in Deep Blue's database.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 Bb4+ Bd2 Be7 Bg2 c6 Bc3
en: Forget the whole 'don't move the same piece twice' advice here. The dance of bishops is considered theory.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3
en: Now that the Black bishop has departed from the h1-a8 diagonal, Kasparov takes it for himself.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O d5 c4
en: Fischer plays simply. Alternatively, after 8.Nd2 Nf6 9.Qe2, White plays for the attack, but Black has queenside and central chances.

line: e4 c6 c4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 cxd5 cxd5 Nxd5 d4 Nc6 Nf3 Bg4 Qb3
en: The ancient move 8.Bb5, which goes back to Nimzovich-Alekhine (Bled 1931), has a worthy defense, as shown by Nimzovich himself: 8...Rc8! 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 e6 11.0-0 Be7.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5
en: After some serious contemplation I noticed 8.Bf4 Nxe5? 9.Bxe5 Bxb5 10.Qxd8+ Rxd8 11.Nxb5 wins, but 8...Bb4 is OK for Black.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 g6 a3
en: An improvement over the classical line 8.Bd3 Nxc3 9.Bd2 (or 9.a3 Na2+ 10.Bd2 Bxd2+ 11.Kxd2 c5 12.Rxa2 Nc6 with advantage to Black) 9...Nxa2 10.c3 Nxc3 11.bxc3 Be7 and Black was better in Yanovsky-Marshall, Ostende 1907.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4
en: Mednis is more a of positional player than a tactical player, so it is not so surprising that he should choose this continuation over the more aggressive 8.g4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5
en: Itâs quite worth another pawn to open the position further.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2
en: With Black's dark-squared bishop gone, White plans to place a bishop on b2 exerting strong pressure along the diagonal.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4
en: Stopping the threat and preparing to put the knight on f5 where it will be powerfully placed.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1
en: Placing the rook in the center and leaving f1 available for the knight which often, from there, goes to e3 or even to g4 via h2.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5
en: This is eventually shown to be a mistake, but it is not a blunder; it is a deliberate pawn sacrifice.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5
en: Pinning the knight and planning Nd5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3
en: White decides that simple development is even stronger than 8. Bxf7+. White's superior development combined with Black's awkwardly placed pieces gives White an overwhelming positional advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7 O-O Qe5 f4
en: White is giving up his rook for an attack.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3
en: White is planning a queenside attack.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5
en: If 8... Bxg5 then 9. Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Nxg5 and White is a pawn ahead.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 cxd4 cxd4
en: White now occupies the center. The question is whether he will be able to use it to advantage or spend all his energy protecting it.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5
en: Notice that the placement of White's bishop prevents a queen exchange.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3
en: Developing his last minor piece.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2
en: White plans to castle queenside in the near future.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6
en: Black has no reason to fear the opening of the king file for after 8...Qxd6 he will be as well developed as White. It is when you are behind in developement that you must be wary of the game becoming more open.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 Bg7 Nc2
en: So, Polgar immediately removes it from the weak square (much as one might with the Black pieces in an English Opening Reversed, Maroczy Bind for Black) .

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nxc6 dxc6 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Bf4
en: This prevents Black from developing ...Bf8-d6 where it would threaten Ph2 and prevent e4-e5. It also prevents ...Kd8-c7, which would help Black to connect his rooks on the back rank.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 e6 Nf3 d5 cxd5 exd5 d4 Bg4 Ne5
en: White doesn't add to his development lead with this.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Be3
en: This is a very unusual square for the bishop; it's vulnerable to ...Nf6-d5 or ...Nf6-g4. But, moving Nf6 makes the a4-e8 diagonal even weaker.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6 Re1 O-O d4 cxd4 cxd4
en: White threatens d4-d5 when Nc6 is awkward.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3
en: White takes away d4 and will also probably play a2-a3, b2-b4 to chase Bc5 and Nc6. The cost is that it blocks in Bc1 for a time. It also prepares to meet ...Nf6xd5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4 b5 Bc2 Bb7 Qe2
en: Clearly one of White's aims is to keep his pawns supported, so he can get in d2-d4 without a major disruption. How does Black prevent this "obvious" plan?

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1 Ne4 Nxe4
en: This continues the plan with no loss of time, but also without as much impact.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Ne5
en: The aim of this is to exploit the weak a4-e8 diagonal.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O h3
en: A Shirov, Anti-Marshall speciality.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6 f4
en: In fact, the capture 8. Qxg7 after 8... Rg8 9. Qh6 Rxg2 would have given a very promising position to Black.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8 Bg2 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6 O-O
en: Again too mach prudent. Better would have been 8. d5 and after 8... Ne7 9. e4 exd5 10. cxd5 d6 11. O-O Ng6 12. Re1 White would have had some advantage in space and developement.

line: c4 Nf6 g3 c5 Bg2 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 Nc6 O-O d6 h3 Bd7 e3
en: This looks like a mistake and Black will not miss the punishment.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 a6 f5 h6 h3
en: In order to fortify the attack immediately by pawn to g4, in case Black attempted to castle on the kingside, or to open the game by pawn to g6, as afterwards done.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2
en: This is routine play, whereas proper timing required 8.Bf4. If the 8...Ng6 in reply, the Bishop can settle down nively at g3. 8...

line: e4 e5 f4 d5 exd5 e4 Nc3 Nf6 d3 Bb4 Bd2 e3 Bxe3 O-O Bd2
en: Black has cleary obtained more than adequate compensation for the sacrificed central pawn: two tempos and an open file. 8...

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 d4 e6 g3 Ba6 Qb3 Nc6 Bd2 Bb7 Bc3 Ne4 a3
en: Prevents intrusion on b4.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5
en: Doing without h4-h5 has also been played quite a lot. Later on the Ph5 could be a weakness as it can quickly be threatened by ...Ng8-f6.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4
en: This allows White to maintain some tension, but would appear to commit the king to the queen-side. Black, on the other hand, is probably wondering if his king would truly be safe on the king-side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6 Rd1 Re8 d3
en: This move admits the failure of Qe2 and Rd1. If he can't achieve Pd4 then Rd1 is bad.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 a3 Bb7 O-O-O Nd7 f4
en: Very aggressive, but in retrospect probably not correct. F3 followed by g4 and h4 was more consistent.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Nf3 c5 Bb5+
en: This appears harmless, because it exchanges black's bad bishop. However, as we will see, white is trying to make use of the a4-e8 diagonal to inflict serious damage before black gets castled.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 c6 a3
en: The well-known "struggle for the tempo." After 8. Bd3 dc4, Black gains a tempo, and hence white delays the development of his Bishop on f1.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3
en: With the threat of e4-e5.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2
en: Glucksberg may have experienced one of Najdorf's attacks before and wanted to cover his Kingside. But this move, taking a tempo to reposition a piece that stood perfectly well, takes too much time.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 Ne7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 Qc7 Nf3 Nd7 O-O
en: Bronstein has been lured into a sharp opening.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4
en: (Designed to prevent the ...g5 break so common in the 08/g3 main lines, or so I read from my books!).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2
en: "This move is relatively unanalysed but has given good results so far," - Tim Harding.

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3 dxc3 Qe7 g4
en: [White has two bishops, an advantage in development, and a tactical initiative!].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe1
en: With this idea in mind I would like to play the bishop back to d3, and then play Qh4, h6 by black results in Bxh6 & after gxh6 Qxh6 black is struggling.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3 Qb6 Qd2
en: The pawn sacrifice offered by this move has rarely been tested in the tournament arena. I was quite surprised when Schwartzman accepted it.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O Nd5 a5 a3 Bc5 Ng5
en: This attempt to refute the black opening strategy at once does not look particularly convincing. Much better is further quiet development, e.g.:.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 g3 d5 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 dxc4 Nxc6 Qxd1+ Nxd1
en: Straight out of the opening the game is heading into an endgame. A fashionable variation of the four knights symmetrical english is been played.

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 c3 f5 fxe5 dxe5 d4 exd4 Bc4 fxe4 Ne5
en: The critical point of the game. White has two continuations here: 8.Ng5 or 8. Ne5. Ng5 looks stronger at first glance since in it the knight covers the important h4-d8 diagonal but black can get acceptable play in it, e.g.:.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Ke6 g3
en: ECO considers 8 c4 to be the stronger main line. I think they are mistaken and was hoping to get the opportunity to show why.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Qg6 Qf3 Ne5 Qe2
en: This seems to be a new move. It's interesting that this year Ivan Sokolov already suffered from a novelty involving Qe2 - in his game against Alexander Morozevich in Sarajevo, which went 1 e4 e5 2 f4 exf4 3 Nf3 Ne7 4 d4 d5 5 Qe2!.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ndf6 Bc4 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3
en: But White prefers more quiet play. Maybe the young Karjakin with his coach (unfortunately I don't know who his coach is ) prepared an improvment in the following extremely sharp line:.

line: d3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c4 Nf6 a3 d6 Nc3 Be7 g3 O-O Bg2 Be6 O-O Qd7
en: I think most humans would be worried about a knight arriving at g5 and would play 8...h6 first.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6 Qe7
en: If 8...fxe6 9 Bg6+, forcing 9...Ke7, would have been even worse.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4
en: Positionally speaking not a good move. Logical is 8 ... Bd6.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8
en: White has the two bishops and is probably better here, but I liked the course of the game sofar. It's no quiet position, in which the number 2 in the world can play positionally.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O g6 b3 Bg7 Bb2 O-O Nc3 d5
en: Black breaks the symmetry of moves and provokes the following flurry of exchanges. In my opinion this move is a little dubious and Black can instead equalize in the variation with 8...Na6!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6
en: It would seem more appropriate to play 8...c6 9.Bg2 d5, but after 10.0-0, White has the freer and easier game to play.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4
en: This treatment has become quite popular.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6
en: Intending Bc8-b7 to pressure White's e4-pawn.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6
en: The king is very secure here.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6
en: Black want to develop the knight on d7 rather than on c6 where it would block the bishop on b7 and the pawn on c7.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6
en: This is more passive than the more usual d5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6
en: Black will soon play ... dxc5 followed by ...b5 and ... c5 and eventually ...Bb7.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+
en: If 9. Kxf2 then 9... fxe4 10. Bxf6 (Not 10. Nxe4 Nxe4+) 10... Qc5+ 11. Ke1 exf3 12. Bb5+ c6 13. Qxf3 (Not 13. Bxg7 Qe3+) gxf6 wins back the piece with a good game for Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6
en: Not a good place for the knight but Ne7 blocks the bishop.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6
en: Protecting the pawn on b7 with the queen and guarding d5.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6
en: This move does nothing other than weaken the Black kingside.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+
en: The side with less space should strive to exchange pieces.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5
en: Recapturing and developing the bishop at the same time.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6
en: The placement of the bishop on b7 is not a good idea in this position because White's pieces are well placed to exploit the holes this pawn move creates at a6 and c6.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6
en: Blocking White's bishop and preparing to develop his own.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3
en: This pawn was doubly threatened.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e3 e5 Bxc4 exd4 exd4 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Be3 c6
en: Taking possession of the central square d5 and planning to plant a knight there.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O O-O b5
en: This is an interesting plan. Black shows he had something more in mind when he played 6...a6.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6 Re1 O-O d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5
en: This is the usual solution: Black fixes White's pawns and then finds some way to chip into them to open the g7-a1 diagonal again.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 Be2 a6 N5c3 Bg5
en: He's exchanging-off his bad bishop, it's blocked by pawns on dark squares. But, which is better, to trade them and weaken Pd6 or to leave it at e7 and have a bad bishop?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7 a3 b6 Be3 Bb7
en: With this it looks like Black is ready for ...d7-d5.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3 a6
en: This isn't to play ...b7-b5, as that would weaken Nc6 far too much. Instead, it gives Bc5 room to retreat.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 c4 O-O Qc2 c5 dxc5 Qa5+ Nc3 dxc4
en: This makes it a little more contentious. Black can easily capture Pc5. Can White get to Pc4?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 Qb6 Nb3 e6 Qe2 Qc7
en: With Be3 coming, the queen was going to have to move anyway.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6 f4 g5
en: An energetic reply, revealing Mikenas character in that period: enthusiasm, courage and imagination. Which is the general strategy of the young people: attack, and don't care about possible losses.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5 Nc6 Nf3 Ne4 Bd2 Nxd2 Nxd2 Bxc5
en: According to the modern theory 8...f5 is preferable. The move in the text is inaccurate.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 h5
en: Double excl amation mark!! Chigorin follows the same moves as the famous game Dubois-Steinitz played in London in 1862, so proving his interest in chess literature at that time.

line: Nf3 Nc6 d4 d5 e3 Bg4 Be2 e6 c3 Nf6 Qb3 Rb8 Nbd2 Bd6 Nf1 Ne4
en: ...and Black profits from it at once.

line: e4 e6 d4 g6 Bd3 Bg7 Be3 c5 c3 cxd4 cxd4 Qb6 Ne2 Qxb2 Nbc3 Qb6
en: White has developed all his minor pieces.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 d4 Qh4+ Ke2 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Bxf4 O-O-O Ke3 Qh5
en: Black is constantly wasting time. 8...Bxf3 was better.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nc3 O-O Rc1 c6 Bd3 a6
en: Pointing out a counterattack on the queenside.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Be7 O-O-O Qa5
en: Attack, no waste of time.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e3 Nd7 Nf3 Bd6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4+ Nc3 Ndf6
en: Quietly, Black has transferred his cavalry to the kingside.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6
en: Initiates an attack on the all-important king pawn.

line: e4 e5 f4 d5 exd5 e4 Nc3 Nf6 d3 Bb4 Bd2 e3 Bxe3 O-O Bd2 Bxc3
en: It stands to reason to get rid of the active Knight.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6
en: While Black gets good piece activity the poor pawn structure must make Gelfand a little nervous.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nf6
en: Essentially Black says White will have an isolated queen's pawn and Black will develop easily and then attempt to exploit his pawn structure advantages (White's disadvantages) .

line: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Be6
en: I've not seen this before. It directly challenges White's light-square bishop and avoids the "obvious" pinning of Nf3, which is an error met quickly by 9. Bxf7+ Kxf7 10. Ng5+.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7 Qf3 Qa5
en: This turned out to be a very astute choice as I was much better prepared for the main line.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7
en: Only move. If 8... Bb7,then 9. e5 9... Bf3 10. Qf3 dxe5 11. Nxe6 fxe6 12. Qxa8+- 9... dxe5 10. Bxb7 exd4 11. Nxb5 axb5 12. Bxa8 +-.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7
en: Shapiro, reasonably enough, figures that there's nothing much to fuss about as long as he covers his c6 square.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6
en: I hope some one later gave Wollner financial compensation for playing this move, because we are all in his debt!

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 e5 Be7 Qg4 O-O O-O-O c5
en: Trying to unravel the pawn chain.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4 c3 Nxd5 Ne4 Qh4
en: Black's pieces swarm around white. Now if 9. d3 then 9... Bg4 10. Qd2 entombs many of white's pieces.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Be3 c5 Qd2 O-O
en: So far on two minutes each. GK.. Garry Kasparov looks tensed, says Mike Valvo. Now Karpov took full 9 minutes to play ...

line: d4 h6 e4 d6 Nc3 a6 f4 b5 Nf3 Bb7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 dxc5 b3 g5
en: #(A typical Basman move, fights for e5, clears the h-file and gets the Bishop to g7, here with tempi on Ktc3.).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7
en: (White takes advantage of the Queen and deploys the second Bishop. 8.Nb5 Qe5+ doesn't look so convincing. Black's retreat may have been too orientated towards stopping Nb5. 8...Qf6 may have been a lesser evil.).

line: b3 g6 Bb2 Nf6 e4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nxe4 Bc4 Nxc3 Bxc3 Bxc3 dxc3 O-O
en: (Well my pawns look pretty healthy to me and the centres on a plate.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 d5 Nce7 Qe2 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 c4 c5
en: Either locking the centre for the moment or giving herself the choice (after dxc6) of a central break with d5 at some point.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Nf6
en: I was expecting 8... Bxd2+. The text takes me out of theory altogether so I was now playing chess.

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3 dxc3 Qe7 g4 Qc5
en: [This was unex pected, but 8. ... h6 9.Bg2 e5 10.h3 Bd7 11.Qe3! Bc6 12.c4 Nbd7 13.Ne2 0-0 14. Ng3 is promising for White. I think that 8. ... Qc5 is better and requires White to play strongly for advantage.].

line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 d6 Qd3 c6 e4 d5
en: [If 8... fxe4 9.Nxe4 Nxe4 10.Qxe4 Bf5 11.Qh4 e6 12.Bg5 with a slight plus.].

line: d4 b5 e4 Bb7 e5 e6 Nf3 a6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 bxc4 Bxc4 d6 Qe2 Nd7
en: Threatening 9...Bxf3, which would either double my f-pawns or win a pawn, liquidating the White centre in the process, so...

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bd3 O-O Ng5 c5
en: Aiming to either destroy Whites pawn centre if he opts for 9.dxc5 Bxe5 or immobolise it completely by playing c4 next. But...

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 Ne5 b5 g3 e6 Bg2 Nd5 e4 Nb4
en: This was an unpleasant surprise, with the tactical point 9.a3 Qxd4! 8...Nxc3 would have been similar to one of my previous games.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 Bf5 f3 Nd6 Nc3 e6 Qe2 Be7 O-O-O Bg6
en: The prophilactic move against e4!

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 Nbd2 f6 exf6 Nxf6 g3 Bg4 a3 Qe7
en: Normal would be 8...Qd7 as mentioned The text is an idea of Nikolay Minev in Inside Chess I'm following the game Lignell-Niemela 1941.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Ke6 g3 b5
en: With the same idea Kasparov attempted in his famous debacle against Deep Blue, making an escape hatch for Black's King. Other moves gives White an advantage.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 a6 Ngf3 c5 exd5 exd5 Be2 c4 O-O Bd6 b3 b5
en: This approach looks too risky.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 f3 b5 g4 Nfd7
en: Kasparov played this variation twice in Cannes and it has became popular. The idea behind the move is to start counter-play on the Queenside (where White will be castling) immediately. Of course it's a bit slow, but how does one exploit it?

line: d3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c4 Nf6 a3 d6 Nc3 Be7 g3 O-O Bg2 Be6 O-O Qd7 Ng5
en: The knight move complicates the position, so it's no wonder that the world champion thought for over twenty minutes before going down this path. Black must preserve the bishop with either 9...Bg4 or...

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 Nf6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Bd6 Nf3 O-O Bd3 Qe7 O-O
en: A strategic error hands the initiative to Black.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1
en: What a clever idea to get the computer out of book and it works. It later turns out that the king is slightly vulnerable on f1 and h2 is undefended but this was naturally quite impossible to foresee.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O g6 b3 Bg7 Bb2 O-O Nc3 d5 Nxd5
en: The only correct way to proceed. If 9.cxd5?! Nxd5 10.Na4 Bxb2 11.Nxb2 Nc6, Black has at least equalized as the White knight on b2 is misplaced.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4
en: This leaves the Be3 unprotected and a tactical liability in some variations. A more modern approach might be 9.Re1 when the bishop on c4 can retreat to f1, if need be.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4
en: If 9.0-0 then 9...Bb7 and White must play 10.f3 after which Black can choose between 10...d5 or 10...Rc8.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+
en: A finely conceived sacrifice.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3
en: The bishop is going to be well placed on b2.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3
en: White is developing normally.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6 a3
en: So that after the bishop recaptures on c4 it can retreat to a2.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2
en: White will soon begin attacking on the queenside.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3
en: A natural developing move.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5
en: This move keeps Black from developing normally. If 9... Bxe5 then 10. Re1 f6 11. f4 would win the bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4
en: White now has the more active pieces and a chance to bring the rook into action on the c file.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3
en: Preparing for an eventual b4 followd by Bb2 while preventing Nb4.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5
en: A strong central position for the knight. Its effect is manifested both by the pressure it exerts on Black's kingside and on Black's weak square c6.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5
en: Pinning the knight and preparing to castle.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3
en: The knight is going to c4 where it will put pressure on Black's e pawn or to d5 via c2 and e3. Black cannot now play 9... exd4 10. cxd4 Nxe4 because 11. Ng5 wins the pinned knight on e4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3
en: 9. g2xg3? would expose White's king too much after 9...gxf3 followed by Bh3+.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e3 e5 Bxc4 exd4 exd4 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Be3 c6 h3
en: To prevent black from playing Bg4 which would be an annoying pin and put indirect pressure on White's isolated Queen pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4
en: White is trying to keep the pressure on and to avoid committal pawn moves. Black has to play this part forcefully.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d6 Nf3 O-O Nc3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Rb8 Rb1
en: Clearly Black wouldn't like to face b2-b4-b5.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Qc2 g6 cxd5 cxd5 Nc3 Bg7 Bf4 Nc6 e3 O-O Be2
en: Now White is ready to O-O, so there's little to be gained by maneuvering ...Nc6-b4-c2. With e5 controlled and the king safe White is probably better. Bg7 can't do much except defend Kg8.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Be3 Qc7 Ne5
en: It seems odd this could be good, but the a4-e8 diagonal is weak.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 e6 Be3 Nc6 Qd2 Be7 g4
en: White keeps Pe4 safe and begins a king-side attack, not entirely unlike the Yugoslav Attack of the Dragon Variation.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 Be2 a6 N5c3 Bg5 Nd2
en: White is weak at d4, so he's not so crazy about exchanging Bc1.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7 a3 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3
en: Kasparov leaves Bf1 at home for the moment. He doesn't want Bb7 to get a free shot at Pg2 if the lines should suddenly open.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3 a6 b3
en: Since Black has spent a tempo on ...a7-a6 White decides to play Bc1-b2 and d2-d4. This seems perfectly reasonable.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4
en: I'm surprised at this, before Kg1-h1. Can Black respond with ...Qd8-b6 to pin Nd4?

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c3 bxc3 O-O O-O c5 e3
en: A modest little move. White intends to build a long-term advantage.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 Qb6 Nb3 e6 g4 Nc6 Qe2
en: Grischuk now intends Be3 and 0-0-0.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5 Nc6 Nf3 Ne4 Bd2 Nxd2 Nxd2 Bxc5 e3
en: Mikenas: "The Yugoslavian Grandmaster Trifunovic indicated the continuation 9.Nde4 Be7 10. 0-0-0 as preferable, with initiative to White. For me it is just matter of taste".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 h5 Nxg5
en: With this move instead, his opponent proves himself naif and little prepared. In fact now the next moves seem to be forced for White. Perhaps it was better to defend himself with.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3
en: This simple developing move was Chigorin's favourite one and proved to be the right one.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 exd5 exd5 Nf3 Bd6 Bd3 O-O O-O h6 Re1 Nc6 Nb5
en: Bird: The opening is much as usual, this move and Mr. Mason's play to preserve his bishop from being changed off taking it a little out of the beaten track.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 O-O e3 b6 cxd5 exd5 Bd3
en: Some simple development moves have the particularity to provoke some adrenalin discharges for the opponent. The move in the text is one of them. The immediate aim of the Bishop on the pawn h7 is little assuring. 9...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5 dxe5 Bg5 h6 Bxc6 bxc6 Be3
en: The attack on Black's weak "c5" will serve as the motif of the ensuing play. 9...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 c5 Ne2 Bd7 Nbc3
en: Instead of this simple development, a more astute mobilisation result from 9. b3. 9...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5
en: The chief protagonist of this move (instead of 9. Bb2 or 9.Nc3) was Anderssen. 9...

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Bb7 d4 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 d5
en: Nimzowitsch's forgotten idea for conducting this opening was revived by Portisch (as Black) in his game with Andersson from Palma 1971.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nf6 h3
en: White is anticipating having an isolated queen's pawn and wants to avoid ...Bc8-g4xf3, undermining Pd4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 O-O Kh1
en: With this move White prepares to move Qd1 without worries that Nd4 might be pinned on the a7-g1 diagonal.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 b5 Bc2 d6 d4 Bb6 a4
en: White probes the queen-side and wonders how Black will defend Pb5, now that Ra8-b8 isn't available.

line: d4 e6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 Nf6 f3 d5 a3 Be7 e4 c5 cxd5 exd5 dxc5 Bxc5 e5
en: This is probably the best way to grab a pawn. I think it is very revealing to see the ways 9.exd5 and 9.Nxd5 get punished. Then one realizes that, assuming he had seen black's idea, he probably would have played it too.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 d6 Nxg4 Nf6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Nc3 c6 Qf3
en: This move carries behind it the devious threat of 10.g4. If white could get that in it would stem black's counterplay on the g-file.

line: Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 c6 d4 Nd7 Bc4 Ngf6 Ng5 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3 g5 Nhg1
en: The knight's journey has already been quite remarkable!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7 Qe2
en: Better than 9. Be3 as in that case Black could have played first...Rd7 followed by...Bb7. After the text move 9... Rd7 would be met by 10. e5 dxe5 11. Nc6 ! Qc7 12. Nxb8 Qxb8 13. Bc6 Qc7 14. Bxd7 Nxd7 with a clear advantage for White.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 Bxc3 bxc3 d6 Bg5 Qe7 Qd2
en: (9. Re1 Nd8 10. d4 c6 11. Bf1 Ne6 12. Bc1 is also played. ).

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5
en: Black's d-pawn becomes a juicy target; isolated, alone.

line: e4 e6 d3 d5 Nd2 e5 exd5 Qxd5 Qe2 Nc6 Ngf3 f5 c3 Nf6 Nb3 Be7 Nfd2
en: This is too passive. 9.d4 or 9.c4 would be more promising.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 cxd5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qd1 exd5 Qxd5 Bd7 Nf3 Nf6 Qd1
en: # Qb3 seems better to me now, but Qd1 shows how much fun the main line is.

line: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 c4 Bc2 b5 Ndf3 Nc6 Ne5 Bb7 f4
en: The Stonewall is established. Black can try 8...Nxe5 9.dxe5 Ne4. This Knight can be a thorn in White's side as either the Kingside pawn structure is weakened or the better hite squared Bishop is traded.

line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 d6 Qd3 c6 e4 d5 exf5
en: [With hindsight, e5 is better.].

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bd3 O-O Ng5 c5 Nxh7
en: Never saw it coming (not quite the words used at the time). Now it is going to be a struggle just to survive.

line: c4 e5 g3 c6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 d5 cxd5 cxd5 Bg2 Be6 Nf3 Nc6 Qa4 Bc5 O-O
en: Now we have a position similar to that in Tarrasch Defence where Black's easy development and active pieces compensate for the supposedly weakpawnatd5.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4 Be3 Qf6 Qg3
en: Black would love to swop off the Queen's, but that is not my poison.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7 Qc2 O-O Ne5
en: White needs to occuly the e5 square at some point, since otherwise Black will eventually play ...e5. As long as White maintains control of e5, Black will find it difficult to activate the light-squared bishop.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3 O-O O-O d6 h3
en: This is probably not necessary, as Black's bishop is headed to b7, but I wanted to make sure it was kept off of g4, where the pin on the knight would weaken my control of d4.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6 Qe7 O-O fxe6
en: If Black captures with the queen, then Re1 is a killer.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4
en: I would prefer 9 ... b6, to get the bishop to a6 or b7.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 O-O-O d5
en: Rebel had 9 ... Ne7 in its book.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5
en: I don't like this because there is no need for it now.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nc3 Ne4 Qc2 Nxc3 Qxc3 c5
en: Such a central pawn thrust, contesting the d4-pawn, is almost always crucial for Black in Queen's pawn openings.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 c6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7 O-O dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5
en: The dark-squared bishops must be exchanged.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6 e3 a6
en: Andersson seeks counterplay with b6-b5, but his lag in development is a cause for concern.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O Kh1 Nbd7
en: 9...Qc7 is more common, but I wanted to go into turbulent, uncharted areas.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5
en: If 9...f5 10.0-0-0 0-0-0 11.Nge2?? Be6, therefore better is 11.Bc4 with an edge according to Tal.

line: c4 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 c5 cxd5 exd5 d4 Nc6 Be2 cxd4 Nxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bd6
en: Now white must spend a couple of tempi to improve the position of the bishop on d2.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 g6 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5
en: Accepting the gambit with 9...Nxc3 10.Bd3 Nc6 can be dangerous after 11.h4 Ne7 (11...Qe7 12.h5 g5 13.f4! was good for White in Klovan-Makarichev, USSR 1978.) 12.f3! with advantage Kurajica-Dvorecki, Wijk aan Zee I 1976.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5
en: Nowadays 9...a6 10.a4 Nbd7 11.Bf4 Qe7 12.0-0 is quite popular.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4
en: A good exchange sacrifice.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4 Qg5 Nf5 c6
en: If now 10. Ba4 then 10... d5 gives Black a satisfactory game.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5
en: Putting some presure on White's center.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6
en: 9... b5 would have given Black better chances.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8
en: Black will move the knight on d7 to f8 so that the bishop on c8 can be developed.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7
en: Black's position is cramped.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5
en: This loses at once, but Black wouldn't have been able to hold out much longer with any move.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4
en: Threatening 10... Bxc3+. However, the move opens up the game which is to White's advantage since he has the better placed pieces.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7
en: Black want to castle to safety as soon as possible.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O
en: Getting the king out of the center and bringing the rook into play.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O
en: Getting the king out of the center and bringing the rook into play.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6
en: Supporting the queenside attack and creating threats on the a7-g1 diagonal.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8
en: To unblock the c pawn so that c6 can be used, if needed, to prevent Nd5. In an open position it would be suicidal to neglect development and move already-developed pieces. In a closed position, both sides can afford positional maneuvering.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7
en: Much better was 9... Nxd7. Black's pieces would then have had much more freedom of movement. The bishop on e7 could have gone to f6 and a rook could have been placed on e8 exerting pressure on the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Nge7
en: Developing his knight. He does not place it on f6 for then White could check on the king file.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7
en: If Qh3+? 10. Ke1 Qg2? 11. Nf2 and the Queen is trapped.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Nc5
en: He's reserving f6 for the dark-square bishop. Karpov is a master of coordination and quiet maneuvering position play. The Nc5 inhibits White from playing Bf1-d3, where it would take aim at Ph7.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 h5
en: This has been around a few years now and it's holding up pretty well. But, some players still choose ...O-O.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4 Nbd7 Qc2 Re8 Rd1 exd4
en: Shirov changes the direction of the game and leaves Qd8 a bit cramped.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Re8
en: This small change doesn't necessarily mean much, though it does allow ...Nd7-f8 to keep Ph7 safer and to leave the queen-side pawns less blocked. Perhaps he'll advance on the queen-side this time.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Na5 Qa4 b6
en: This move might just be a way of defending Na5 without committing to ...c5 (yet) , but it could also be a way of offering a light square bishop trade by ...Bc8-b7 (if White opens the diagonal further) .

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 g6
en: The more blocked d-file makes pressure on Pd6 less significant, but weakening f6 has to be dangerous.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Be3 Qc7 Ne5 a6
en: This prevents Bf1-b5, but not Qd1-a4+. It does force White to commit to one way of utilizing the queen, rather than waiting until Bb5+ forces Black into a rigid defensive position before Qd1-a4 or Qd1-f3 might win outright.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6 Re1 O-O d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e5 Ne4
en: This is risky. If Nf3 can move to allow f2-f3 then where would Ne4 run away to?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 Be2 a6 N5c3 Bg5 Nd2 Nf6
en: Bg5 certainly looks odd, but as long as it can be exchanged for Nd2 or Bc1 it's fine. White isn't about to go chasing after it with pawns.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7 a3 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3 Nc6
en: After this it's difficult for Black to get ...d7-d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 Bb7 O-O Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 Ne7
en: This takes care of the immediate threat, but also leaves Black's position awkward.
