line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 Qb6 Nf3 e6 Be2 Ne7 O-O Bg4 Na4 Qc7 b3 b5
en: This may be a bit too committal - Grischuk can take advantage of Karpov's lack of development to open the game now. Maybe the cautious 9 ..Nd7 was to be preffered.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 Qb6 Nb3 e6 g4 Nc6 Qe2 d5
en: It's an early visit to Planet Shirov! Only someone like Alexei could contemplate such a move at an early stage. Still underdeveloped and with his king in the center, Shirov simply sacrifices a pawn.

line: c4 c5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nc7 b3 e5 Bb2 Be7 Rc1 O-O Na4 Nd7
en: A reply which is not unpleasant at all for White: the right square for this Knight was c6. The c5 Pawn should be protected in a different way.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 h4 c5 Qg4 f5 Qh5+ g6 Qh6 Bf8
en: There is nothing better! After 9... Bxg5 10. hxg5 White threatens Qh6-g7 and Nc3-b5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3 Na5
en: Now, however, this Knight jump near the fence is not so good and makes a lot of troubles to its conductor. Right was 9... Bg4 10. Bb5 Kf8 (!) 11. Be3 Nge7 and Black would have kept his extra pawn and a solid position.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 Nf6 Bc4 d5 exd5 Bd6 d4 Nh5 Bb5+ c6
en: Anderssen in action! It's time to change colours and play white!

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 c5
en: White's position is already clearly better. Black has pushed his pawn in order to allow his Knight to go out to c6 and allow a further control of the center. The position required, instead, a better control of the square h7.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Bd6 Nf3 Nge7 Qc2 Bg4 Nbd2 Qd7 O-O f6
en: Move to prepare an imminent attack.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 c5 Ne2 Bd7 Nbc3 O-O-O
en: After his rapid and straighforward development, Black has already overcome all the difficulties of the opening.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Qh4 Nb5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qxe4+ Be2 Kd8 O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 a6
en: This is superior to 9...Nf6, adopted by Steinitz at this point in the second game of the match. It has the effect of blocking the king's knight for some time.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5 Na5
en: This manoeuvre, if effected without delay, does not represent loss of time, as White's Bishop must react sooner or later, and Black can find the necessary breathing space to consolidate his position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 Bb6 dxe5 Nge7 O-O O-O Ba3 h6
en: Necessary to prevent the Knight from coming to g5 and to be able to play 10...Re8 which at present is not possible on account of 10.Bxf7+! followed by 11.Ng5.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bb4 e3 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 f3 c4 Ne2 Nc6
en: The knight intends Nb8-c6-a5-b3.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6 b6 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 Bg7 a4 Qxb6
en: Nd7 holds square e5 and Qb6 does better on the b-file than a Nb6 would.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 Nc3 g6 e4 Bg7 Be2 O-O O-O Na6
en: This is a very typical maneuver in the Benoni before a6, b5, although 9...a6 isn't a mistake. The knight can be well-placed on c7 in conjunction with ...b5, even as a sack. Also, unlike on d7, it doesn't get in the way from that square.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2
en: This basically just hands white a pleasant position. After I became disillusioned with 9...Nxc3 I didn't see anything else, but the situation actually should not be considered so desperate.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Re8
en: Black puts pressure on the e - Pawn and also prevents its advance. Later Black plays on the Queenside for... b5,... b4 etc.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+
en: Obviously, if White captures this Bishop, Black has 10...Ng4+ and 11...Qxg5 recovering the piece and remaining a pawn to the good with a strong attack.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7
en: This pulls the Rook away from the eighth rank. Now the d-pawn is pinned against the undefended Queen. Hence:.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6
en: Black cannot afford the loss of his entire center. He wastes no time bolstering the weakling.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 d6 g3 Nc6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O Nge7 Rb1 O-O d3 h6 b4 f5
en: Both players have their strategic aims. White charges on the queenside and Black on the other flank.

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8
en: #(Again White can bring more firepower to bear at the expence of the Queen's vulnerable position. the reply 9...Qf5 may have been tried but that White Knight would be ready to spring to b5 again.).

line: b3 g6 Bb2 Nf6 e4 Bg7 e5 Ne4 d3 Ng5 h4 Ne6 h5 d6 d4 O-O hxg6 fxg6
en: # Here's that f-file again.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6
en: A less quiet possibility here would be 9 ... c5 or 9 ... dxc4 followed by c5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 O-O d6 c3 Bb6 b4 Nf6 d3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bxd5 Qxd5
en: Now he can attack the Queen and trap the Bishop.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bd3 O-O Ng5 c5 Nxh7 Kxh7
en: Looks no better a position than playing.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 Ne5 b5 g3 e6 Bg2 Nd5 e4 Nb4 O-O Nd7
en: In this position i spent some time trying to make 10.Nxc6 work, but without success.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Nb3 Nbd7 Qf3 Qc7
en: Trying to improve on 9...Be7 with which I had scored 0/2. My opponent also favours the Najdorf.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 g6 Bxc4 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Nfd7 Qe2 Nb6 Bb3 Nc6
en: An attempt to improve on Golombek - Smyslov, Budapest 1952, which saw 9...a5.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 e6 Nge2 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Be3 Nf6 g4 h5 g5 Ng4 Bc1 Qb6
en: A novelty, which runs somewhat counter to the theme of the opening, which usually involves b7-b5 and the placement of the queen at c7. Still, there is some logic behind the move, as it inhibits the development of the bishop at c1.

line: c4 c6 e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 cxd5 d4 e6 Nf3 Bb4 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Qc7 Bd2 Nd7
en: Positions with the isolated d-pawn are quite popular in New Delhi and a number of very interesting games on this topic have been played here.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 Nc3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 O-O Nd7 f4 Ngf6
en: The treat was 10.f5 e6 11. Ne6, but now black neglects the "credo" of holding back the kings-knigt development. The safer move is 9. ...Qc7, and 9. ...b6-b5 also deserves attention. Now white has got a target...

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ndf6 Bc4 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+
en: I think the exchange of dark-squares bishops is in White's favour because Black has some problems with development of his second bishop. Also the d6-square can become weak.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O Bd7 f4 b5
en: One of the main positions of Sicilian Rauzer.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 b3 Nd7 Bb2 e6 Bg2 Ngf6 O-O c6 d3 Bd6 Nbd2 O-O h3 Bh5 e3
en: Kasparov once again proves he doesn't want a violent confrontation, by playing e3, instead of e4.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 O-O-O d5 g4
en: Rebel was debating between this and 10 f5!? After a longer think Rebel would have preferred 10 f5!?, which is an interesting continuation. But also 10 g4 is perfectly playable, of course.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5 Bxb5
en: 10.Nxb5?! is dubious after 10...Nxe4! 11.Bxe4 Qa5+ 12.Nc3 Bxc3+ 13.bxc3 Re8 which is good for Black.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4 Qg5 Nf5 c6 Rg1
en: A splendid piece sacrifice.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4
en: White now has a strong positon in the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O
en: Getting the king out of the center and developing the king's rook.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5
en: Beginning an eloquent combination.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7 O-O Qe5 f4 dxc3+ Kh1 cxb2 Bxf7+
en: If 10... Kxf7 then 11. fxe5+ followed by 12. Bxb2.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4
en: This provides strong support for the knight and opens the way for a kingside attack.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5
en: Putting pressure on the weak dark squares.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6 Nd2 Nd7 c4
en: Attacking the center and making room for the queen to develop.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3
en: The bishop has designs on the Black king.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4
en: Reinforcing the knight's position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4
en: White now has a clear advantage in space because the pawn on e4 controls more space than the pawn on d6 and because of the powerfully placed queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Nge7 Ng5
en: A premature attack. White has nothing better than Ba3 followed by 11. cxd4 when he does not have sufficient compensation for his pawn minus.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3
en: Developing and guarding the king pawn.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nce7 c4 Nxd5 exd5
en: This makes the pawns a bit unbalanced with White advancing on the queen-side. Aside from Pb5 Black shouldn't have much difficulty completing his development.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3
en: White might be threatening Nxg5 to force the position open (though it wins no material) .

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 h5 Be2
en: I think he must be considering f3-f4 to threaten Ph5 and to open the position while Ke8 isn't as safe as he would normally be. Or, he's still just preparing g2-g4-g5.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Na5 Qa4 b6 Nd5
en: This is probably over-reaching and Black's play will show that soon.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4 Bb4 d3 d6 h3 O-O Be2 Ne7 O-O c6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3
en: White will have use of the open file, but in an endgame, or late middle-game, his pawns might be targets. On the king-side White's pieces are pretty well situated to meet the oncoming attack, but can do nothing aggressive.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O O-O b5 a3 Rb8 Kh1
en: White is interested in prosecuting his offensive plan on his terms. He'd rather not be pushed into something by ... b5-b4.

line: Nf3 c5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O Nc6 c3 d5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 e6 Nc3 Nge7 b3 O-O Qd2
en: Before Bc1-b2 or Bc1-a3 he takes the c1-h6 diagonal to prevent ...Bg7-h6. This preserves control of c1 without having to also play e2-e3.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6 Re1 O-O d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e5 Ne4 Nc3
en: I would have loved to see White find a move to challenge Ne4 with f2-f3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3
en: This is certainly more contentious and forceful than Nb1-d2. He tries to force Pb5 away, so he can move Na3-c4 to add pressure to Pe5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nbd2
en: Shirov chooses a less confusing course, but does leave open a possibility for Black to play ...d7-d5.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3 a6 b3 Ba7 Nxf6+
en: I don't quite know why he'd allow Black's queen to come out so easily. Leaving Nf6 kept Qd8 blocked.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 Bb7 O-O Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 Ne7 Bd2
en: With Bf8 blocked from action on the queen-side White decides to threaten Pb5. Bd2 prepares a2-a4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Qf3 Nbd7 Be2 h5 Bg5 Qa5 Bd2
en: Apparently he's willing to go to some length to not create any weaknesses Kasparov might utilize/exploit.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 Be7 f5
en: This is where his approach differs with Ivanchuk's. Ivanchuk played Kg1-h1, Qd1-e2 and slowly developed while Vallejo Pons self-destructed. Here Adams goes for the throat.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6 Bg5 Bb4 f3 c5 dxc5 Qa5 Qd4
en: Perhaps the strongest reply against Black's choice. Now 11.Nxc4 is threatened, and if 10... Bxc5 11.Qxc4 the threat is 12.e4.

line: Nf3 Nc6 d4 d5 e3 Bg4 Be2 e6 c3 Nf6 Qb3 Rb8 Nbd2 Bd6 Nf1 Ne4 Ng3 O-O Bd3
en: The first mistake. It was better to play immediatly 10. Ng1 to force the Bishop exchange and to open the kingside to the air, since it is beginning to "smell sweat".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5
en: (!) Bird is not afraid of Steinitz threat to replace the Knight in c5 with the Bishop, and with the intention to exploit the position of his opponent's King, he continues with his attacking plan.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 d4 Qh4+ Ke2 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Bxf4 O-O-O Ke3 Qh5 Be2 Qa5 a3
en: The black queen cannot find a single pleasant square on the board.

line: e4 c5 Ne2 Nf6 Nbc3 Nc6 g3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 O-O Be7 Rb1 O-O c4
en: This move has an advantage and a disadvantage. The advantage: White can place a Bishop on the diagonal a1-g8; the disadvantage: it weakens the control of the d4 square, which can become a good base for Black counterplay. 10...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Re1
en: Preparing 11.Nf3-d4. 10...

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 e3 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 O-O Ne5 dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5 f4 Be6 Qb3
en: The opening in this games deserves long commentaries, addressed to the opening lovers only. I think that actually it is not meaningfull to discuss all the refinements, so ... let's go on. 10...

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 f4 d5 d3 Bb4 fxe5 Nxe4 dxe4 Qh4+ Ke2 Bxc3 bxc3 Bg4+ Nf3 dxe4 Qd4
en: The saving clause which redeems White's game, and leaves the opponent no option but to lose a move with the only piece he has got in play besides his queen.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e5 dxe5 Ng4 Nf3 Bc5 e3 Nc6 Bd2 O-O Bc3 Re8 Be2 d6 exd6 Bxe3 fxe3
en: Capablanca was not one to refuse a challenge. He could castle instead, with a defensible game but not much more. 10...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 Ne7 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 Qg4 Qc7 Bd3 cxd4 Ne2 Nbc6 cxd4
en: Now white simply has more space, and has whatever chances exist on both sides of the board.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 Nc3 g6 e4 Bg7 Be2 O-O O-O Na6 Nd2
en: Also a weird-looking move but you won't even glance twice if you've played through a lot of Benoni games. Playing the knight to c4 puts pressure on d6 and frees the path for the f-pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Re8 Qc2
en: White plans to develop his Bishop to f4 before playing Nd2. As will be seen, Tal brilliantly refutes this idea. It looks better to play 10. Nd2 as recommended by theory.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7
en: Let your imagination run wild and you will see that Nxf7 has all the earmarks of an excellent investment. First point: it's an offer Black can't refuse.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1
en: Glucksberg therefore leaves the Bishop where it sits, possibly already envisaging an encirclement with ...g3 to trap and win it.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5
en: Only this move is a just followup to the Knight sacrifice. Black's N/f6 must move (or he has lost material for nothing), and White will push this pawn up to e6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4 c3 Nxd5 Ne4 Qh4 Ng3 Bg4 f3
en: How should black respond with two pieces hanging? Attack of course!

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4 Nf3 Qxd5 Be2 Nc6 c4 Qh5 d5 Ne5 Nbd2 O-O-O O-O e6 Qa4
en: Too aggressive! White has no chance of attack, because his own King-side is weak. More reasonable would be 10. dxe6.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 e3 Nbd7 f3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bb3 e6 Nge2 Bb7 a3 a6 e4
en: (White is building a very imposing centre which Black must try and breach at some point in the future.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 c5 exd5 Qxd5 Ngf3 cxd4 Bc4 Qd6 O-O Nf6 Re1 a6 a4 Nc6 Qe2
en: (10.Nb3 might have transposed in the direction of the main line possibly.).

line: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 c4 Bc2 b5 Ndf3 Nc6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nxe5 fxe5
en: I decided it was better to keep the centre closed and try to control the f-file.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5
en: I had decided Black would not want 10 ... Qxd5 11 Bxc7 but after 11 . .. Qc6 he does OK. My main intention was to have a position with d5 blocked, thus making a queen side fianchetto unattractive.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 Qd7 O-O b6 Qd3
en: Be3 is recommended as more flexible (Baumbach, SCC no 29.). Whatever, as Black I don't like the threats from White's d and e pawns advancing.

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 e4 d6 Nf3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Qe2 Nc6 d5 Na5 Bd3 c5 O-O a6 a4
en: Played to prevent the obvious b5 & c4, winning the Bishop.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4 Be3 Qf6 Qg3 e5 O-O-O
en: White has now reached a safe castled position, and has much more artillery at his disposal.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7 Qc2 O-O Ne5 Nbd7 Ndf3
en: This is a standard anti-Dutch plan. The knight at e5 is supported by both a pawn at d4 and another knight at either f3 or d3.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3 Qb6 Qd2 Qxb2 Rb1 Qa3 dxc5
en: This was my own idea. 10.Be2 was recommended in an old book by Harding, but it did not impress me at all. I decided to eliminate the dark-squared bishops and use Kasparov's attacking formation on the kingside.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Ke6 g3 b5 a4 b4 Nd2
en: A nasty surprise. White alertly notices that c4 is now available for this Knight.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6 Qe7 O-O fxe6 Bg6+ Kd8
en: Black is a piece up but his position is horrendous.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4 h3 cxd4
en: A little trick: If 11 hxg4, then 11 ... dxc3 and if the bishop moves, 12 ... c2 will follow.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4 bxc4 Ne5 Qe2 Bb4
en: Striving for complications. On 11 d4 it's possible to play 11 ... Ne4.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O
en: I was very satisfied with the outcome of the opening: Rebel has a solid position, with no weaknesses and a clear aim: Attack the White king.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8
en: Out of book. Rebel only knows 10 ... Be7 and 10 ... cxd4. I must confess that I thought that 10 ... Qc8 was a novelty, because I had never seen it before.

line: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Be2 O-O O-O c5 d5 Na6 Re1 Nc7 Bf4 b6 Qd2 Re8
en: Black plays another passive move.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6 e3 a6 b4 b5
en: After 10...d5 11.Bb2 Be7 12.Rc1 Qd7 13.Bg2 0-0 14.cxd5 exd5 15.Qb3, White has a clear advantage.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O Kh1 Nbd7 a4 b6
en: Possible is 10...Qc7!? 11.a5 b5 12.axb6 Nxb6.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O
en: Now it is safe to castle. Note that 10...d5?! is premature because of 11.Bb5+, as after 11...Bd7 12.Bxd7+ Qxd7 13.e5 Nc6 14.b4! Black cannot hang on to the advanced d-pawn for long.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5
en: With this pawn break, Black equalizes easily. As play unfolds, we will see that Black develops an initiative by virtue of having the more active minor pieces.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 Bg5 Be7 Qa4+ Bc6 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 O-O e3 Bb7
en: Returning the bishop to its natural Queen's Indian square is necessary in order to develop my knight from b8 and to free my c-pawn. The loss of time involved is more than offset by the three White queen moves.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8
en: With a view to sacrificing the Exchange on c3. The solid 10...Be7 is also possible.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 a3 f6 Bd3 Qc7 O-O O-O-O Re1 fxe5 dxe5 c4
en: White planned a strike c3-c4, so Black radically prevents it, bearing in mind that it is difficult for a white knight to occupy the ideal square d4, because the pawn e5 is weak.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 Be7 O-O-O O-O f4 Nxd4 Qxd4 a6
en: Rather rare move. Main discussions there are now around 10...Qa5.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+
en: Perhaps better was 10...Qg7 at once.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4 Qxa8 Nf6
en: Developing, guarding his king bishop, and preventing 11. qe8+.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8
en: Black wants the bishop to be protected so that after ... Ne4 the knight will not become pinned to the bishop after White moves his queen and knight. However, this is a passive place for the rook.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4
en: Although this move gains space on the queenside, it takes pressure off the center. White now strives to play e4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4 Qc7
en: In a few moves White will have threats based on playing Bf4 and attacking both the queen and the rook.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6 a3 h6 Bh4 Re8
en: Black is waiting until White develops his bishop before playing ... dxc4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7
en: The knight is moving to c5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O
en: Black's king is not safe in the center but it is not safe on the kingside either.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5
en: It is correct to try to undermine the powerful knight by attacking its defenders.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6 Nd2 Nd7 c4 b6
en: Possibly thinking that he should prevent 11. c5, which was not a good move anyway. Black should castle.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5
en: Attempting to put pressure on the queenside.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6
en: To develop the bishop on b7.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5
en: White would like to castle now but that would allow Black to move the knight on d4 checking with the bishop. For example, 11. 0-0 Nxf3+ 12. Kh1 Nxg5.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6
en: 10... Nd5 may have turned out better.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8
en: This allows Black to play f6 in response to 11. Nc4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6
en: Developing and offering the exchange of bishops. After 11. Bxe6 fxe6 White's queen knight would no longer exert pressure on his d5. 11. Bb3 is best now.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Re8 Bc4 Nb6
en: It's not exactly easy to criticize this move, but after Bc4-d3 then what is Nb6 doing? Does he intend to invade at c4 after ...Bc8-e6?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3
en: This might be considered a downside of 10. Na3 since it stops White's plan, or it might be considered a positional gain since Black is giving a bishop for the knight. Such exchanges can be difficult to evaluate.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nf6 c4 b4 Nxf6+ Qxf6
en: Though this leaves d5 weak Black can use it as an opportunity to do some damage on the king-side; usually Black doesn't get the queen out in front until much later in the middle-game.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 Nc3 Nd5 Qxc4 Nb6 Qb3 e5 dxe5 Be6 Qc2 Nd4 Qd3 Bc5
en: This makes ...Be6-c4 possible.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Bxc4 Nb6 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nb4 Be4 f5 exf6 exf6 Nc3 f5
en: Consistently Black uses a pawn to block Be4 and this incidentally (and usefully) prevents Qd1-h5+ from being effective. Now Nb4 could retreat if necessary.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 Be7 f5 Nc6
en: Black takes the pressure off Pe6 immediately. Black can hardly afford to play ...e6-e5 and leave Pd5 completely in White's hands.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O h3 Bb7 d3 h6 Nc3 Bc5
en: Up to now, 10 ..Re8 or ..d6 has been the only moves here. However, Leko's move fits in with his Archangel\Moeller set-up with ..Bb7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3 Na5 d4 exd4 Nxd4 c5 Nf5 Nxf5 exf5 Nxb3
en: Of course now it is too late to play 10...c4 because of 11.Qe2+.

line: e4 e6 d4 g6 Bd3 Bg7 Be3 c5 c3 cxd4 cxd4 Qb6 Ne2 Qxb2 Nbc3 Qb6 Rc1 Na6 Nb5 Bf8
en: (?!) Protecting the square d6, but Black's pieces are completly misplaced.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O c5 Ne5 Nxe5
en: After this move White has advantage.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Bf5 Qb3 Qb6 Qxb6 axb6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 cxd5 e3 Nc6 Bd2 Bd7
en: Black is planning - after the preliminary move Pb6-b5 - to bring his Knight to c4. In order to support the advance of the b-Pawn, the Bishop goes back to d7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 d6 Bg5 Bxc3 bxc3 Qe7 Re1 Nd8 d4 Bg4
en: Capablanca's favourite move, and probably stronger than the usual 10... Ne6 11.Bc1 c5. With this move, in fact, Black developes his last light piece, keeping the pressure on the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5 Na5 Bb2 Ne7
en: By this move Black shows that he has no fear of 11.Bxg7, because of 11...Rg8; and Black would have the initiative.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O
en: Playing a Nh4 or Nd4 to add pressure to the pin on Nf3 would be desirable, but White can step out of the pin with Qd1-e1. Black has to do more, so he castles and prepares to bring more forces into play.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2 cxd4 Nb3 Qb6 cxd4 Nf6 d5 d6 Nf3 O-O O-O Na6
en: Black is probably taking aim at Pd5 (though there is also ...Nb4 followed by ...Bc8-f5-c2) , but I think Black needs to ensure space on the queen-side for Qb6 and the knight by first playing ...a7-a5 and ...a5-a4 if possible.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4 c5 Qd2 cxd4 Nxd4 h6
en: Without Nf3 to defend Ph4 White has to think twice about retreating Bg5-e3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6 Rd1 Re8 d3 a6 Bxc6 bxc6 Nbd2 a5
en: This serves several purposes. One is to prevent b2-b4, thereby keeping Pb2 a little backward. It also clears the way for ...Bc8-a6 to target the weak Pd3 and Qe2.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 Bb7 Bg2 Bb4+ Bd2 c5 O-O O-O Bxb4 cxb4 Qd3 d5
en: Black doesn't worry about Pd5 blocking Bb7 forever. Since there's a Pc4 Black will have ...dxc4 to reopen the diagonal.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bb5 Bd7 O-O Bg7 d3 a6 Bxc6 Bxc6 Kh1 Qd7 Qe2 f5
en: 10... Nh6 was probably better. Far from stopping white's kingside play, this weakens e6, forming the basis for some nice knight maneuvers in the next few moves.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 c6 a3 h6 Bf4 a6 h3 dxc4
en: Black could have continued the struggle with 10...Re8 when 11 Qc2 is best.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Re8 Qc2 Na6
en: Black's idea is to play... Nc7,... Rb8 followed by... b5. Also the Knight can be used for other purpose as demonstrated in the game.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4
en: Najdorf consistently brings his forces over to the Kingside with a gain of time thanks to the unveiled attack on the N/g5. But has he overlooked something?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Bb7 d3 Nd7
en: Black, for his part, evolves a plan to bring his forces to the Queenside and open the center, believing that he has superiority in piece activity.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 d6 Qh4 Rb8
en: White is allowed to take the initiative.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 Qc7 Qe1 O-O Qg3 Qb6
en: A furious fight for a place at the interzonal tournament has started.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nc3 d5 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Qc8 Bg5 Qe6
en: This position stems from Eliskases-Najdorf, Buenos Aires 1947.

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8
en: (With such a lead in development and potential to embarrass the King, I was happy to give up the Rook for the poor defending Knight. 10...Qxd8? 11.Bxf7+ Kd7 12.Qe6++.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 Nc3 Nf6 Nd5 Nxe4 Qe2 Bxf2+ Kd1 f5 d3 Nd4 Nxd4 Bxd4 dxe4 f4
en: #(This blocks off the diagonal for the Black squared Bishop. White's pieces have more space, however.).

line: Nf3 d6 d4 Nf6 c4 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g3 Ne4 Bd2 Be7 Bg2 Nd7 O-O c5 d5 Qb6 b3 O-O
en: #(At this point , not having achieved very much in the opening, I decided on radical action to seize the initiative, Remember Fischer's 1...Nh5 against Spassky?).

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7 Nbd2 g6 Bd3 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 d6 Bb2 Nbd7 c4 e5 Qc2 Re8
en: Black has snatched a small initiative with the threat of 11...e4.

line: e4 Nc6 d4 d5 Nc3 e5 exd5 Nxd4 Nf3 Bg4 Be2 Nxf3+ Bxf3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Bb4 Bd2 Nf6 O-O-O O-O
en: I quite fancy White's chances here.

line: d3 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e4 dxe4 d5 Ne5 Qa4+ Nd7 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 g6 Nb5 Nxd5
en: [I looked here at 11.Qxe4. Now 11... Nxf4 and 11... N5f6 both lose to 12.Nd6#. If 11... e6 then 12.0-0-0 seems fine for White. But 11... N7f6 solves all Black's problems! So...].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe1 c5 Be3 a6 dxc5 Qa5
en: A lovely idea this, black gives back the gambit pawn, with the idea of ..Bxc5 Bxc5 Qxc5+ picking up the Bishop on c4!!

line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 d6 Qd3 c6 e4 d5 exf5 Bxf5 Qe3 Na6
en: [If 10... Bxc2 11.Qe6+ Kh8 12.Ng5 pressurising e6 and f7.].

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5
en: Black goes for the pawn capture anyway. After all, the c8 h3 diagonal is available again.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 O-O d6 c3 Bb6 b4 Nf6 d3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bxd5 Qxd5 c4 Qd6
en: Now at least I get two pawns for the Bishop.

line: c4 e5 g3 c6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 d5 cxd5 cxd5 Bg2 Be6 Nf3 Nc6 Qa4 Bc5 O-O h6 Nc3 Ne7
en: Again unexpected! After his previous I thought he was playing.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 Bf5 f3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 g4 Bg6 h4 h6 Qb3 b6
en: I was confident that Iain would not play 10...Qb6. In the last two Championship tournaments Iain had given me a lesson on how to play and literally ripped my Kings head off! I was sure he would want to keep Queens on.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 dxe5 Nxe5 Nd7 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Ke6 g3 b5 a4 b4 Nd2 N7f6
en: Forced. Any other move loses the Knight on d5 for nothing, or worse. For example, 10 Ncf6 allows White mate in three.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 Nc3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 O-O Nd7 f4 Ngf6 Re1 Qc7
en: I was not confident with this move, but I felt forced to do so. My prefered move, the alternative ...h5!?, looks interesting, but the analyse suggests a littlel but forced advantage for white:.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 O-O-O d5 g4 Ne7 h4
en: Impressive, these white pawns!

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4 bxc4 Ne5 Qe2 Bb4 f4
en: A mistake, missing Black's reply. Probably 11 d4 is best anyway.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1
en: The tournament bulletin condemns this move, claiming it's a routine move. They propose 11 e4 instead.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 h6 b3 Ke8 Bb2
en: All typical Berlin Defence fare. White has all his pieces out and Black does not a lot.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3
en: So that d6-d5 does not arrive with tempo and can thus be met by e4-e5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5 Bxb5 Nxe4 Nxe4
en: Forced, as are the next moves.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5 exd5
en: White cannot play 11.e5? because of 11...c5, followed by the pawn fork 12...d4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3
en: The piquant point, Black can not play 11...Qxe3+? because after QxQ Blackâs Bishop Pawn is pinned and cannot recapture. Notice how all of Whiteâs moves gain time and development.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4 Qxa8 Nf6 Na3
en: Unfortuneatly for white, he must develop the knight to the side to guard his c2 pawn.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4 Qg5 Nf5 c6 Rg1 cxb5 g4
en: Black cannot play 11... fxg3 en passant because of 12. Bxg5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4 Qc7 e5
en: The center pawns are on the move. Black's best is now 11... dxe5 12. dxe5 Nd7 although Black's position would be cramped and his pieces would be in each other's way.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7 c3
en: Supporting the center and providing an escape hole for the bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1
en: Bringing the rook to an active central position.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3
en: White hopes to be able to use the open g file to attack the Black king.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+
en: If 11... Kd8 then 12. Bxf6 Qxf6 13. Qd5+ Qd6 14. Qxa8 wins.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4
en: White has her pawn back and is still in an excellent position.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O Bc4
en: A natural developing move.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4
en: Attacking the bishop and preparing Bb2 where the bishop will exert strong pressure on the Black kingside.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5 Rf1
en: Developing the rook for a kingside attack and protecting f2. If now 11... b4 then 12. Na4 and White can trade his knight for Black's powerful bishop.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nbd7 Qe2
en: Preparing Ba6 to exchange off Black's bishop on b7, the defender of his queenside holes. Black should now try 11... c5 attacking White's center, although White would still have a significant advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8 Nc4
en: Attacking the pawn on e5. If 11... exd4 12. cxd4 White's pawn center would cause Black serious trouble.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4 O-O b3
en: The bishop on the a1-h8 diagonal will menace the Black king.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5
en: The prelude to an enterprising knight sacrifice which Anderssen however with ingenious play refutes.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 Nbd2 Bg7 Nf1 O-O Ba4 Nd7 Ne3 Nc5 Bc2 Ne6 h4
en: Starting an attack against Black's king. White plans to play h5 and hxg6 opening his rook file. By playing this move White has definitely committed himself to queenside castling for his kingside will be too exposed for him to castle there.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Nh6 h3
en: Although this gives an escape square for Bg3 it seriously weakens the king-side, where White's king might soon be residing.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 e6 Bb3 b5 O-O Be7 Qf3 Qc7 Qg3 O-O Bh6
en: This forces ...Nf6-e8 which removes pressure from Pe4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d6 Nf3 O-O Nc3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Rb8 Rb1 Na5 Qa4 b6 c5
en: It would appear this is something especially prepared for Shirov. By preventing ...c7-c5 he undermines Black's plan and still can play b2-b4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4 b5 Bc2 Bb7 Qe2 Ng6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nh4 Nbd2
en: This blocks Bc1 for the moment, but it makes room for Bc2-b1 (if needed) and defends Pe4 again.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 d3 Bb7 e4 O-O d4
en: This is an interesting change of tack. White opens things up, but he doesn't have the best grip on d5 since Nc3 is gone. Maybe now Black can play on the dark squares a little more actively.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Ne5 Nd7 Bb5 Bd6 Qg4 Kf8 O-O
en: Kasparov has a lot of courage. Here he offers a pawn, so he can spend the tempo developing pieces. He obviously thinks there's a way to fight for a win if his piece activity is sufficient.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 e6 Bb3 Be7 O-O O-O c3 Nc6 Re1 b5 Nbd2 d5 e5 Nd7 d4
en: White supports Pe5 and prepares for Bb3-c2 to take aim at Ph7 (and Kg8) .

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3 Na5 d4 exd4 Nxd4 c5 Nf5 Nxf5 exf5 Nxb3 Re1+
en: Maybe Steinitz has been too quick in willing to eliminate the dangerous lightsquare Bishop. Maybe, probably, surely indeed, Janowsky will show us that his opponent "fell out the frying pan into the fire"!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 c5 dxc5 Na6 a3 Bxc3+ Qxc3 Nxc5 f3 d6 e4 e5 Be3 Qc7 Ne2
en: This knight is aiming to take the strong d5 square.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5 Nb3 Qe4
en: "Do you want a Rook? Just take it!".

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7 e3 O-O c5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Qc2 f5 Bc4 Nc6 a3 Bf6 O-O-O
en: A concrete decision: White's advance on the queenside will be met by e6-e5, which is why Steinitz changes direction, preparing an attack against the weakened black centre and potentially on the kingside.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Bd6 Nf3 Nge7 Qc2 Bg4 Nbd2 Qd7 O-O f6 Re1 g5 h3
en: Removes the lightsquared Bishop, but also weakens the castling. 11...

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nc3 O-O Rc1 c6 Bd3 a6 O-O dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bd3
en: A further control on the d4 square.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Be7 O-O Nc6 Re1 Bg4 c3 f5 Qb3 O-O Bf4
en: Lasker agrees, and resists to the temptation of capturing the pawn b7.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3
en: Preparation for an attack by 12.h4 and 13.h5, but the king knight loses a pawn support - a circumstance thet will not escape Botvinnik's notice.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 e6 Nxe4 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 Nf3 b6 Ne5 O-O Bd3 Bb7 Qh5 Qe7 Qxh7+
en: A sacrifice of the Queen leading to a forced mate of rare beauty: with a King move! 11...

line: c4 e5 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 g6 a3 a5 Nf3 Bg7 d3 Nge7 Nd2 d6 Nf1 Be6 Ne3 O-O Ned5
en: The knight feels good on d5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4
en: Though White needs to clear the way for Bc1 to develop it's a little odd to see him weaken Nf3 this way. Does he intend to move Bc1 and then play Ne4-d2 to re-establish the defense of Nf3, or is g2-g4 still being considered?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 a6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Qc7 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxf6 gxf6 Qg4
en: Naturally White does his best to avoid Rh8-g8.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Bd3 O-O Nge2 Re8 Qc2 c6 h3 Ne4 Bf4
en: Refusing to exchange pieces on black's terms. 9...Ne4 looks silly as white can push through f2-f3, etc. with tempo.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb6 O-O Be7 f4 g6 a3
en: 11.Nf3 looks better as it isn't clear yet that ...Nb4 will be a problem.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 a3 Bb7 O-O-O Nd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Ngf6 e5 Ng4 Bg1
en: This drops a pawn, but white was probably overextended anyway. Black appears to be at least equal.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7 Qe2 Rc7 Rd1 Nbd7 a4
en: A common move in such positions.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Re8 Qc2 Na6 Bf4
en: Better was 11. Re1 Nc7 12. Bf4 Rb8 13. a4 a6 14. a5 b5 15. axb5 Rb6 with chances for both the sides.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5
partai: Donald Byrne vs Robert James Fischer (1956)
en: 11. Be2 followed by 12 O-O would have been more prudent. The bishop move played allows a sudden crescendo of tactical points to be uncovered by Fischer. -- Wade.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+
en: This prepares for the eventual advance of White's d-pawn. The idea is to soften up the center with f4 first, and if the Black e-pawn can be deflected, then d4 will establish a dominant center for White.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6
en: A bad idea by white. Black reconnects a strong central pair of pawns, opens up the f-file for his Rooks. White cannot generate counter play against the central pawns in time.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 h5 Nxc6 bxc6 Bc4 Qc7 O-O
en: With Douglas seemingly intent on not castling, I thought I'd be a touch perverse and invite a further K-side advance.

line: d3 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e4 dxe4 d5 Ne5 Qa4+ Nd7 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 g6 Nb5 Nxd5 Be5
en: [The bishop cannot be taken because of Nc7#].

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3 dxc3 Qe7 g4 Qc5 h4 h6 Bg2 Nc6 Bxe4
en: [I was a little reluctant to exchange one of my bishops for a knight, but White must open up lines quickly.].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe1 c5 Be3 a6 dxc5 Qa5 Nd5
en: Oops, someone left the coral gate open, and the stallion goes berserk. If black plays Qxe1 white gains a bishop by virtue of the check on e7!

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 b3 Nf6 g3 Bf5 Bg2 Nbd7 cxd5 cxd5 Bb2 e6 Nc3 Bb4 O-O O-O Rc1 Rc8 Nh4
en: This move forces some sort of Knight for Bishop exchange, leaving me with doubled and/or isolated pawns. I try and pick the least unatractive option.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4 Be3 Qf6 Qg3 e5 O-O-O Nd7 Bc4
en: Eyeing up the weak f7 square, the Rook on h1 will come to f1 and further embarace the black Queen.

line: d4 Nf6 e3 d5 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 b6 Ndf3 c4 Bc2 Bd6 Ne5 O-O f4 b5 Qf3 g6 Nh3
partai: A Petrie vs T F McAinsh
en: ,but is creating weaknesses on the black squares around the King.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O Nf3 d6 O-O Nbd7 Nc3 e5 e4 c6 h3 exd4 Nxd4 Qb6 Nde2
en: More and more popular move.

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 Nbd2 f6 exf6 Nxf6 g3 Bg4 a3 Qe7 Bg2 d3 e3 Nd4 O-O
en: 11 h3 was obligatory according to Minev.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7 Qc2 O-O Ne5 Nbd7 Ndf3 Ne4 Bf4
en: White invites Black to advance the g-pawn. This is a double-edged strategy.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3 O-O O-O d6 h3 Bb7 Rd1 Re8 a4
en: I believe this was a novelty.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 Nf3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb4 Bb5+ N8c6 d4 cxd4 a3 dxc3 Qxd8+ Kxd8 axb4 Nxb4 Ke2
en: An idea of Garri Kasparov which I found in a book collection of his games. Other replies are much weaker, e. g.:.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 a6 Ngf3 c5 exd5 exd5 Be2 c4 O-O Bd6 b3 b5 a4 Bb7 bxc4 bxc4 Bxc4
en: Excellent! Perhaps Alexey Dreev did not expect this sacrifice from such an "elderly" player?!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 b5 cxb5 Bxb5 Bg2 c5 O-O Bc6 Ba3 Na6 Nbd2 Be7 dxc5
en: Vladimir plays in a classical manner - he simply develops his pieces and will try to use his extra-tempos.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 f3 b5 g4 Nfd7 Qd2 Nb6 O-O-O N8d7 Nb3
en: It's a novelty. The Guests of Cannes played As I understand, Ponomarev's idea is to prevent the Knight's maneuvre, Nd7-c5-a4 etc.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 c5 O-O Nc6 Be3 Bg4 f3 Bd7
en: An unusual variation. More usual is 11 ... Na5. Rebel's following move was still in its book.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 O-O-O d5 g4 Ne7 h4 b5
en: Preparing a counterattack on the queen's side. Rebel expected 11 ... h5.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4 bxc4 Ne5 Qe2 Bb4 f4 Bxc3
en: Not a trivial move! But the point comes one move later.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3 e5 h3 Be6 a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bb2 Nd7 Nbd2 O-O e3 f5
en: Active play, like Rebel always does.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 h6 b3 Ke8 Bb2 Be7
en: Designed to take Fritz out of book which it appeared to do.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 O-O Bg7 Nbd2 O-O Re1 Re8 d4 Bd7 d5 Ne7 Bxd7 Nxd7
en: The structure reminds us of the King's Indian, an opening in which computers have traditionally not fared too well.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 Bb3 cxd4 exd4 Nc6 Nc3 Be7 Re1 O-O Bf4 Na5
en: Attacking the bishop. Exchanges are usually to the defender's benefit, especially in a cramped position.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O g6 b3 Bg7 Bb2 O-O Nc3 d5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Bxg7 Kxg7 cxd5 Qxd5
en: The exchanging sequence is forcing, as 11...Bxd5 12.d4, is good for White. Note that White wins immediately after 12...cxd4? 13.Qxd4+ Kg8 14.Rfd1, pinning and winning Black's bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5
en: Risky, yet 11...0-0-0 12.Rc1! f5 13.exf6 favors White.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3 Nc6
en: Aiming to knock out the bishop from a5. In his notes Short suggests 11...f5!? with similar play to Game 22.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 O-O d4 Bb6 Qd3 d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Bd7 Nbd2 a6 Bc4 exd4
en: Together with 12...g5, this is too loosening. Normal and best would be 11...Qe7. If 11...g5 instead then 12.Nxg5! hxg5 13.Bxg5 and thanks to White's 7th move the attack looks very dangerous.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 Be7 O-O-O O-O f4 Nxd4 Qxd4 a6 Bc4 Qc7
en: Early Black automatically played 11...b5, but if White in any case ought to take away his bishop on b3, why Black would not use this tempo for more useful pieses regrouping.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4 Qxa8 Nf6 Na3 f3
en: Breaking in to White's king position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8 Rad1 Ne4
en: The knight is Black's best-placed piece.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7 c3 Nc5
en: Attacking the pawn on d3.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3 Be7
en: Breaking the pin and threatening 12... Nxd5 13. Bxe7 Nxe7 winning a piece.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4
en: A strategic error: Black relieves the tension in the center. Black's queenside attack is no match for White's kingside attack.".

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6
en: If now 12. Bxd8 then 12... Nxd4. Or, if 12. Bxc6 then 12... Qxg5.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6 Nd2 Nd7 c4 b6 b4 f6
en: Attempting to chase away the powerful knight. But Black has made too many weakening pawn moves already.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O Bc4 Nc6
en: Developing and beginning to put pressure on White's center.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5 Rf1 a4
en: Now Black is prepared for ... b4.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nbd7 Qe2 Nd5
en: Removing an important defender from the kingside.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4
en: Hoping to exchange the bishops and castle.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4 O-O b3 Rfe8
en: Placing the rook on the half-open file and leaving f8 open for the bishop where it will help guard g7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Nge7 Ng5 O-O Bd3 Bf5
en: A good exchange sacrifice. 11...h6 was also an adequate defense.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Nc5 Be3 Be6 Kb1 Qc8
en: I'm not quite certain what his plan is.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Nh6 h3 Nc6
en: Black wants to trade at d4 and then use ...f6-f5 to uncover another threat before playing ...f5-f4 to mash Bg3.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Na5 Qa4 b6 Nd5 Bd7 Qc2 c5
en: Black had no intention of playing ...Nxd5 to allow White cxd5, securing control of c6 and removing Pc4 as a target.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 e6 Nf3 d5 cxd5 exd5 d4 Bg4 Ne5 cxd4 Nxc6 bxc6 Qxd4 Be7 Bg5 Be6
en: Black hunkers down just a bit, hoping to castle and develop enough to support the advance of her central pawns.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4 Bb4 d3 d6 h3 O-O Be2 Ne7 O-O c6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ng6 Re1 Re8
en: This seems to indicate Kasparov is considering ...d6-d5, but one would think opening the center could only be good for White's bishops.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 e5 Bc4 d6 d3 Be7 Nd2 Bg5 h4 Bxd2+ Bxd2 Nf6 Bg5 Be6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 h6
en: Now that White has the two bishops v. two knights he decides to regain one of them. Though his position is fine it's hard to know how valuable those bishops might become later.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3 Bg7
en: Sometimes Bg7 is useful to enable ...Nc6-e7 to challenge the light squares.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3 O-O b4 Be6 Rb1 f6 d3 Nd4
en: This is a surprising move. Usually Black would avoid a trade of Nf3 in order to keep Bg2 under cover. But, in this case it appears Black intends to get his queen-side better organized before White could play Bc1-e3 and Nc3-e4-c5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nf6 c4 b4 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Nc2 Qg6
en: This creates an opportunity for White to show d5 isn't sufficiently guarded, or to be more precise that d5 and all of Black's queen-side is weak.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3 a6 b3 Ba7 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Bb2 Bg4
en: This pin is important and has to be broken with h2-h3. The immediate threat is NOT ...e5-e4 because Bb2 still pins Pe5 to Qf6. But, Black might play ...Qf6-e6 to prepare ...e5-e4 and/or ...Bg4-h3xg2.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4 Re8 Kh1 Nbd7 Qe2 g6
en: It's amazing how a move like this can be appealing and yet it weakens Nf6 quite a lot. And, after f4-f5 (whenever White chooses to play it) open lines would soon follow.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7 a3 Be7 Be3 O-O Rc1 Nc6 Be2 Nxd4 Qxd4 d6
en: Black's position isn't very enterprising. It's quite passive. He's traded off one minor piece, so his cramp won't be too terrible, but he will have to be in a mood to counter-attack if he's to find any chance to win.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Qf3 Nbd7 Be2 h5 Bg5 Qa5 Bd2 Qb6 Nb3 Qc7
en: It would appear Black wants to play ...Nd7-e5-c4 or ...b7-b5 and ...Bc8-b7.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 e6 Bb3 Be7 O-O O-O c3 Nc6 Re1 b5 Nbd2 d5 e5 Nd7 d4 Ba6
en: I wonder if later he might miss this piece from c8 where it could defend Pe6 in a few critical cases when Black would want to play ...f7-f5 to block the b1-h7 diagonal.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 Qb6 Nb3 e6 Qe2 Qc7 g4 b5 Be3 b4 Na4 Nbd7
en: The scene is set: White is looking to exploit the queenside, Black is staking his claim in the centre.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Na5 Bc2 c5 d4 Bb7
en: The Romanishin Variation. Named after one the most original thinkers in the game, the Ukrainian GM Oleg Romanishin, who is one of the world's leading experts on this line. It's also one of Grischuk's favourite pet-lines.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6 f4 g5 Nf3 gxf4 exf4 Rg8 Qf2 Nxd4
en: The right continuation even if comes from intuition rather than calculation. The consequences of 11... Rxg2 12. Qxg2 Nxd4 13. Qg7 Nxf3+ 14. Kf2 were unclear. Not even convincing 11... Nh5 12. Bxh7.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8 Bg2 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6 O-O Ne7 Qc2 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Bxf6 gxf6
en: If Black would have not resisted from winning a Pawn with 11... dxc3 12. Bxc3 Qxc4 13. Ne5 Qc7 14. Bxb7 Qxb7 15. Nc4 he would have been in severe delay in developement and would have given very good chances to the opponent.

line: c4 Nf6 g3 c5 Bg2 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 Nc6 O-O d6 h3 Bd7 e3 Qc8 Kh2 h5 d4 h4 gxh4 g5
en: (!) This move is now possible thanks to White's mistake at the 8th move: The Bc1 has his way blocked by his own pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5 Nb3 Qe4 Nxa1
en: "Did you take it? Good. Do you think that now I want to take your Rook in a8? You are wrong!".

line: e4 c5 Ne2 Nf6 Nbc3 Nc6 g3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 O-O Be7 Rb1 O-O c4 Qd7 Bb2 b6
en: "A natural move, nevertheless a mistake. I thought Black would have prepared this push with.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Nf3 b6 Bg5 Bxc3+ bxc3 Bb7 e3 d6 Bd3 Nbd7 O-O Qe7 Nd2 h6 Bh4 g5
en: Since Black has already decided to castle, his attack on the kingside is made easier by the presence of this Bishop. (Le Lionnais).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5 dxe5 Bg5 h6 Bxc6 bxc6 Be3 Ng6 Qd3 Bd6 Nd2 Ne7
en: Black has a bad game but this move makes it even worse.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Qh4 Nb5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qxe4+ Be2 Kd8 O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 a6 N5c3 Qe5 Na3 b5
en: Best at once, but not so much with the view of attacking the two pieces as with the object of paralysing the action of one of the knights.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e5 Nfd7 f4 e6 Nf3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O d3 Nb6 Ne2 d4 g4 f6
en: Questa mossa, per ben due volte omessa dal Nero, ora porta a risultati meno soddisfacenti a causa della debolezza della casa e4. (N).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6
en: A third attack on the king pawn. White must now either give up the center by 12.exf6, or part with his precious king bishop.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qd4 O-O Qxe5 Re1 Be6 d4 Qf5 Bg5 Bd6
en: This is normally given a question mark, but the real error only comes nextmove.

line: e4 e5 f4 d5 exd5 e4 Nc3 Nf6 d3 Bb4 Bd2 e3 Bxe3 O-O Bd2 Bxc3 bxc3 Re8+ Be2 Bg4 c4 c6
en: Undermining the center, Black intends to force the development of his Queenside pieces.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 d6 g4 a6 Be3 Nge7 Nb3 b5 f4 Bb7 Qf3 g5 fxg5 Ne5
en: A comfortable square for the black knight. Black is in command.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nf6 h3 O-O Nc3 Nb4 Be2 dxc4
en: Finally Black feels it's safe, or necessary, to get rid of Pc4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 b5 Nxc6 Qxc6 O-O Bb7 a3 Nf6 Qe2 h5
en: This is unusual in most Sicilian Defense variations, but normal in this one. Black aligns bishops and queen to aim at Kg1 and then throws forward the king-side pawn and Nf6-g4 to add more pressure.

line: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Be6 Na3 Bxb3 Qxb3 Qd3 Qb5 O-O-O
en: There is an obvious weakness at f7, so I'd presume Gelfand has given this careful thought. If he can tactically support O-O-O then he'll have a clear advantage -- already.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3 fxe4
en: He falls for it. On the one hand the refutation is not trivial, in fact I had some trouble remembering it. However, I was still very surprised as it is something one should know if they are going to play the Pelikan.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Be2 h5 Bxg4 Bxg4
en: Remember that in last week's game black played 11...hxg4. The bishop recapture certainly appears more natural, however, and I think that you have to know this game to understand why someone would take with the pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2 Qxd2 O-O Be2 b6
en: This appears to be almost the only way for black to play. The idea is to play 12...bc and to gain the c6-square if white re-captures with the b-pawn. If white takes with the d-pawn, as in the game, then black gets a central majority.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7 Qe2 Rc7 Rd1 Nbd7 a4 bxa4
en: Only move. If 11... b4 12. Na2! a5 13. Nb5 with an almost winning position.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4 f4 Qe8
en: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit fans the world over know and love this move, preparing to swing the Queen up to h5 for the Kingside assault. But Stonewall fanatics are likely to say that they took out the patent first!

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4
en: No points for subtlety, but full marks for bravery.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4 c3 Nxd5 Ne4 Qh4 Ng3 Bg4 f3 e4 cxd4 Bd6
en: Black sacrifices material until it hurts. Play is now razor sharp on the king side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 c3 Nf6 d4 b5 Bb3 Be7 Be3 O-O Nbd2 d5
en: Boris plays his favourite move in the Ruy Lopez. The opening of the centre sharpens the game.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 e3 Nbd7 f3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bb3 e6 Nge2 Bb7 a3 a6 e4 Be7 Nf4 Qb6
en: (I didn't appreciate the full force of Whire's next move.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Kf2 f6 Be3 fxe5
en: (Against Paul McDonald in Section 'A' Alan played the alternative 11...Be7.).

line: Nf3 d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c5 Nxc4 Nc6 b3 Bf5 Bb2 Nf6 Rc1 e6 g3 Be7 Bg2 Qc7 O-O O-O d3 Rad8
en: The Black Rooks surely belong on c8 and d8, and his next move invites occupation of e5 with tempo.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 d4 g3 c5 b4 cxb4 a3 e6 Bg2 Nc6 O-O Nf6 Bb2 bxa3 Nxa3 Bc5 Ne1 e5 Nd3 Bd6
en: [Black makes the critical decision to allow the capture of the black-squared bishop. 11...Be7 would of course permit White to regain his pawn by 12.Bxc6+, but it would by no means clearly good to do so.].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 e4 d6 Nf3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Qe2 Nc6 d5 Na5 Bd3 c5 O-O a6 a4 b6 Bd2 Qc7
en: Intending 12...c4, winning the Bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Bc2 d5 e5 Nd7 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Be7 Nc3 a6 Be3 Nb6 Nd2 h5
en: I felt it was the only move to prevent WQ going to g4 or h5. It meant BQ side castling likely.

line: d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O Qc2 c5 d5 exd5 Ng5 h6 Nxd5 Bxd5 cxd5 Bd6
en: #I think this is new. 11...d6 was played in van der Stemen - Karner Tallin 1987 and 11...hxg5!? between Balashov - Tiviakov St. Petersburg 1993 which continued 12.d6 Nc6 13.dxe7 Qxe7 14.Bxg5 d5 but I didn't fancy ny two N's v 2 B's!

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7 Qc2 O-O Ne5 Nbd7 Ndf3 Ne4 Bf4 g5
en: Black accepts the challenge.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O Nd5 a5 a3 Bc5 Ng5 g6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Ne4 Qe7 b3 Ba7
en: Not letting the bishop be exchanged. Although it did not do much of anything in the actual game, some variations later proved this decision has been right.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 O-O O-O d6 d3 h6 Na4 Bb6 b3 Re8 Bb2 Bd7 e3 Bg4
en: This only allows white to move the h-pawn with tempo. The purpose of the move is rather unclear.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6 Qe7 O-O fxe6 Bg6+ Kd8 Bf4 b5 a4
en: White is able to open more files in front of the king.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4 h3 cxd4 cxd4 Bf5 Nfd2
en: Anand continues to play passively. More logical was 12 Nh4 and then 13 Nd2 to get rid of the e4-knight.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3 e5 h3 Be6 a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bb2 Nd7 Nbd2 O-O e3 f5 c4
en: With a little trick in mind: 13 Ng5! Bxg5 14 cxd5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 c6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7 O-O dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5 Bxe7 Qxe7 Rc1 Nxc3 Rxc3
en: Recapturing with the rook saves a tempo.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 Bb3 cxd4 exd4 Nc6 Nc3 Be7 Re1 O-O Bf4 Na5 d5
en: Wantonly giving up the weak pawn in order to open lines and create complications. Kasparov himself played 12.Bc2 against world #3 Anand in 1999.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Nf6 Qh4 Ke7 Ne5
en: The most ambitious decision. White sacrifices a pawn, noting that the enemy king is stranded in the center. Of course, 12.Bf4 Bb4+ 13.Bd2 (otherwise 13...g5) 13...Bxd2+ 14.Kxd2, hardly suits him.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O d5 c4 Nf6 cxd5 cxd5 exd5 exd5 Nc3 Be7 Qa4+
en: This is a very unpleasant check.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 g6 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 Bd3 Qa5 Ne2 cxd4 Bxd4
en: White's pieces are well developed and ready to attack the weakened Black kingside.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 Kf8 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nxc3 Bd3 b6 h4 Ba6 Rh3
en: Threatening 13.Rg3 g6 14.Bxg6 winning.

line: d4 d5 c4 c5 cxd5 Nf6 Nf3 cxd4 Qxd4 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 b4 e5 Qc4 Bxb4 Qxc8+ Ke7 Qxh8 Bxc3+ Bd2 Ne4 Rd1
en: White has defended all his weak points and is ready to start development - e3, Bd3 etc. Pay attention to the strong position of the queen on h8 - it holds black pieces of the queenside and doesn't let them to enter play.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3 Qg7 Bxf4
en: Black has two extra pieces, but he is far behind in developement and his King is very exposed.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8 Rad1 Ne4 Qe3
en: White would like to trade off the knight with 13. Nd2.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4 Bc2 Qe7 O-O
en: The rook will go to e1 to support the pawn move to e4.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8 O-O Nf8 h3 Be6 Rfc1
en: Moving the rook to the half-open file. White plans to place his other rook on b1 to support the pawn advance.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7 c3 Nc5 axb5
en: If 12... Nxb3 then 13. Qxb3 axb5 14. Rxa8 Bxa8 15. Qxb5 winning a pawn.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6
en: To make room for the knight on d5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O Qc4+ Kh8 Nd4
en: The knight is very well placed in this central square. It now threatens Ne6 forking the rook and queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ Nbd7 O-O-O
en: Threatening 13. Bxf6 gxf6 14. Bxd7+. Notice how all White's pieces are developed and working together.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4 Bb2 exd3 Qxd3 a6 h4
en: White begins an attack on the king.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5 O-O Bb7 Rc1
en: Rooks work best when not blocked by their own pawns.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4
en: Now if 12... Bxh4 then 13. gxf5 Nxf2 14. fxe6 fxe6 15. Nxh4 Qxh4 16. Rhe1 Nxd1 17. Qxe6+ Kd8 18. Qd6+ Kc8 19. Be6#.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8 Nc4 f6 a4
en: Threatening a5 trapping the bishop.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5 Bd7 e5
en: Without this follow up White's last move would simply be bad for it blocks his king bishop diagonal denies his knight d5 and leaves his e5 and d4 squares weak.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4 Nbd7 Qc2 Re8 Rd1 exd4 Nxd4 a5 e4 Nc5 f3
en: Often h2-h3 is used to guard g4, but in this case Pf3 defends Pe4 and guards g4. Later on it might advance further and Pg3 won't have been weakened. It's hard to say at this point whether it's especially better.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 e3 Nc6 d4 d5 cxd5 exd5 Bb5 Bd6 O-O O-O dxc5 Bxc5 h3 Bf5 b3 Qd7 Ne2
en: Is he aiming for Ne2-g3 to chase away Bf5 or Ne2-d4 to pressure Nc6?

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Na5 Qa4 b6 Nd5 Bd7 Qc2 c5 Nxf6+
en: Helping to uncover Bg7 can't be recommended.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Ne7 Qg4 O-O Bd3 f5 exf6 Rxf6 Bg5 Rf7 Qh5 g6 Qd1
en: Although he could have played 12. Qh4 I think he might have had it in mind to play h2-h4-h5xg6 to continue the attack on Kg8. In any event after Qd8 moves Black would have ...Ne7-f5, so Qd1 is safer.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Ne7 Re1 h6 h3 Ng6 Bd2
en: This is a modest move which leaves the bishop capable of moving to c3 to back up Pe5 or simply guarding square f4. One noticable key thing about the move is it doesn't weaken his queen-side the way the b2-b3, Bc1-b2 plan does.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Re8 d4 Bb7 Nbd2 Bf8 d5
en: White keeps the center closed and will willingly fight around the perimeter to keep Bf8, Re8 and Bb7 quiet.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O O-O b5 a3 Rb8 Kh1 a5 Bg5 h6 Bh4
en: This is certainly intersting and puts in question 7...O-O. How does Black continue on both wings when his king wouldn't be safe after ...g7-g5?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3 bxa3 d5 exd5
en: White naturally seeks simplifying exchanges now, and more open positions should be good for his bishops.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Bxc4 Nb6 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nb4 Be4 f5 exf6 exf6 Nc3 f5 Bb1 N4d5 Nf3
en: It doesn't look like any stodgy closed Queen's Gambit Declined!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 Bb7 O-O Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 Ne7 Bd2 Ng6 a4 b4 Nd5
en: Now he's combining both tactics (pressure on Pb4 and Nc3-d5) which might have the effect of overwhelming Black.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Qf3 Nbd7 Be2 h5 Bg5 Qa5 Bd2 Qb6 Nb3 Qc7 a4
en: This move is slightly effective. It prevents ...b7-b5, so that after ...b7-b6 Pa6 will still need a defender. It also indicates White won't be castling to the queen-side and if he goes king-side one has to ask, "Is Qf3 well placed?".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3 Na5 Bg5 Ne7 Nd5 f6 Bxf6
en: A risky decision. Against Steinitz our hero played the stronger move 12.Bf4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bc5 O-O O-O Nxe5 Re8 Nxc6 dxc6 Bc4 b5 Be2 Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 Bf3 Re6 c3
en: (?) It take few microseconds only to notice the enormous hole in d3. One of the usual moves that are played automatically and are severely punished.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 Bd2 Ne7 Nb5 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O c3 b6 f4 Ba6 Nf3 Qd7 a4 Nbc6 b4
en: Prevents ..Na5 and makes clearer the situation at the center. "It is surprising that a player like Nimzowitsch did not consider this move when he began his strategical plan with 8...b6." (Alekhine).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 d4 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 exd4 Nxd4 Bd7 O-O Be7 b3 O-O Bb2
en: Now White places his Bishop on the milky way. 12...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 c5 Ne2 Bd7 Nbc3 O-O-O Bf4 Bc6 O-O Nf6 f3
en: Thus White's majority in the centre is held for a long time to come. 12...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qd4 O-O Qxe5 Re1 Be6 d4 Qf5 Bg5 Bd6 g4
en: This is probably less effective than the simple 12.Qd2, when White has the same type of slight advantage. 12...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 Bb6 dxe5 Nge7 O-O O-O Ba3 h6 Nbd2 Re8 Nb3 Ng6 Bxf7+
en: A desperate decision, but one which all the same hase some very good points to it. 12...

line: b3 e5 Bb2 d6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 e3 Nc6 d3 O-O Nf3 h6 c4 Be6 O-O Qd7 d4 exd4 exd4 Bf5 a3
en: Prevents intrusion on b4.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 g6 a3 a5 Nf3 Bg7 d3 Nge7 Nd2 d6 Nf1 Be6 Ne3 O-O Ned5 Rb8 O-O
en: White is behind in development.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1
en: White's pawn structure is quite modest, but from that his pieces might spring forward. Only the pin on Nf3 is troublesome.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4 c5 Qd2 cxd4 Nxd4 h6 Bxf6 Nxf6 Qb4
en: White takes control of the queen-side dark squares and Qd8 now appears exposed on the open d-file (after O-O-O) , so ...Qd8-e7 seems sensible.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxc5 Qxc5 Kh1 b5 Qe1
en: White prepares e4-e5, Nc3-e4-d6+.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 b5 Nxc6 Qxc6 O-O Bb7 a3 Nf6 Qe2 h5 f4
en: I can't imagine why White would allow Nf6-g4 this way. To weaken the dark squares so seriously has to be very bad.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5 d5 e6 O-O O-O Nbc3 Na6 h3 exd5 exd5
en: White would like to cramp Black's pieces, but the one pawn at d5 can't do much damage by itself.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 c5 d5 b5 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Bb7 a4 Qa5+ Nbd2 Bxd5 axb5 Qd8 Ra4 Nxd2 Nxd2 d6 e4 Bb7 Qa1
en: There is no way to defend a7, so white has a big advantage after only 12 moves. Impressive, but now black digs in.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bb5 Bd7 O-O Bg7 d3 a6 Bxc6 Bxc6 Kh1 Qd7 Qe2 f5 Nd5 Rd8 Ng5
en: The knights are homing in on the weak e6 and b6 squares.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Be2 h5 Bxg4 hxg4 Qd2
en: 12.0-0 first is more common.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb6 O-O Be7 f4 g6 a3 a5 b3
en: I agree that this is a good move for more or less the same reasons as Brogan states in his notes.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 d6 Nxg4 Nf6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Nc3 c6 Qf3 Rg8 Qf2 Bg4 d3 Bh6 Ne2
en: White decides he would like to be a pawn ahead, but in doing so he spends precious time and fails to solve the problem of exactly how to develop. Furthermore, now if the c1-bishop ever moves the b2-pawn will hang.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4 Qa3
partai: Donald Byrne vs Robert James Fischer (1956)
en: On 12. Nxa4 Nxe4 and White faces considerable difficulties.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+
en: Charousek doesn't need to be asked twice.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Kh1
en: As advertised: White is preparing f4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Be2 a6 O-O Be7 Be3 Qc7 f4 O-O g4 Nc6 g5 Nd7 f5
en: Black meets great problems.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 c5 Rb1 Bg7 Nf3 O-O Be3 Qa5 Qd2 cxd4 cxd4 Qxd2+ Kxd2
en: (In this line White has to accept some risks. The king can be an attacking piece (Steinitz). The idea is to leave the King on the Queen side to help in the control of Black's Pawns.).

line: d4 d5 Nf3 f5 c4 Nf6 g3 e6 Bg2 Bb4+ Nc3 Nc6 O-O Bxc3 bxc3 dxc4 Qa4 h6 Ba3 Bd7 Qxc4 Ng4 Rae1
en: (I think this is a mistake. Instead Rfe1 looks healthier.)#.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7 Nbd2 g6 Bd3 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 d6 Bb2 Nbd7 c4 e5 Qc2 Re8 d5 Nc5 Be2
en: I felt 12.e4 was better. Black is unlikely to exchange the c5 knight for a Bishop with little future.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 c5 exd5 Qxd5 Ngf3 cxd4 Bc4 Qd6 O-O Nf6 Re1 a6 a4 Nc6 Qe2 Be7 Bb3 O-O Nc4
en: (Establishing a firm grip on the square e5, as well as attacking the Black Queen on d6.).

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5 g6 Qf3 f5 Qd5 Qe7 Nxc7+ Kd8 Nxa8 b6 d3 Bb7 h4
en: A one move threat which gains a little space.

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 e6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe1 c5 Be3 a6 dxc5 Qa5 Nd5 Qd8 Nb6
en: David threw in the towel to avoid further mutilation, as 12...Ra7 13.c6 Nxc6 14.c3 Ng4 15.Nxc8 Qxc8 16.Bxa7 Nxa7 17.Bb3!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 c4 h6 Nc3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 Qc7 O-O Nf6 f4 Bc5+ Kh1 O-O Qf3
en: The White pieces are beginning to take up good positions.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 d5 Qb6 Nc3 Qxb2 Nge2 a6 g3 d6 Bg2 Nbd7 O-O Be7 Rb1 Qa3 dxe6 fxe6 Bd2
en: With the idea of 13.Nf4 and played in preference to.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O Nf3 d6 O-O Nbd7 Nc3 e5 e4 c6 h3 exd4 Nxd4 Qb6 Nde2 Nc5 Be3
en: An active move, but it seems to be better to defend first the pawn b2, and to play Be3 thereafter.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O a3 Bxc3+ Qxc3 b6 Bg5 Ba6 e3 d6 Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 c5 O-O Rc8 Qb3
en: Recommended in 'Beating the Indian Defences'.

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 c3 f5 fxe5 dxe5 d4 exd4 Bc4 fxe4 Ne5 Qh4+ g3 Qf6 cxd4 Bb4+ Nc3 Ne7 Rf1
en: The moves order has to be precise or else black can get counterchances:.

line: c4 c6 e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 cxd5 d4 e6 Nf3 Bb4 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Qc7 Bd2 Nd7 Bd3 Bxc3 bxc3 N5f6 a4
en: Perhaps White anticipated ...b6 and thus planned creating tension on the queenside with a4-a5. However this move wastes time and allows Black to develop his pieces comfortably.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ndf6 Bc4 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Qxd2 Ne7 O-O-O O-O Rhg1
en: White prepares the adavnce of the g-pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 c5 O-O Nc6 Be3 Bg4 f3 Bd7 Rb1 Qc7
en: Rebel's book expected 12 ... Na5. Now the chessprogram had to think for the very first time.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4 h3 cxd4 cxd4 Bf5 Nfd2 Nf6
en: Preventing piece exchanges.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4 bxc4 Ne5 Qe2 Bb4 f4 Bxc3 Bxc3 Ne4
en: Threatening 13 ... Ng3, 13 ... Qh4+ and 13 ... Nxc3.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1 Nxd5 cxd5 Ne5
en: Nicely played by Rebel. Of course 13 exd4 wins a pawn, but after 13 ... Ng6 Black controls f4 and the White pawns are very weak.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 h6 b3 Ke8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5
en: Although this is the first novelty but again a normal move.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5 Be2 Bb7 Nbd2 Nbd7 Nb3 Bf8
en: Fritz just thought Kramnik had to play 13.Nbd2 now when it would merrily play 13...Bc5 Of course 13...Be7 was more sensible.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O e3 Ne4 Bxe7 Qxe7 cxd5 Nxc3 bxc3 exd5 Qb3 Rd8 c4 dxc4
en: Instead of this, the GM team of commentators were examining what looks like a forced queen exchange.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 c6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7 O-O dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5 Bxe7 Qxe7 Rc1 Nxc3 Rxc3 e5
en: With this, White must either exchange his pawn on d4 or isolate it.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O g6 b3 Bg7 Bb2 O-O Nc3 d5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Bxg7 Kxg7 cxd5 Qxd5 d4 cxd4
en: Black's last opportunity to avoid the endgame that occurs in the game is 12...Na6, when it is probably easier for Black to demonstrate equality.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O Kh1 Nbd7 a4 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3 Rc8
en: Has 12...Qb8!? 13.Qd2 Rc8 ever been tried?

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5 Nd5 f5
en: After 12...Qd6 13.Nf3 Bxb5 14.Nxe5 0-0-0 15.Rc1+ Kb8 16.Nd7+! Crunch!

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 g6 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 Bd3 Qa5 Ne2 cxd4 Bxd4 Nc5
en: Provoking the following piece sacrifice. More reliable was 12...Bd7 or 12...Nc6.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 Kf8 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nxc3 Bd3 b6 h4 Ba6 Rh3 h5
en: 12...Bxd3 is met strongly by 13.cxd3 Nd7 14.h5 (Idea 15.Rg3). However, after the text, the g5-square becomes weak and serves as a nice outpost for the White pieces.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3 Nc6 Bd2 d5
en: 12...Bd7 13.Kh1 also slightly favors White, while after; 12...a5 13.a4 Qb6 14.Qh4 White can prepare the usual assault.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4
en: Black's compensation for the sacrificed Exchange includes the capture of White's valuable e-pawn, play against White's fractured queenside pawn structure and good prospects for his minor pieces.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 d6 d4 Nbd7 Nc3 e5 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 O-O O-O d5 a5 Ne1 Nc5 Qc2 b6 Bg5 h6 Be3 Ng4
en: Georgy Lisitsyn was a very strong player, who wrote three excellent books - on the opening, middlegame, and endgame. I confidently played 12...Ng4, and was very surprised by the exchange of first one bishop for a knight, and then the other.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5 a4 Rb8 c3 d6 d4 Bb6 Na3 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Nxb5 O-O
en: One of the strangest tabyias of modern times. Black is a pawn down and is prepared to take on f3, strengthening White's centre and giving him the advantage of two Bishops.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Be7 d4 Na5 Be2 d6 Qa4+ c6 dxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf6 O-O b5 Qc2 O-O
en: Svidler chosed the line where White's chances, in my opinion, are obviously better.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 a3 f6 Bd3 Qc7 O-O O-O-O Re1 fxe5 dxe5 c4 Bc2 Bc5 Nbd2 Nh6
en: Looking closely not only to the pawn e5, but also to the square f2.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8 Rad1 Ne4 Qe3 f5
en: Now Black can meet 13. Nd2 with Ndf6.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8 O-O Nf8 h3 Be6 Rfc1 N6d7
en: Black hopes to simplify by exchanging bishops.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Qb6
en: Attacking the bishop and threatening 14... Bxe5.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 d4 c5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O Bc4 Nc6 O-O b6
en: The bishop is better placed on b7 then d7.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5 Rf1 a4 Nxd4 Bxd4
en: White should now play 13. Bd2 to help defend the dark squares on the queenside.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nbd7 Qe2 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5
en: Very bad since Black's queen bishop is now shut in. Better was 12... Bxd5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8 Nc4 f6 a4 c6
en: This gives the bishop an escape hatch, but it loses a pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Nc5 Be3 Be6 Kb1 Qc8 Nd4 Bd7
en: It might seem he could develop more actively by ...Be6-g4, but White's pawns would simply advance on light squares and chase it back, gaining time for the pawn assault on Kg8.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Nh6 h3 Nc6 dxe5 fxe5
