en: Black sees reason to allow a queen trade; especially when ...g5-g4 might still allow the king-side to open nicely for Black's pieces. The only cost is in leaving d5 to White.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 h5 Be2 Nbd7 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf5
en: It's unclear how well Bf5 coordinates with the other pieces in this position, but retaining the two bishops appeals to many players.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4 Nbd7 Qc2 Re8 Rd1 exd4 Nxd4 a5 e4 Nc5 f3 c6
en: Finally Shirov activates his queen at the cost of weakening Pd6. A lot of games have been won with the Black pieces from this opening and many have been tense dramatic struggles.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d6 Nf3 O-O Nc3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Rb8 Rb1 Na5 Qa4 b6 c5 Bd7 Qa3 Nc4
en: The knight would seem to be a little too far afield.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Re8 d4 Bb7 Nbd2 Bf8 d5 Nb8
en: Black generally retreats just for the moment and regroups with ...Nb8-d7 and ...c7-c6xd5; producing a position (for Black) which is much like a Sicilian Defense.

line: c4 c5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nc7 b3 e5 Bb2 Be7 Rc1 O-O Na4 Nd7 Nf3 f6 Qc2 Ne6 Nh4 Nb6
en: Not 12... Nd4 for 13. Bxd4 cxd4 14. Bd5+ Kh8 15. Qe4 with the threats 16.Bxb7 and, more important, 16. Ng6+ hxg6 17.Qh4+ mate.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8 Bg2 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6 O-O Ne7 Qc2 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Bxf6 gxf6 Ne4 Ng8
en: The best, maybe. The exchange 12...Bxe4 would have been favourable to White.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 Bc5 Bc4 Nf6 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O O-O Re1 Nf4 Ne4 Ne7
en: A useless Knight maneuver.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 d6 Bg5 Ne7 Nh4 c6 Bc4 Ne8 f4 Bxc3 bxc3 d5 Bb3 f6
en: Here it is! Raise a hand who would have made a different move!

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 exd5 exd5 Nf3 Bd6 Bd3 O-O O-O h6 Re1 Nc6 Nb5 Bb4 c3 Ba5 Na3 Bg4 Nc2 Qd7
en: 12...Re8 would have provided easy equality.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bc5 O-O O-O Nxe5 Re8 Nxc6 dxc6 Bc4 b5 Be2 Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 Bf3 Re6 c3 Qd3
en: (!) The hole is immediately filled...

line: c4 e6 e3 Nf6 Nf3 b6 Be2 Bb7 O-O d5 d4 Bd6 Nc3 O-O b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Qe7 Nb5 Ne4 Nxd6 cxd6 Nd2 Ndf6
en: "This waste of time gives me the opportunity to prepare tha attack which will follow." (Zukertort).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Nf3 b6 Bg5 Bxc3+ bxc3 Bb7 e3 d6 Bd3 Nbd7 O-O Qe7 Nd2 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 O-O-O
en: Now we can imagine our Mario putting his wrist watch on the table, taking his jacket off (even if it was not so polite at that time) and prepare himself to his best fist fight in his lifetime.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Be7 O-O Nc6 Re1 Bg4 c3 f5 Qb3 O-O Bf4 Bxf3 gxf3 Ng5
en: The present Black's aggressive position is a direct consequence of White's 10th move.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 d4 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 exd4 Nxd4 Bd7 O-O Be7 b3 O-O Bb2 b5
en: Interesting. Black threatens to win the exchange forcing the Knights to be removed and putting the Queen in e2 and the Rook in f1 with the Bishop in b5: 13...c5 14. Nf3 b4 Nd1 15.Bb5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 Be6 Bxe6 fxe6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Ne7 Bg5 Nc6 Bxd8 Nxd4 O-O-O Nb5
en: Here Steinitz shows poor judgment, since he will be left with a doubled, isolated "b" pawn and a weak "d" pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Qh4 Nb5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qxe4+ Be2 Kd8 O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 Nf6 N1c3 Qe5 Rfe1 a6 Na3 Qd4
en: 12...b5, blocking out the opponent's a-knight, was tempting, but would have been thoroughly unsound, e.g., 12...b5 13.Bf3 Qc5 (best) 14.b4 Qb6 (best) 15.Qg5 Rg8 16.Nd5 and wins.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6 Bxg6+ hxg6
en: The open rook file is bound to benefit Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qd4 O-O Qxe5 Re1 Be6 d4 Qf5 Bg5 Bd6 g4 Qg6
en: A serious error. After 12...Qd5 or 12...Qb5 White has no forcing continuation, and the weakening of his kingside resulting from the move g4 improves Black's long-term chances for counterplay.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bb4 e3 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 f3 c4 Ne2 Nc6 g4 h6 Bg2 Na5 O-O Nb3
en: The black knight is well posted.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Ne7 O-O Nbc6 c3 Ne5 f4 Nxd3 Qxd3 Qc7 Be3 Nc6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7
en: Black is behind in development.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8
en: It appears Black might want to play ...e6-e5 to secure control of d4 and f4, but he might also have in mind to play ...Bd6-f8 to keep the bishop on the board.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Qa5+ Bd2 Bb4
en: This is an interesting move which I've only seen recently. It essentially forces a weakening of White's queen-side pawn structure. In times past Black used to play ...Qa5-c7 and possibly aim for a bishop trade by ...Bf8-d6-f4xd2.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 Ne7 f4 c5 h4 h5 f5 exf5 g5 Nec6 Bg2 cxd4 Nxd5 Nd7
en: Black intends to get rid of Pe5 before it can be supported at e6, so White has to get rid of Pd4 to keep material equality or White can gambit Pe5, knowing the open e-file will be of use: 13. O-O Ndxe5 (keeping Pd4 defended) 14. Nef4.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4 c5 Qd2 cxd4 Nxd4 h6 Bxf6 Nxf6 Qb4 Nd5
en: I'm not so certain the knight is better here. It blocks the d-file and chases Qb4, but it also loses contact with d7, where it was useful preventing difficulties on the a4-e8 diagonal.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 Bg7 c3 f5 Bd3 Ne7
en: After Ne7 it appears Black might prefer ...Bc8-b7, as is played in many Sicilian Defense games, to cut through the center of the board and to aim at Pg2, where White's king might soon reside.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O e5 c3 g5 d4 g4 Nfd2 cxd4 cxd4 exd4 Nc4 c5 Re1 Be6 Nba3 Be7
en: Developing this piece to this square is usually normal, but in this case it's very strange. It helps keep the e-file blocked, but how are the king-side pieces to be developed and used? I'm not certain what Black's plan might be.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Ng8 f4 f6 Bd4 Qa5 Qd2 fxe5 fxe5 c5
en: Black greedily chases Bd4, so he can capture Pe5 without offering a bishop trade, but he also weakens b5 & d5 which should give White some opportunities.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Be2 Be7 a4 Nc6 O-O O-O f4 Qc7 Kh1 Re8 Bf3 Bf8
en: Black doesn't fear White's plan and plans the counter strike ...e6-e5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5 d5 e6 O-O O-O Nbc3 Na6 h3 exd5 exd5 Nc4
en: Though this is a square which is nearly always in White's hands it is easily utilized by Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 b5 Bc2 d6 d4 Bb6 a4 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 Qxa8 h3 Bh5
en: This is bound to get Black into trouble. What's wrong with the simple exchanges?

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 Nc3 g6 e4 Bg7 Be2 O-O O-O Na6 Nd2 Re8 f3 Nc7 a4 b6
en: This might seem inconsistent with what I said earlier about ...b5, but black isn't changing his plans. Rather, he is just going to play ...Ba6 and exchange it off for something first.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6 d5 Ne7 b4 a5 bxa5 Rxa5 a4 Nd7 Ba3 Bh6
en: This seems like a good plan. First of all it prepares ...f5. The other point is that on Nd2 he can take it now. I realized this, but I was lured to play it anyway because I saw a pretty tactic that would be nice to get on the board!

line: e4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 d4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bd3 Nc6 Bf4 f6 Qe2 fxe5 Nxe5 Ndxe5 Bxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 O-O
en: He doesn't want to play the endgame either. Good.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 c6 a3 h6 Bf4 a6 h3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Ba2 Bb7
en: (12... c5 is less good because of 13. d5).

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7 Qe2 Rc7 Rd1 Nbd7 a4 bxa4 Nxa4 Bb7
en: If 12... Be7 13. Bd2 e5 14. Nf5 g6 15. Nxe7 Qxe7 16. Bb4 Rc6 17. Qd2 Nc5 18. Nxc5 dxc5 19. Ba5 O-O 20. Ra3! Bb7 21. Rd3 Rcc8 22. Bd8! Rcxd8 only move when 23. Rxd8 Rxd8 24. Qxd8 Qxd8 25. Rxd8 + Kg7 26. Rd6!+- is a sample variation.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 d5 exd5 cxd5 d6 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Re8 Qc2 Na6 Bf4 Nb4 Qb1 Nxe4
en: It was not possible to play 12...Nfd5 due to 13. exd Bc3 14. bxc Re2 15. cxb.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 Bxc3 bxc3 d6 Bg5 Qe7 Qd2 Nd8 Bc4 Be6 Bb3 Bxb3 axb3 Ne6
en: The mobility of this knight, which always aims to occupy f4, is the greatest obstacle for white.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 f5 d4 e4 Ng5 Bb4 Nh3 Nf6 e3 Bxc3+ bxc3 d6 Nf4 O-O h4 Qe7 c5 Nd8 Qb3+ Ne6
en: Possibly it's odd that black wants to get rid of his knight in a situation favorable to knights. But he's willing to get rid of one of his knights for the only active white bishop, the (soon to be) c4 bishop.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Re1 Nf8
en: Shapiro hunkers down to defend. Najdorf decides he'd like more open diagonals, thank-you-very-much.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4 f4 Qe8 g3 Qh5
en: Experienced players know enough to find this concentration of force on the Kingside rather alarming. True, there is no instant mate. But Najdorf shows his tactical mastery in making the most of his pieces' firepower.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+ Kf8
en: But now, how to meet the threats at h2 and f2?

line: c4 e6 g3 d5 Bg2 Nf6 Nf3 Be7 O-O O-O d4 c6 Qc2 b6 b3 Bb7 Bb2 Na6 Rd1 Qc8 e3 c5 Qe2 dxc4
en: Black brings life to a dull game.

line: d4 h6 e4 d6 Nc3 a6 f4 b5 Nf3 Bb7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 dxc5 b3 g5 fxg5 Bg7 Bb2 hxg5 Nxg5 Nd7 Qf3 Bf6
en: (To forestall 0-0-0 and tell Ktg5 not to be too optimistic about f7.).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 Bxf7 Nf6 Be6 Qb8
en: (White's Bishop imposes a blockade as well as driving away the Queen. 12...Nd7 would invite 13.0-0 with Rd1 to follow.).

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7 Nbd2 g6 Bd3 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 d6 Bb2 Nbd7 c4 e5 Qc2 Re8 d5 Nc5 Be2 Bc8
en: The Bishop threatens to come to f5.

line: e4 e6 c4 d5 exd5 exd5 Qb3 d4 c5 Bxc5 Bc4 Qe7+ Kd1 Nf6 Nf3 O-O Re1 Qd6 Ng5 Qxh2 Bxf7+ Kh8 Be8 h6
en: 12...Nxe8 and 12...Rxe8 are inferior.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 cxd5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qd1 exd5 Qxd5 Bd7 Nf3 Nf6 Qd1 Bc5 e3 Qc7 Be2 O-O-O O-O g5
en: # Ouch!! Clearly taking on g5 gives Black a gory g file attack.

line: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 c4 Bc2 b5 Ndf3 Nc6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nxe5 fxe5 Nd7 Nh3 Qc7 Qf3 f6
en: Weakening the King side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 d5 Nce7 Qe2 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 c4 c5 O-O g6 Bd2 a5 Nc3 h6 Qd1 Nc8
en: The start of some complicated (To me!) and patient manoevring. The Knight has access to better squares from d7 than from a7.

line: Nf3 Nf6 g3 b5 Bg2 Bb7 O-O e6 b3 Bd6 d4 O-O Na3 a6 c4 bxc4 Nxc4 Bb4 Bb2 d5 a3 dxc4 axb4 cxb3
en: Don't underestimate that pawn.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6
en: The Bishop is driven back but it may still be a sacrificial force to be reckoned with if there is a build up against h3.

line: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3 g6 d4 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bd3 O-O Ng5 c5 Nxh7 Kxh7 Qh5+ Kg8 Qh4 c4 Be2 f5
en: A desperate attempt to create space. I need to be able to move around the blocked centre if I am to defend against White's kingside pawns.

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4 Be3 Qf6 Qg3 e5 O-O-O Nd7 Bc4 Nh6 Rhf1 Qg6
en: This time I will oblige Black with the Queen swop, and then hack away the remnants of the defence.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ng5 d6 d4 h6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Bc4+ Kg7 Bxf4 Be7 O-O Bxh4 Qd2 a6
en: [This move is slow and White will be able to build some initiative before Black's play on the queenside can become dangerous. I think Black's development should have been taking priority.].

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 g6 Bxc4 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Nfd7 Qe2 Nb6 Bb3 Nc6 Rd1 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qe8
en: This move has the goal of blasting open the center. After the king moves to the h-file Black can advance both e- and f-pawns.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3 O-O O-O d6 h3 Bb7 Rd1 Re8 a4 b4 a5 Qb8
en: In retrospect, this is an error. The simple 12...Qe7 would have given Black an equal game.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 Nf3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb4 Bb5+ N8c6 d4 cxd4 a3 dxc3 Qxd8+ Kxd8 axb4 Nxb4 Ke2 c2 Ra4 a5
en: Black still does not see how dangerous his position is. Here 12...e5 was already obligatory. In that case white would have still kept his advantage but black's chances would have been much better.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 c5 O-O Nc6 Be3 Bg4 f3 Bd7 Rb1 Qc7 Nf4
en: Also after a longer think Rebel sticks to this logical move. White tries to take advantage of the unusual c7-square for the Black queen by means of Nf4-d5.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4 h3 cxd4 cxd4 Bf5 Nfd2 Nf6 Nc3
en: Now the black c6-knights enters the White position. It was possible to play 13 a3 to prevent this.

line: d4 d6 e4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 f4 c6 Nf3 Bg4 Be3 Nd7 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 O-O-O d5 g4 Ne7 h4 b5 h5 b4 h6
en: This isn't good. White should open the king's side, not close it. The normal move was 13 Ne2, with an interesting fight coming up.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 h5 Bh7 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Be7 O-O-O O-O Ne5
en: With the idea of f4, Ne4 and g4 to start an attack on the Black king.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 c6 e3 Nf6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Bd6 Nf3 O-O Bd3 Qe7 O-O e5 Be2 e4 Nd2 a6 cxd5 cxd5 b4
en: Maybe Bareev worried about an attack on the kingside. It does not justify the sacrifice sufficiently.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5 Be2 Bb7 Nbd2 Nbd7 Nb3 Bf8 a4
en: With the Black rook on h8 a long way from the action its time to attack the weak queenside pawns.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nxc6 Qf6 Qd2 dxc6 Nc3 Ne7 Qf4 Be6 Qxf6 gxf6 Na4 Bb4+ c3 Bd6 Be3 b6 f4
en: White grabs some more space on the kingside and anticipates Black's f5 pawn advance.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 Bb4+ Bd2 Be7 Bg2 c6 Bc3 d5 Ne5 Nfd7 Nxd7 Nxd7 Nd2 O-O O-O Rc8 a4
en: Black's next move prepares to hit the d4-pawn with ...c5.

line: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Be2 O-O O-O c5 d5 Na6 Re1 Nc7 Bf4 b6 Qd2 Re8 a4 Bb7 Bc4 a6 Ra3
en: A rook manoeuvre restricts the queenside.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 O-O Bg7 Nbd2 O-O Re1 Re8 d4 Bd7 d5 Ne7 Bxd7 Nxd7 a4 h6 a5
en: A positionally justified advance of the a-pawn.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O g6 b3 Bg7 Bb2 O-O Nc3 d5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Bxg7 Kxg7 cxd5 Qxd5 d4 cxd4 Qxd4+
en: Less effective is 13.Nh4 Qd7 14.Bxb7 Qxb7 15.Qxd4+ Kg8 16.Rfd1 Nc6 17.Qd7 (17.Qe4 Rfd8 18.Nf3 0.5-0.5 Sanguinetti-Panno, Buenos Aires 1977) 17...Qxd7 18.Rxd7 Rfd8 0.5-0.5 Tal-Salov, Brussels 1988. In both cases Black equalized.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6 e3 a6 b4 b5 cxb5 axb5 Bb2 Na7 h4
en: Exploiting the misplaced "Queen's Indian bishop. ".

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O d5 c4 Nf6 cxd5 cxd5 exd5 exd5 Nc3 Be7 Qa4+ Qd7 Re1
en: Very simple - pinning the bishop on e7. If 13.Bb5 axb5 14.Qxa8 0-0, when Black can continue with Bc8-b7, and d5-d4, when Black is better developed with a strong passed d-pawn, and the White queen is out of play.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5 Nd5 f5 Qe2
en: Tempting is 13.Nxe7 fxe4 14.Nf5! yet I saw that after 14...Bf6 15.Nd6+ Ke7 16.Bxd7 Kxd6 17.0-0-0+ Ke7 18.Bf5 Nd3+ would give Tal some chances.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 c3
en: Necessary - now White's cluster of minor pieces on the central files have a loose feel to them.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Ne2
en: Passive. Probably better is 13.c4. Note that 13.f5 e5 14.Ne2 Qc7 is promising for Black. After 13.Bxe4 Bxe4 14.Nf3 Be7 15.Nd2 Bb7, I would be very happy, as my bishop is even stronger here than in the main line.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5 a4 Rb8 c3 d6 d4 Bb6 Na3 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Nxb5 O-O Re1
en: This position saw also 13.Bc2 and 13.Be3, but Black is doing relatively fine there.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3 Qg7 Bxf4 Nf6 Ne4
en: White must strike while the iron is hot. The text starts on attack against Blackâs knight, which covers his King. Black cannot play 13...Nxe4 because 14. Be5 or Bh6 dis. + wins the Queen.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4 Bc2 Qe7 O-O a6 Rfe1
en: White now threatens 14. e4 dxe4 15. Bxe4 with an overwhelming position. The pin of the knight prevents 15... Nxe4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4 Qc7 e5 Nd5 exd6 Bxd6 Ne4
en: If 13... Be7 then 14. c4 Nf6 15. Bf4. If 13... cxd4 then 14. Nxd6 Qxd6 15. c4 Nf6 16. Bf4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6 a3 h6 Bh4 Re8 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Ba2
en: From here the bishop can move to b1 supporting the queen in the attack on the king.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8 O-O Nf8 h3 Be6 Rfc1 N6d7 Bf4
en: White prefers not to exchange.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6 cxd6 Nd5
en: If 13... Qd8 then 14. Nxf4 exf4 15. e5 winning back the knight with a crushing attack.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3 Be7 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Qd2
en: If Black plays passively, White will gain a huge advantage by castling queenside and using the open g file for an attack.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O Qc4+ Kh8 Nd4 Qd7 Rad1
en: Another developing move that reinforces White's hold on the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Qe7 O-O Qe5 f4 dxc3+ Kh1 cxb2 Bxf7+ Kd8 fxe5 bxa1=Q Bxg8 Be7 Qb3
en: Threatening 14. Bb2 trapping the queen. Black should try 13... Qxe5 leading to unclear complications.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4 Bc2 a6 Qf3
en: Bringing the queen into the attack.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Qb6 Nc3
en: White is delighted to sacrifice the pawn for the attack.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6 Nd2 Nd7 c4 b6 b4 f6 Nxc6 Nxc6 cxd5
en: If 13... Ne7 then 14. dxe6 and Black's rook and knight are both attacked.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5 O-O Bb7 Rc1 Re8 Ne5
en: Centralizing the knight and putting pressure on the Black king.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5
en: Chasing away the knight so that White can play Ne5.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5 Rf1 a4 Nxd4 Bxd4 Bxf6
en: Instead he begins an attack on the kingside.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4 O-O b3 Rfe8 Bb2 Bf8 Rad1
en: Developing the rook to the center. 14. e5 is now threatened becuase 14... dxe5 would be met by 15. Qxd7 Nxd7 16. Rxd7. If 14... Rxe5 then the same thing would happen after 15. Rxe5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Re8 Bc4 Nb6 Bd3 Be6 Ng5 Bxg5 Bxg5
en: Now White has f4 for his queen, so ...f6 might be good, though it's not like Karpov to voluntarily weaken his king's position even for a useful tempo.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 g6 Be3 Bg7 Qf3 O-O Rad1 Nbd7 Bf2
en: I'm not certain where she thinks the bishop will be better placed, but it's difficult to marshall the forces better before making a committing move such as f4-f5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d6 Nf3 O-O Nc3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Rb8 Rb1 Na5 Qa4 b6 c5 Bd7 Qa3 Nc4 Qxa6
en: But, perhaps the same can be said of White's queen! If she had just retreated the game would be interesting, but now it's a walk on a razor's edge.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1 d6 e4 Nbd7 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Rb8 b3 a6 Bb2 O-O h3
en: It might appear that Bb2 is going to play a big part in a king-side advance, but White has to be careful to not expose Kg1 too much by making rash pawn moves.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Qc2 g6 cxd5 cxd5 Nc3 Bg7 Bf4 Nc6 e3 O-O Be2 Ne4 O-O Bf5 Nh4 Nxc3 Qxc3 Be4 Nf3
en: Ivanchuk didn't seem to be in an adventurous mood, but I like that he achieved a draw without the histrionics he sometimes displays.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nc3 b4 Nd5 Na5 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Ba2
en: White's Pe4 is under assault, so it's difficult for him to consider d3-d4. However, White has the two bishops, so at some point he'll want (or need) open lines and seek out targets.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O O-O b5 a3 Rb8 Kh1 a5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Be6 Nd5
en: How else could White proceed?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O a3 Nc6 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3
en: White has gotten rid of Ne4, but Black has Qd5 and no significant cramp. His pieces can maneuver freely.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Be3 Qc7 Ne5 a6 Qa4+ Nd7 O-O-O cxd4 Nxd7 Qxd7 Qc2
en: This is an interesting move since he could have immediately captured Pd4, allowing a queen trade. He could have also used 13. Qb3 to keep an eye on Pb7 and square d5 (though that doesn't necessarily prevent 13...Qd5) .

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Ne7 h3 Ng6 Bg5+ Ke8 Rad1 Be7 Bxe7
en: This seems to end Black's cramp and White's chances to play for a win. But, perhaps I'm overestimating it's importance. White still has the king-side pawn majority and safer king.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 e6 Be3 Nc6 Qd2 Be7 g4 O-O O-O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 b5 a3 Nd7 h4
en: White would be happy to give Ph4 to open the h-file for Rh1 (and possibly Qh2) to attack Ph7 and Kg8.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 Nf6 Re1 O-O d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 e5 Ne4 Nc3 Bf5 Nh4 Be6 Bxc6 bxc6 Na4
en: Ne4 has no easy way out. White threatens f2-f3xe4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nbd2 Bf8 c3 Na5 Ba2 c5 d4
en: The glass shatters and White simply steps over it. He says there never was a "bind" or pressure.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4 Re8 Kh1 Nbd7 Qe2 g6 Bd2 Bf8 Rad1
en: Mysterious? No, he expects ...Bf8-g7, so Pd6 would be the big weakness. Of course this will leave Black wondering what to do with Bf8.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 Re1 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 d3 Bb7 e4 O-O d4 cxd4 Nxd4 d6 b3
en: White quickly moves everything off the f6-a1 diagonal, so now Black will have to open the position up.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Qf3 Nbd7 Be2 h5 Bg5 Qa5 Bd2 Qb6 Nb3 Qc7 a4 b6 Bg5
en: In many instances this freezes Nd7 as defender of Nf6. But, Black could spend a tempo on ...Bf8-e7 to take over that duty.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 e6 Bb3 Be7 O-O O-O c3 Nc6 Re1 b5 Nbd2 d5 e5 Nd7 d4 Ba6 Nf1 b4 Ba4
en: This is certainly an odd utilization of the bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 f4 Be7 Be3 O-O g4 d5 e5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 g5 Qb6 Nf5
en: If Rb1 or Qc1, ..Bc5 is awkward. As for 0-0? It looks as if Black can simply take on b2 safely as there's no real attack or threat from White.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qc7 Qg4 Kf8 O-O c5 dxc5
en: New - but not a novelty. 13 Re1 and 13 c3 is more standard. The idea is, at the cost of the White pawn structure, to open as many lines as possible to try and take advantage of Black's underdevelopment.

line: c4 c5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nc7 b3 e5 Bb2 Be7 Rc1 O-O Na4 Nd7 Nf3 f6 Qc2 Ne6 Nh4 Nb6 Nf5
en: Not wasting time in the Knight exchange. Flohr wants to have a clear edge in the middlegame and is not afraid of doubling the a-file pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 d4 Qh4+ Ke2 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Bxf4 O-O-O Ke3 Qh5 Be2 Qa5 a3 Bxf3 Kxf3 Qh5+ Ke3 Qh4 b4
en: While tenaciously chesing the black queen Steinitz prepares an attack against his opponent's king.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 dxc4 e4 Bb4 Bg5 c5 e5 cxd4 Qa4+ Nc6 O-O-O Bd7 Ne4 Be7 exf6 gxf6 Bh4 Nb4 Qxb4
en: Aaah! What is that? A shot on Grunfeld's head.

line: e4 c5 Ne2 Nf6 Nbc3 Nc6 g3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 O-O Be7 Rb1 O-O c4 Qd7 Bb2 b6 d4 Bb7 d5
en: This pawn is annoying (for Black).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Nf3 b6 Bg5 Bxc3+ bxc3 Bb7 e3 d6 Bd3 Nbd7 O-O Qe7 Nd2 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 O-O-O a4
en: White begins a counterplay on the queenside.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5 Na5 Bb2 Ne7 Bd3 O-O Nc3 Ng6 Ne2
en: After the violent initial skirmishes, the play is now characterised by subtle manoeuvres. This "positional" aspect of the Evans Gambit shows its wide resources. 13...

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8 Ng3
en: So, this is the idea behind Nd2-e4. Black has to either retreat and give up on the pin on Nf3 or give up one of the bishops for a knight. He could trade off Bd6 (13...Bxg3 14. fxg3) or Bh5 (13...Bxf3 14. Qxf3) .

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4 c5 Qd2 cxd4 Nxd4 h6 Bxf6 Nxf6 Qb4 Nd5 Qa3
en: Black already has some difficulties.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O h6 Be3 Nxd4 Bxd4 b5 f3 Qa5 a3 Be7 Kb1
en: This could be an indication White has no advantage, but Anand is a patient person who doesn't feel he has to constantly be at the opponent's throat to have a chance to win.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 O-O Kh1 Qc7 a4 Nc6 Be3 Re8 Bf3 Rb8 Qd2
en: This isn't the best location for the queen, though it could go to f2. He seems to be begging Black to invade on the c-file!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 a6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Qc7 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxf6 gxf6 Qg4 Kf8 Kh1 h5 Qh4
en: To this point it looks like White's efforts might bear fruit because all the play will be focused on the king-side. But, Black has yet to bring all his pieces into play.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 c5 d5 b5 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Bb7 a4 Qa5+ Nbd2 Bxd5 axb5 Qd8 Ra4 Nxd2 Nxd2 d6 e4 Bb7 Qa1 e5 Bg5
en: A very nice shot, but 13. Be3 was also strong, when there remains nothing for black to do to avoid 14. Rxa7.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 e3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 d4 cxd4 exd4 Be7 Bd3 Nc6 O-O O-O Re1 Nf6 a3 b6 Bc2 Bb7 Qd3
en: The thematic plan. White intends Bg5, which threatens Bxf6 and would force a weakness.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb6 O-O Be7 f4 g6 a3 a5 b3 Bd7 g4
en: This looks OK to me. True, white will have to be patient before a direct assault with f4-f5 is going to work. However, this stakes out some space and prevents ...h5, so I don't see a problem.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 c6 a3 h6 Bf4 a6 h3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Ba2 Bb7 O-O
en: (13. b4 allows counterplay with 13... a5).

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O b5 Bf3 Ra7 Qe2 Rc7 Rd1 Nbd7 a4 bxa4 Nxa4 Bb7 e5
en: This guarantees White a great positional superiority. 13... dxe5 14. Bxb7 exd4 (14... Rxb7 15. Qxa6 clear plus for White.. Bxa6 Black faces great difficulties.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Re1 Nf8 Rxe6
en: And yes, he'd like fries with that. Crispy french-fried Black pieces, please!

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+ Kf8 Bf4
en: The only move! Charousek displays not only great attacking elan but also defensive savvy here. Consider the alternative: 13.h3 Nxf2 Now it is Black who has the attack, with a sacrifice on h3 threatened (in addition to the obvious ..Nxd1).

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4 Nf3 Qxd5 Be2 Nc6 c4 Qh5 d5 Ne5 Nbd2 O-O-O O-O e6 Qa4 Bd6 h3 Bxh3 gxh3 Qxh3 Qxa7
en: Too greedy. Rather 13. Nxe5 Bxe5 14. Nf3 Ng4!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Be3 c5 Qd2 O-O Rc1 Qa5 Nf3 e6 d5 exd5 exd5 Re8 Be2
en: Time: White: 0:53 Black: 0:24. Valvo observed GK tapping his fingers impatiently on the table after move Re8. It just might all be preparations! Both are sitting deeply concentrated at the table.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nc3 d5 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Qc8 Bg5 Qe6 Rc1 c5 Nd3 cxd4 Bxf6
en: Korchnoi collapses completely.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 c5 Rb1 Bg7 Nf3 O-O Be3 Qa5 Qd2 cxd4 cxd4 Qxd2+ Kxd2 Rd8 d5
en: (The first step of White's strategical plan: the creation of a pawn wedge.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 Nc3 Nf6 Nd5 Nxe4 Qe2 Bxf2+ Kd1 f5 d3 Nd4 Nxd4 Bxd4 dxe4 f4 c3 c6 cxd4 cxd5 Qh5+
en: (Black's King is very exposed.).

line: Nf3 d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c5 Nxc4 Nc6 b3 Bf5 Bb2 Nf6 Rc1 e6 g3 Be7 Bg2 Qc7 O-O O-O d3 Rad8 Rc2 Rd7 Qa1
en: # The authentic Reti formation - see for example the classic Reti - Rubinstein, Karlsbad 1923. But my favourite example, indeed my all time favourite game is Larsen - Geller, Copenhagen 1960, culminating in the wonderful move Qa1-h8!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 d5 Nce7 Qe2 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 c4 c5 O-O g6 Bd2 a5 Nc3 h6 Qd1 Nc8 Qa4
en: I don't know why an exchange of Queens seemed good at this point.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5 g6 Qf3 f5 Qd5 Qe7 Nxc7+ Kd8 Nxa8 b6 d3 Bb7 h4 f4 Qf3
en: White has to retreat otherwise the Queen is lost after 13...Na5.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6 Ne5
en: A probing move, eyeing c6.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ng5 d6 d4 h6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Bc4+ Kg7 Bxf4 Be7 O-O Bxh4 Qd2 a6 g3
en: [This was played to allow White's rooks to double up on the f-file. Control of this file is the most important feature of the game. All White's efforts are aimed at this goal.].

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 Nbd2 f6 exf6 Nxf6 g3 Bg4 a3 Qe7 Bg2 d3 e3 Nd4 O-O Ne2+ Kh1 O-O-O Qa4
en: 13 b4 was played in the above mentioned game (if 13 h3 h5! )I'm now on my own!

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 g6 Bxc4 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Nfd7 Qe2 Nb6 Bb3 Nc6 Rd1 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qe8 Nb5
en: Gligoric improved against me a week or two later with 13. Ne4!, with the threat of Nc5. Serves me right for getting the game published in the New York Times!

line: e4 c5 Nc3 e6 Nge2 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Be3 Nf6 g4 h5 g5 Ng4 Bc1 Qb6 h3 Ne5 Be2 g6 Nb3 Nbc6 f4
en: This exposes the entire kingside and commits White to a do or die battle.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3 O-O O-O d6 h3 Bb7 Rd1 Re8 a4 b4 a5 Qb8 d4
en: This is a deliberate sacrifice. I saw the Black forces huddled on the queenside and felt that a pawn could safely be invested for good attacking chances.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O Nd5 a5 a3 Bc5 Ng5 g6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Ne4 Qe7 b3 Ba7 Bb2 d6 Ng3
en: A pure waiting move. Black does not want to make any decisive moves before white has castled. Early pawn moves on the king side could prove verydangerous indeed, should white later decide to castle long.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bc4 Bd6 Qe2+ Kf8 O-O Nbd7 d4 Nb6 Bb3 Nbxd5 c4 Ne3 Bxe3 fxe3 Qxe3 c5 Nc3
en: I did not like 13.d5 because of the following line:.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 c6 Bc4 Bf5 Bd2 e6 Bb3 Bb4 O-O O-O Ne5 Nbd7 a3 Bxc3 Bxc3 Qc7 Nxd7
en: Morozevich doesn't avoid simplifications. But he invents a rather sharp plan...

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nf6 Ne5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Qa5+ c3 Qa6 Ne4
en: This seems to be a novelty.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 O-O Bc4 Bd7 Bb3 Rc8 O-O-O Ne5 Kb1 Re8 h4
en: A typical for Dragon very sharp situation is arisen - the kings are castled to the opposite sides and both players are trying to organise an attack. At first sight White is coming quicker but Black has a lot of counter recourses.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 b4 d3 d6 a5 Be6 Nbd2 Bxb3 Nxb3 Re8 h3
en: This modest move is a novelty.

line: d3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c4 Nf6 a3 d6 Nc3 Be7 g3 O-O Bg2 Be6 O-O Qd7 Ng5 Bf5 e4 Bg4 f3 Bh5 Nh3 Nd4 Nf2 h6
en: A cautious, but probably wise, decision giving the bishop an escape square in case Kasparov does attempt a pawn storm.

line: c4 c6 Nf3 d5 b3 Bg4 Bb2 Nd7 e3 Ngf6 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 Nc3 dxc4 bxc4 Ne5 Qe2 Bb4 f4 Bxc3 Bxc3 Ne4 O-O-O Ng3
en: This is wrong. Rebel needs a few minutes on the AMD K6 450 MHz to find the right move: 13 ... Nxc3! 14 dxc3 Nd7, followed by 15 ... Qe7 and 16 ... Nc5 with advantage to Black.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Ne5 Qc8
en: Rebel expected 13 ... Qd8 14 Rd1.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 h6 b3 Ke8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5 a4 h5
en: Nigel Short asked Vlad about this - he did not want to answer in detail. It just does not matter if you lose a tempo in this line hesaid.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O d5 c4 Nf6 cxd5 cxd5 exd5 exd5 Nc3 Be7 Qa4+ Qd7 Re1 Qxa4
en: If 13...d4 14.Nb5 0-0 15.Qxd4 axb5 16.Qxd7 Bxd7 17.Rxe7, or 13...0-0? 14.Qxd7 Bxd7 15.Rxe7 and White is winning.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O Kh1 Nbd7 a4 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3 Rc8 Qd2 Qc7
en: 13...h6 is a feasible alternative.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5 Nd5 f5 Qe2 Qd6
en: If 13...Bxb5 14.Qxb5+ Qd7 15.Nc7+ wins.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5 Bxb5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qa5+ Nfd2 Qxb5 Nxd6 Qa6
e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 c3 Rd8
en: A very strong move, threatening 14...c5, so White must move his queen off the d-file.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7 Qf3 Qc7 O-O-O Nbd7 g4 b5 Bxf6 Nxf6 g5 Nd7 f5 Bxg5+
en: White's variation after 13...Nc5 14.f6 gxf6 15.gxf6 Bf8 16.Rg1! is a tough nut to crack.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4 Bc2 Qe7 O-O a6 Rfe1 Qe6
en: Breaking the pin. Note that White has developed all his pieces except the rook on a1; Black hasn't developed either rook or the queen's bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4 Qc7 e5 Nd5 exd6 Bxd6 Ne4 c4
en: This is the only move to avoid the loss of material. However, it takes the pressure off of White's center leaving him free to conduct a kingside attack. Black has no prospects for a counterattack in the center or for a queenside attack.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8 O-O Nf8 h3 Be6 Rfc1 N6d7 Bf4 Nb6
en: So that Black can play 14... Bd6 and the queen will protect the bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6 cxd6 Nd5 Nxd5
en: A striking conception. Black's two minor pieces will be more powerful than White's queen.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3 Be7 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Qd2 d5
en: Taking advantage of the fact that White hasn't yet castled and that the e pawn is pinned.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O Qc4+ Kh8 Nd4 Qd7 Rad1 Rf7
en: Black can think of nothing better to do than wait. Better was 13... Nf7 followed by Nd8 to defend the weak square on e6.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4 Bb2 exd3 Qxd3 a6 h4 axb5 cxb5 Ne7
en: Black is preparing to castle; however, the kingside is almost as dangerous as the center.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Qb6 Nc3 Bxe5
en: It is dangerous to grab a pawn when behind in development, but the pawn on e5 kept Black's queen bishop hemmed in. Besides, Black now threatens 15... Bxc3 16. bxc3 17. Qxb5.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5 Na5
en: There is an old saying that a knight on the rim is dim. But where else can the knight go?

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nbd7 Qe2 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 Rf3 f5
en: To block the range of White's bishop.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4 Bh7 Bg3 Nxg3
en: So as to be able to play 14... Qc7 and 15... 0-0-0 getting the king to safety.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 e6 Bb3 b5 O-O Be7 Qf3 Qc7 Qg3 O-O Bh6 Ne8 Rad1 Bd7 Nce2 Bf6
en: This defends Pg7 and is well positioned to threaten White's queen-side, but it leaves Ne8 very awkward. White shouldn't try to force things now. Aiming to trade bishops and play against the weakened Pd6 might be effective.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 Bg7 Nc2 O-O Be2 Qa5 Bd2 a6 O-O Bd7 Rc1 Rac8 f4 Rfe8
en: Black prepares the ...Qa5-b6+, so Bd2-e3, Kg1-h1 or b2-b3 are immediately candidates to consider.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Ne7 Re1 h6 h3 Ng6 Bd2 Bd7 Ne4 Kc8
en: Black is far from completing his development, but if White doesn't execute a concrete attack he'll have time. That was the idea Kramnik utilized (as Black) to slow Kasparov.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bc5 Bg2 d6 d3 a6 h3 O-O O-O b5 a3 Rb8 Kh1 a5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Be6 Nd5 Bxd5
en: Black is forced to give up one of his valuable bishops and Pd5, though doubled, will be well supported by Bg2.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 e5 Bc4 d6 d3 Be7 Nd2 Bg5 h4 Bxd2+ Bxd2 Nf6 Bg5 Be6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Qd2 Ne7
en: With this move Black doesn't commit himself to a queen-side action, but he certainly makes it clear White's bishop is a target.

line: Nf3 c5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O Nc6 c3 d5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 e6 Nc3 Nge7 b3 O-O Qd2 b6 Ba3 Ba6 Rac1 Qd7 Rfd1 Rfd8
en: This breaks the pin on Ne7 and also prepares to meet e2-e4 with pressure on Pd4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 Be2 a6 N5c3 Bg5 Nd2 Nf6 O-O O-O b3 Nd4 Nf3 Bxc1 Rxc1 Nxf3+
en: Be2 is blocked by his pawns, so Nf3 could be more dangerous to Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3 bxa3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bb2 Nf4
en: Black takes advantage of the moment and hops right in; this also opens the diagonal for Bb7.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4 Re8 Kh1 Nbd7 Qe2 g6 Bd2 Bf8 Rad1 Nh5
en: In his 9th round game (Vallejo Pons - Anand) he had to meet an f-file attack against his castled king and Nf3-h4 was played to gain space for f2-f4. Is he replaying that game or does he have some original idea here?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O Nc3 Bf5 a3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nc6 cxd5 Qxd5
en: By transposition they've arrived at the same position as Kasparov-Adams.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5 Ra4 b4 Qh4
en: Black enters the attack vs. counterattack situation and makes room at d8 for Black's king to move around a bit. The center is clogged up, so he plays with Ra4 and Qh4 on the wings.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 c3 e6 Be3 Qb6 Qb3 Nd7 Nd2 f6 f4 g5 Ngf3 gxf4 Bxf4 Bh6 Bxh6 Nxh6 exf6 Nxf6 Be2 Rg8
en: Black's equalised already; the half-point can be taken anytime now.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Qc2 c6 a3 dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5 Bxe7 Qxe7 Ne4 N5f6 Bd3 Nxe4 Bxe4 h6
en: Vanek does not play 13...Nf6 in order to keep control over the e5 square.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6 f4 g5 Nf3 gxf4 exf4 Rg8 Qf2 Nxd4 Nxd4 Rxg2 Qf1 Bc5
en: A serious mistake would have been 13... Ng4 for 14. Be4 Qh4+ 15.Kd1 Nf2+ 16. Kc2 and the attack vanishes.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3 Na5 d4 exd4 Nxd4 c5 Nf5 Nxf5 exf5 Nxb3 Re1+ Be7 f6 gxf6 axb3 d5
en: Perhaps, as a last attempt to stop the imminent catastrophe, Steinitz could have tried 13...Be6 14.Qh5 Qd7.

line: e4 e6 d4 g6 Bd3 Bg7 Be3 c5 c3 cxd4 cxd4 Qb6 Ne2 Qxb2 Nbc3 Qb6 Rc1 Na6 Nb5 Bf8 O-O d6 d5 Qa5 Bd4 e5
en: (!) Black is happy to close the position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5 Nb3 Qe4 Nxa1 f6 Bc5+ Kh1 Rb8
en: It seems that Steinitz want to keep all the advantages he has apparently obtained.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7 e3 O-O c5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Qc2 f5 Bc4 Nc6 a3 Bf6 O-O-O Kh8 f3 Qe7 Bg3 f4
en: Very typical for Lasker - by complicating dubious positions he won many great games. Now he hoped for 14.Bxf4... #.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Ng3 e6 Bd3 c5 O-O Be7 c3 O-O Qe2 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 cxd4 cxd4 Nb8
en: With the idea of recycling the Knight with Nb8-c6 to attack the Pd4 or to force the exchange with the Knight in e5, believing that in such a way the position will improve.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nc3 O-O Rc1 c6 Bd3 a6 O-O dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bd3 c5 a4 c4 Bb1 Nd5
en: In search of a clarification.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Be7 O-O-O Qa5 e3 Bd7 Kb1 h6 cxd5 exd5 Nd4 O-O Bxf6 Bxf6
en: The unclear strategy of White has brought Black to possess a darksquared Bishop which shines now of his own light.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e3 Nd7 Nf3 Bd6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4+ Nc3 Ndf6 Bd3 Qa5 Bd2 Ne7 O-O O-O a3 Bxc3 Bxc3 Qc7
en: Now White has the advantage of the Bishop pair.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 e3 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 O-O Ne5 dxc4 Bxc4 Nd5 f4 Be6 Qb3 b5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Qxd5 cxd5
en: We are nearly skipping the middle game.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Qh4 Nb5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qxe4+ Be2 Kd8 O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 a6 N5c3 Qe5 Na3 b5 Bf3 Nge7 Rad1 Qf5
en: It may be observed, that on this and the previous moves Black had to avoid the temptation of forking the two knights by ...b4, as on each occasion White could have obtained a winning attack by the reply of Nd5.

line: e4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 e5 Nfd7 f4 e6 Nf3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O d3 Nb6 Ne2 d4 g4 f6 exf6 gxf6 Ng3 Nd5
en: Il Nero cerca di difendere l'ala minacciata dal centro, ma cio non dovrebbe essere sufficiente. (N).

line: e4 e5 f4 Bc5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Qe2 Qe7 d3 Bg4 f5 O-O-O b4 Bxf3 gxf3 d5 exd5 Nxb4 d4 Bb6 Ba3 Nfxd5
en: Aiming at the h4 square.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5 Na5 Bb2 Ne7 Bd3 O-O Nc3 Ng6 Ne2 c5
en: Following up the advantage which he has acquired on the Queen side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qd4 O-O Qxe5 Re1 Be6 d4 Qf5 Bg5 Bd6 g4 Qg6 f4 f5
en: The rest is a nightmare for Black:.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8 Ng3 Bg6
en: Apparently he didn't see any immediate value to trading, so he keeps the two bishops in hopes of some future time when they'll be especially valuable.

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2 cxd4 Nb3 Qb6 cxd4 Nf6 d5 d6 Nf3 O-O O-O Na6 Nfd4 Bd7 Bd2 Nc5 Ba5 Qa6
en: It's odd to note this, but this is the same awkward place for the queen which occurred in the Leko-Bareev Caro-Kann game. Now Bareev is on the other side.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 Ne7 f4 c5 h4 h5 f5 exf5 g5 Nec6 Bg2 cxd4 Nxd5 Nd7 Nxd4 Ndxe5
en: Black's central pawn chain is destroyed, but the knights have replaced them. Probably one of the knights has to be removed to weaken Black's control of the e-file. White has to make threats before Black can simply move ...Bf8 and ...O-O.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6 b6 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 Bg7 a4 Qxb6 Nd2 O-O Be2 Rb8 O-O Qa7 Nc4 Nb6
en: It looks like he's just trying to trade pieces to ease his cramp, but this can be risky because White has mobile central pawns and is close to having them very well supported.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O h6 Be3 Nxd4 Bxd4 b5 f3 Qa5 a3 Be7 Kb1 e5
en: I'd generally not be in favor of this move, as it helps White play through the center.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxc5 Qxc5 Kh1 b5 Qe1 Bb7 f3 d6
en: Black covers the dark squares and awaits White's next threat (s) .

line: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Be6 Na3 Bxb3 Qxb3 Qd3 Qb5 O-O-O Ng5 c4 Nxf7 Rd5
en: Qb5 is trapped and the following trades will give Black a tremendous opportunity to win material quickly. White's pieces are on the periphery and inactive.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5 d5 e6 O-O O-O Nbc3 Na6 h3 exd5 exd5 Nc4 b3 Nd6
en: Black's position is relatively harmonious and only the passed Pd5 is a problem. That the Pd5 also happens to block Bg2 and Nc3 is a happy "coincidence".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 b5 Bc2 d6 d4 Bb6 a4 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 Qxa8 h3 Bh5 d5 Na7
en: Now Black's pieces are on the perimeter. It's only ...c7-c6 which gives him a chance to counter against White's center. White might bolster Pd5 with b2-b3 and c3-c4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3 fxe4 Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5 Qg5
en: Definitely the most resiliant. My memory did not serve here so we were both on our own, but I used the process of elimination to guide me through the next couple moves, knowing the resulting position should be winning for white.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 O-O Bc4 Bd7 O-O-O Qa5 h4 Ne5 Bb3 Rfc8 g4 b5
en: The standard move 13...Nc4, or possibly 13...Rc4!, is probably better, unless my 22... Ne8 idea actually holds up.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 e3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 d4 cxd4 exd4 Be7 Bd3 Nc6 O-O O-O Re1 Nf6 a3 b6 Bc2 Bb7 Qd3 g6
en: Supposed mistake number one. 13...Rc8 should be better.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2 Qxd2 O-O Be2 b6 b4 bxc5 dxc5 Nc6
en: This was the crux of my idea, and it seems to be the best try. The knight goes to e7 so it can support the center.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 Bxc3 bxc3 d6 Bg5 Qe7 Qd2 Nd8 Bc4 Be6 Bb3 Bxb3 axb3 Ne6 Bh4 h6
en: (13... Nf4? 14. Nd4! exd4 15. Qxf4 dxc3 16. Rae1 intending Qe3 and f4 with a powerful attack is good for white. ).

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4 Qa3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nxe4
partai: Donald Byrne vs Robert James Fischer (1956)
en: The natural continuation of Black's plan.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Re1 Nf8 Rxe6 Nxe6
en: The gift cannot be refused. But now White's lightsquare Bishop becomes a brilliant laser pinning down the Knight on the e-file.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4 f4 Qe8 g3 Qh5 Kg2 Bg1
en: A shot! Najdorf clears off the h2 square for a Queen check. There is only one way to capture this Bishop: taking with the King is self-mate.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Kh1 d5 f4 exf4
en: Here Mieses makes a small mis-step, which his opponent declines to capitalize on.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4 c3 Nxd5 Ne4 Qh4 Ng3 Bg4 f3 e4 cxd4 Bd6 Bxb5+ Kd8 O-O exf3
en: White is a piece up with no peace. How should white respond to black's threat of 14... fxg2 attacking both white's Rook and Queen? The natural 14. gxf3 is refuted by 14... Bxg3 15. hxg3 Qxg3+ 16. Kh1 Nf4 17. Qe2 (forced) Nxe2 winning.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 c5 Rb1 Bg7 Nf3 O-O Be3 Qa5 Qd2 cxd4 cxd4 Qxd2+ Kxd2 Rd8 d5 Nc6
en: (Taking advantage of the pin.).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 Bxf7 Nf6 Be6 Qb8 Qd1+ Ke8
en: (White was intent on using the d file for attacking and so it seemed the King on e8 would stop Black's Knight from redeploying via that square onto d6. However 13.Bf4 is unpleasant, as in 13...Ne8 14.Qa4 Nf6 15.Nd5.).

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 b6 e3 Bb7 Nbd2 g6 Bd3 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 d6 Bb2 Nbd7 c4 e5 Qc2 Re8 d5 Nc5 Be2 Bc8 e4 Nh5
en: White creates a new weakness at f4.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 e3 Nbd7 f3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bb3 e6 Nge2 Bb7 a3 a6 e4 Be7 Nf4 Qb6 Bxe6 fxe6 Nxe6 Bf8
en: (Is there an alternative move for Black here? There seemed an Rg8 which didn't seem all that attractive but neither is my eventual choice of Bf8 either.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 c5 exd5 Qxd5 Ngf3 cxd4 Bc4 Qd6 O-O Nf6 Re1 a6 a4 Nc6 Qe2 Be7 Bb3 O-O Nc4 Qc7 g3 Nd5
en: (Guarding against a subsequent Bf4.).

line: d4 e6 c4 d5 Nc3 c6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4+ Bd2 Qxd4 Bxb4 Qxe4+ Be2 Na6 Bc3 Ne7 Bxg7 Rg8 Bf6 Qf4 Bc3 Rxg2 Nf3 f6
en: Analysis by Lautier and Wells suggests that 13...Rg8 should be looked at as an alternative to 13...f6.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 cxd5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qd1 exd5 Qxd5 Bd7 Nf3 Nf6 Qd1 Bc5 e3 Qc7 Be2 O-O-O O-O g5 Nd4 Qe5
en: # I start to feel this game slipping away after this move.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 Nd4 c3 b5 cxd4 bxc4 dxe5 Qxd5 exf6 Qxg5 Qf3 Rb8 Qc6+ Bd7 Qxc7 Rc8 fxg7 Rxc7
en: Why didn't I prefer 13...Bxg7. Maybe because of 14.Qg3.

line: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 c4 Bc2 b5 Ndf3 Nc6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nxe5 fxe5 Nd7 Nh3 Qc7 Qf3 f6 O-O O-O-O
en: # White has more space and the idea of opening the f-file looks even more appealing.

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3 dxc3 Qe7 g4 Qc5 h4 h6 Bg2 Nc6 Bxe4 h5 g5 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qxf2
en: [Here a computer would probably give a favourable assessment to Black, but the position is clearly better for White.].

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6 Ne5 f6
en: A response that looks weakening.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 b3 Nf6 g3 Bf5 Bg2 Nbd7 cxd5 cxd5 Bb2 e6 Nc3 Bb4 O-O O-O Rc1 Rc8 Nh4 Nb6 Nxf5 exf5 e3 Ne4
en: Rose tinted spectacle time. Nice would be Nxe4 dxe4 uniting my pawns. Even better d3 and Nxc3 wins a piece. But...

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 Bf5 f3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 g4 Bg6 h4 h6 Qb3 b6 Nh3 Be7 h5 Bh7 Nf2 O-O
en: Castling into the attack.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Nb3 Nbd7 Qf3 Qc7 Bd3 b5 O-O-O Bb7 Bxf6 Nxf6 Kb1 Be7
en: #In reply to this I received an interesting letter which contained no moves; my hopes rose accordingly.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c6 Nbd2 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 O-O Qe7 Qc2 O-O Ne5 Nbd7 Ndf3 Ne4 Bf4 g5 Nxd7 Bxd7 Bxd6 Nxd6
en: White now owns a superior bishop, but Black has plenty of room to maneuver.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3 Qb6 Qd2 Qxb2 Rb1 Qa3 dxc5 Bxc5 Bxc5 Qxc5 Bd3 a6 h4 Nb6
en: 13...Qe7 would have made it harder for me to justify the investment of the pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Qg6 Qf3 Ne5 Qe2 Nh6 f4 Neg4 f5 Qf6 Bg1 O-O Nd2 Ne5 O-O-O Qa6
en: It is easy to criticise Black's decision to settle for a unpleasant ending, but White's pawn storm on the kingside could be even more unpleasant!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 O-O Bc4 Bd7 Bb3 Rc8 O-O-O Ne5 Kb1 Re8 h4 h5
en: A necessary move to slow down White's activity.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Bd7 b3 Kc8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5 h3 Re8
en: This is a novelty, and maybe not good. As you have seen Kramnik never forgot to play h5 after h2-h3. It's very important to take care of the knight on f5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 c5 O-O Nc6 Be3 Bg4 f3 Bd7 Rb1 Qc7 Nf4 e6 Be2
en: A serious alternative would have been 14. d5. Rebel's move removes the bishop to Nc6-a5 attacks.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1 Nxd5 cxd5 Ne5 Be2 Re8 h4
en: To push the pawn to h5, after which exd4 becomes a threat (the Black knight cannot go to g6 anymore).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Ne5 Qc8 Qd3
en: An interesting move. First Rebel wanted to play 14 Nc4, but the reply 14 ... Qc6 is sufficient in that case.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5 Be2 Bb7 Nbd2 Nbd7 Nb3 Bf8 a4 b4 Nfd2
en: The standard move to head for the newly available c4 square.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nxc6 Qf6 Qd2 dxc6 Nc3 Ne7 Qf4 Be6 Qxf6 gxf6 Na4 Bb4+ c3 Bd6 Be3 b6 f4 O-O-O Kf2
en: Preparing to advance his c-pawn in order to reactivate the knight and get a nice hold on the white squares.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O e3 Ne4 Bxe7 Qxe7 cxd5 Nxc3 bxc3 exd5 Qb3 Rd8 c4 dxc4 Bxc4 Nc6 Be2
en: This avoids the possibility of losing a tempo and the capture of White's good bishop after.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 Bb3 cxd4 exd4 Nc6 Nc3 Be7 Re1 O-O Bf4 Na5 d5 Nxb3 Qxb3 exd5 Rad1
en: Played instantly, showing that X3D Fritz was still in its opening library. Black is unable to hold on to the extra pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6 e3 a6 b4 b5 cxb5 axb5 Bb2 Na7 h4 h6 d5
en: A strong positional pawn sacrifice that opens the long diagonal for White's dark-squared bishop.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Nf6 Qh4 Ke7 Ne5 Bxe5 dxe5 Qa5+ c3
en: Also possible is 14.Bd2 Qxe5+ 15.Be3, and it is quite unsafe for black to grab the second pawn on b2. But the position of the white pawn on c3 is more convenient for him than on c2.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 Kf8 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nxc3 Bd3 b6 h4 Ba6 Rh3 h5 Qf4 Qe7 Rf3
en: White now threatens 15.Bxg6 (and also Nh3-g5). Therefore Black's reply is practically forced.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 c3 Rd8 Qc2
en: White plans to answer 14...c5 with 15.Be4.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3 Qg7 Bxf4 Nf6 Ne4 Be7 Bg5
en: Continuing the pressure against the Knight.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4 Qxa8 Nf6 Na3 f3 g3 Bh3+ Ke1 Qg4 Be3
en: Developing and attacking black's queen knight.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4 Qg5 Nf5 c6 Rg1 cxb5 g4 Nf6 h4 Qg6 h5 Qg5 Qf3
en: Threatening 15. Bxf4 trapping the queen. The bottled up position of the Black queen is amusing.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4 Bc2 Qe7 O-O a6 Rfe1 Qe6 Nd2
en: The point is to play 15. e4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6 a3 h6 Bh4 Re8 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Ba2 c5 Rd1
en: Putting pressure on the soon-to-be opened d file. However, it is usually not a good idea to move a piece twice in the opening and neglect the development of other pieces.

line: c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 Nbd7 Nf3 c6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8 O-O Nf8 h3 Be6 Rfc1 N6d7 Bf4 Nb6 Rab1
en: Preparing for an eventual b4.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7 c3 Nc5 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 Bxa8 Bc2
en: Although the bishop looks passive, WhIte will play b4 to chase away the knight and then return the bishop to b3. White is threatening d4 giving him a strong center.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3 Be7 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Qd2 d5 O-O-O
en: White was faced with the choice of a passive defense and sacrificing a pawn for an attack. He chose the latter.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O Qc4+ Kh8 Nd4 Qd7 Rad1 Rf7 f4
en: White is preparing to control e6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ Nbd7 O-O-O Rd8 Rxd7 Rxd7 Rd1
en: The pinned rook is doomed. White threatens 15. Bxd7+ and 15... Nxd7 could not be played because the knight is pinned.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4 Bb2 exd3 Qxd3 a6 h4 axb5 cxb5 Ne7 Qd2
en: White guards the bishop on b2 so that he threatens Nce4 taking control of f6.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4 Bc2 a6 Qf3 b5 Qh3
en: Threatening 15. Nxd7 Qxd7 (if 15... Nxd7 then Qxh7#) 16. Bxh7+ Kh8 (If 16... Nxh7 17. Qxd7) 17. Bf5+ Kg8 18. Bxd7. If Black plays 14... h6 then 15. Bxh6 gxh6 16. Qxh6 Ne4 17. Rf3 Bf6 18. Rg3+ Nxg3 19. Qh7#.

line: f4 e6 Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Bd6 d4 Nc6 Ne5 Ne7 Be3 c6 a3 h6 Nd2 Nd7 c4 b6 b4 f6 Nxc6 Nxc6 cxd5 exd5 Bxd5
en: Attacking the knight on c6 and pinning it to the rook.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5 Na5 Ne5
en: A knight posted in the center is a very powerful piece. Bishops work best at a distance.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd8 d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4 Nbd7 Qe2 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 Rf3 f5 Rh3
en: Threatening 15. Qh5 h6 16. Qg6 with many threats including 17. Rxh6, 17. Bxf5 and 17. Qe6+. If after 15. Qh5 Black were to play 15... Nf6 then 16. Qxf5 Bc8 (appearing to win the rook on h3) 17. Qxh7+ Nxh7 18. Bxh7+ Kh8 19. Ng6#.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4 Bh7 Bg3 Nxg3 fxg3
en: It is normally better to capture toward the center (hxg3) but White wants the f file open.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4 O-O b3 Rfe8 Bb2 Bf8 Rad1 Qc6 Rd3
en: The rook can attack Black's kingside and protect the pawn on e4 if necessary.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5 Bd7 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 Bf4
en: Bringing the bishop to this active position with tempo the beginning of the attack.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 Nbd2 Bg7 Nf1 O-O Ba4 Nd7 Ne3 Nc5 Bc2 Ne6 h4 Ne7 h5 d5 hxg6 fxg6 exd5
en: Surprising at first glance for White eliminates his strong center pawn and is left with a backward pawn on d3.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4 Nbd7 Qc2 Re8 Rd1 exd4 Nxd4 a5 e4 Nc5 f3 c6 Be3 Qe7 Bf2
en: It's easier to retreat off the e-file than to defend Be3.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nxc6 dxc6 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Bf4 Bb4 O-O-O+ Ke7 f3 Rd8 Be2 Bd7 a3 Bxc3 Bd6+ Ke8 bxc3
en: Now White has a chance to use c3-c4 to control d5 and e4-e5 to chase Nf6 while creating a bind on Black, so that Bd7 and the rooks can't become active.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6 O-O Nf6 Be3 Bb4 Na4 Be7 Nxc6 bxc6 Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Qxc8 Bd4 O-O e5
en: Earlier in the tournament Shirov played 14. Qd3, which gave a small advantage.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3 bxa3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bb2 Nf4 Bc1
en: Ivanchuk recognizes his mistake and tries to rectify it, even at the cost of another tempo. But, this gain of time surely gives some initiative to Black.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 Bb4 Nd5 Bc5 Bg2 d6 O-O O-O e3 a6 b3 Ba7 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Bb2 Bg4 h3 Bh5 d3 Qe7 Qd2
en: This position doesn't offer many possibilities for White to win, but Ba7 and Nc6 are blocked, so Black doesn't have much either.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4 Re8 Kh1 Nbd7 Qe2 g6 Bd2 Bf8 Rad1 Nh5 Nf3
en: Ivanchuk doesn't appear to be in a hurry, but he's not going to allow ...Qd8-h4 either. He's incidentally (?) clearing the d-file and may plan Bd2-e3-d4. This is an amazingly quiet maneuvering noncomittal game for Ivanchuk.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Bxc4 Nb6 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nb4 Be4 f5 exf6 exf6 Nc3 f5 Bb1 N4d5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 Be7 Bd2
en: Now who's lost the tempo?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 Bb7 O-O Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 Ne7 Bd2 Ng6 a4 b4 Nd5 a5 c3 b3 g3
en: He's preparing Nd5-e3 and disallowing ...Ng6-f4. It's not terribly pretty, but Nd5 will have to move eventually.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 Be7 f5 Nc6 Be3 Nxd4 Bxd4 O-O fxe6 fxe6 Qe2
en: White may attack Pb6 to peck away at Black's weak points while he maneuvers into some formation to attack Kg8. Threatening at two or three points can help the White cause.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6 O-O Nf6 Kh1 Nxd4 Qxd4 Bc5 Qd3 b5 f4 Bb7 Bf3 O-O e5 Ne8 a4
en: Taking on b7 and either f5 or Ne4 is par for the course here - usually White doesn't commit the queenside pawns.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Nbd7 Qd2 b5 a4 b4 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Nb6 Bxb6 Qxb6 a5
en: The idea is simple: White is going to stymie Black's play by rounding up on the vulnerable b-pawn.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c3 bxc3 O-O O-O c5 e3 Nc6 Qe2 Bf5 Rd1 Qb6 Bb2 Rfd8 Nc4 Qa6 a4
en: Karpov obviously doesn't like the idea of Kasparov fixing the a-pawn with a ..Qa4.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 Ne5 e6 Bg5 Bb4 f3 c5 dxc5 Qa5 Qd4 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 e4 Bxc5 Qxc4 Bg6 Bd2
en: Now, if 14.0-0 15.Nd1! Qb6 16.a5 White wins a piece. Black has no choice.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 b6 Qf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bb7 Qg3 Bd6 f4 g5 Nf3 gxf4 exf4 Rg8 Qf2 Nxd4 Nxd4 Rxg2 Qf1 Bc5 Nf3
en: Again an inaccurate move which will cost material. 14. Nce2 was relatively better but after 14... Ng4 Black's attack would be irresistible.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3 Na5 Bg5 Ne7 Nd5 f6 Bxf6 gxf6 Nxf6+ Kf8 Ng5
en: The cavalry is sent audaciously to the attack. (Different times, different spirit, different phylosophy of the game!).

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 O-O O-O c5 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 dxc5 Na6 a3 Nxc5 b4 Ne6 Bb2 a5 b5
en: Mikenas: "Alekhine looked nervous. It was necessary to realize the wrong opening strategy and try to keep equality with 14.Nc3.".

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 Nf6 Bc4 d5 exd5 Bd6 d4 Nh5 Bb5+ c6 dxc6 bxc6 Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc6+ Kf8 Bxa8 Ng3 Rh2
en: Obviously the unknown club player who was playing white it wasn't clear whether Black had sufficient compensation for the sacrificed rook. And what do you think now about the options, e.g.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5 Nb3 Qe4 Nxa1 f6 Bc5+ Kh1 Rb8 e6
en: It looks like a mistake, and probably it is. Maybe is it a "terroristic" move?

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e3 Nd7 Nf3 Bd6 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Bb4+ Nc3 Ndf6 Bd3 Qa5 Bd2 Ne7 O-O O-O a3 Bxc3 Bxc3 Qc7 Ne5
en: Steinitz, for now has nothing in view. He has placed his Knight in e5 ... just to bother his opponent which is now to act in a resctricted space.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5 dxe5 Bg5 h6 Bxc6 bxc6 Be3 Ng6 Qd3 Bd6 Nd2 Ne7 Nc4 Nc8 O-O-O Qe7 f4
en: Opening the "f" file as a basis for future operations. 14...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6 Bxg6+ hxg6 Qd3 Kf7 h4
en: A necessary provision for 15.Bf4, which if playedat once meets 14...g5 in reply. Botvinnik's next move is a profound one. It deserves a an exclamation point or two. 14...

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Bb7 d4 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 d5 e5 Be3 f5 Ne1 Bxg2 Nxg2 d6 Qd2 Nd7 f3
en: A useful consolidating move directed against the mobility of Black's KP and KBP. 14...

line: d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 c5 c3 Qa5 Nd2 cxd4 Nb3 Qb6 cxd4 Nf6 d5 d6 Nf3 O-O O-O Na6 Nfd4 Bd7 Bd2 Nc5 Ba5 Qa6 Qd2
en: White just keeps moving forward into the breech and Black can't easily challenge any of White'spieces!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bd3 Be6 O-O Bxd5 exd5 Ne7 c3
en: It seems to me Pd5 needs more support and White should play on the queen-side as part of that.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 Ne7 f4 c5 h4 h5 f5 exf5 g5 Nec6 Bg2 cxd4 Nxd5 Nd7 Nxd4 Ndxe5 Nb5
en: White sees ...Bf8-d6 as essential to Black's effort to secure Ne5, but after Nb5 there's less force available to break up the knights. It's a difficult choice for White. He chooses to threaten Nc7+.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 Nf3 g6 cxb5 a6 b6 d6 Nc3 Nbd7 e4 Bg7 a4 Qxb6 Nd2 O-O Be2 Rb8 O-O Qa7 Nc4 Nb6 Na5
en: White decides he would rather leave the pieces on the board and fight for e4-e5 (a major strategic theme) or perhaps a direct king-side attack. Black has to commit to some other way of fighting actively.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxc5 Qxc5 Kh1 b5 Qe1 Bb7 f3 d6 a4
en: This is very often a swift rejoinder to an early ...b7-b5. It's usually difficult for Black to defend Pb5 or to avoid a pawn trade after ...b5-b4, c2-c3. This queen-side line opening gives White some possibilities for offense.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c3 Ne7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Bd3 Bb7 Qe2
en: Keeping his castling options open, but soon he will have to choose and he will certainly go kingside...

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2 Qxd2 O-O Be2 b6 b4 bxc5 dxc5 Nc6 b5
en: Of course nothing could be more natural, and I was counting on this. Nonetheless, 14.Rb1 should be considered for reasons that I will explain in a moment.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7 Qf3 Qc7 O-O-O Nbd7 Bd3 h6 Bh4 g5 fxg5 Ne5 Qe2 Nfg4 Nf3
en: This is the correct plan - to put every resource towards overcoming the e5-square.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 d5 Bg2 Bb4+ Nfd2 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bb2 O-O O-O Nc6 Nc3 Rc8 cxd5 exd5 Na4 Nd4 Nc3
en: What else ? If 14. Re1 Nc2 15. Qxc2 Bxf2+ 16. Kxf2 Rxc2 -+){.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4 f4 Qe8 g3 Qh5 Kg2 Bg1 Nxg1
en: Taking with the Rook allows mate in two as well. Only the Knight capture is acceptable -- or so it seems.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+ Kf8 Bf4 Nxf2 Qe2
en: By threatening mate at e8, Charousek ensures that his B/f4 cannot be taken.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5 exd5 b5 Bf1 Nd4 c3 Nxd5 Ne4 Qh4 Ng3 Bg4 f3 e4 cxd4 Bd6 Bxb5+ Kd8 O-O exf3 Rxf3
en: This may be the losing move. After 14. Qe1!, black will find it hard to justify his material sacrifice.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2
en: White should have played a3 to control the important b4 square.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Be3 c5 Qd2 O-O Rc1 Qa5 Nf3 e6 d5 exd5 exd5 Re8 Be2 Bf5 O-O
en: The atmosphere in the pressroom is a bit "fuzzy." The game hasn't found its own personality yet, and the fact that the US plays the Soviets at the Chess Olympiad in Novi Sad at this very moment is also widely discussed.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Be2 Be7 O-O O-O Be3 Nc6 f4 Bd7 Qe1 Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc6 Qg3 g6 Qe3 Qa5 e5
en: Kholmov pressures in the centre.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 h5 Nxc6 bxc6 Bc4 Qc7 O-O h4 h3 Bd7 Rad1 Nh5 Bd4
en: Trying to be consistent with one of the original objectives of the opening - removal of the fianchettoed Bishop.

line: d4 b5 e4 Bb7 e5 e6 Nf3 a6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 bxc4 Bxc4 d6 Qe2 Nd7 Bf4 d5 Bd3 c5 Be3 cxd4 Bxd4 Ne7 a3 Bc5 O-O
en: 14.Rc1 should have been preffered here.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 b3 Nf6 g3 Bf5 Bg2 Nbd7 cxd5 cxd5 Bb2 e6 Nc3 Bb4 O-O O-O Rc1 Rc8 Nh4 Nb6 Nxf5 exf5 e3 Ne4 Qh5
en: So much for strategy and tactics. I need some good ideas quickly now: the obvious g6 Qh6 leaves an Nxe4 mate threat. Why not get rid of the Knight?

line: c4 e5 g3 c6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 d5 cxd5 cxd5 Bg2 Be6 Nf3 Nc6 Qa4 Bc5 O-O h6 Nc3 Ne7 Bf4 a6 Rad1 O-O a3 Rc8 Ne5
en: I was reluctant to play this but the alternatives didn't look too good.

line: d4 Nf6 e3 d5 Bd3 e6 Nd2 c5 c3 b6 Ndf3 c4 Bc2 Bd6 Ne5 O-O f4 b5 Qf3 g6 Nh3 Bd7 Nf2 Be8 O-O Na6 e4
partai: A Petrie vs T F McAinsh
en: Attacks the pawn chain,Ifelt that the time was right for this move. The Bishops will soon be free to move to more aggresive squares leaving the Black position cramped.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 f6 exf6 Nxf6 O-O Bd6 Nf3 Qc7 Nc3 a6 Bg5 O-O Bh4
en: White's idea is to reduce pressure alonge the b8-h2 diagonal by offering an exchange of Bishops on g3. Black needs a good counter to this plan...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 a6 Ngf3 c5 exd5 exd5 Be2 c4 O-O Bd6 b3 b5 a4 Bb7 bxc4 bxc4 Bxc4 dxc4 Nxc4 Be7 Re1 Qc7 Rb1
en: White's pieces quickly comes into play. By the way, Rb7 is threatened.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 b5 cxb5 Bxb5 Bg2 c5 O-O Bc6 Ba3 Na6 Nbd2 Be7 dxc5 Bxc5 Bxc5 Nxc5 Rc1 Nb7 e4
en: Very interesting pawn sacrifice.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ndf6 Bc4 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Qxd2 Ne7 O-O-O O-O Rhg1 Ned5 Bd3 Ng4 Ne5
en: The correct decision: White wants to exchange the knight on g4 and drive away the knight on d5. And bishop c8 is off-side still.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Ne2 c5 O-O Nc6 Be3 Bg4 f3 Bd7 Rb1 Qc7 Nf4 e6 Be2 Ne7
en: Preventing 15 d5, but the knight is very passive at e7. More active was 14 ... Rad8 or Rfd8.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O b3 c5 Bb2 Ne4 c3 Nc6 e3 Bg4 h3 cxd4 cxd4 Bf5 Nfd2 Nf6 Nc3 Nb4 Nf3 Nd3
en: A so called 'octopus'. It appears that it is very difficult to get rid of this awsome knight.

line: Nf3 d5 g3 Bg4 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Nc6 d3 e5 h3 Be6 a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bb2 Nd7 Nbd2 O-O e3 f5 c4 dxc4 dxc4 Bf6 Qc2 e4
en: This move is possible, because White is not able to retake on d4 with a piece. Still, white's centre is getting stronger, but also after 10 minutes of thought Rebel would have played e5-e4.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1 Nxd5 cxd5 Ne5 Be2 Re8 h4 c5
en: Starting the counterattack and defending the pawn on d4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Ne5 Qc8 Qd3 b5
en: Stops 15 Nc4, but overlooks White's next move. Maybe it was better to complete development first.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nxc6 Qf6 Qd2 dxc6 Nc3 Ne7 Qf4 Be6 Qxf6 gxf6 Na4 Bb4+ c3 Bd6 Be3 b6 f4 O-O-O Kf2 c5
en: Black would like to bring his own knight into play with this.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O d5 c4 Nf6 cxd5 cxd5 exd5 exd5 Nc3 Be7 Qa4+ Qd7 Re1 Qxa4 Nxa4 Be6
en: The position is almost equal but Fischer shows good technique in this position.

line: Nf3 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 a3 Nxd4 Qxd4 b6 Bf4 Bc5 Qd2 O-O Rd1 Bb7 Bd6 Bxd6 Qxd6 Rc8 e3 Re8 f3 Rc6
en: Less effective was 14...Ba6, as this enables White to reply 15.b3 Rc6 16.Qc6.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5 Nd5 f5 Qe2 Qd6 Nf3 f4
en: If 14...Qxd5 15.Bxd7+ Qxd7 (if 15...Kxd7 16.Rd1 winning) 16.Nxe5 Qe7 17.0-0-0 with a raging attack as 17...Nf6 18.Qb5+ Kf8 19.Nd7+ Nxd7 20.Bd6 wins for White.

line: c4 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 Nf6 b3 c5 cxd5 exd5 d4 Nc6 Be2 cxd4 Nxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bd6 Nxc6 bxc6 Nc3 O-O O-O Bf5 g3 Qd7 Re1 h5
en: The h-pawn is used as a battering ram in a classical attack against the king's fortress.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 g6 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 Bd3 Qa5 Ne2 cxd4 Bxd4 Nc5 O-O Nc6 Bxg6 Rg8
en: Of course, Black cannot take the bishop immediately - 14...fxg6? 15.Qxg6+ Kf8 when either 16.Be3 or 16.f4 gives White a strong attack.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nge7 Bc4 d6 O-O O-O f4 Na5 Bd3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 c3 Rd8 Qc2 Nc4
en: Because of the loose Be3, White is more or less forced to part with the bishop pair.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Bc5 c3 O-O d4 Bb6 Qd3 d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 Bd7 Nbd2 a6 Bc4 exd4 cxd4 g5 Bg3 Nh5 e5 Kg7
en: Unfortunate but necessary, as 14...Nxg3? 15.Qg6+ is winning for White, as is 14...Ne7 15.exd6.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Ne2 Qc7 Qe1 d5
en: Increasing my grip on the center, but it was also possible to play simply with 14...Be7.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 d6 d4 Nbd7 Nc3 e5 e4 g6 Be2 Bg7 O-O O-O d5 a5 Ne1 Nc5 Qc2 b6 Bg5 h6 Be3 Ng4 Bxg4 Bxg4 Nd3 Bd7
en: Today, of course, I would have taken the knight at d3 and then played ...Bd7.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5 a4 Rb8 c3 d6 d4 Bb6 Na3 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Nxb5 O-O Re1 Bxf3 gxf3 Nh5
en: Shirov is repeating his game vs Ivanchuk from Belgrade, where he had no problems whatsoever.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8 Rad1 Ne4 Qe3 f5 d5 exd5 cxd5 Ndf6
en: Attacking the pawn on d5. It doesn't look like it can be defended.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ Nbd7 O-O-O Rd8 Rxd7 Rxd7 Rd1 Qe6
en: This unpins the knight. White could win material now with 16. Bxf6, but, instead, plays a combination that puts this game into the history books.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Qb6 Nc3 Bxe5 Rae1 Bxc3
en: The dark squares now belong to White.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5 O-O Bb7 Rc1 Re8 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 cxd4
en: The losing move. It lets White's rook slip in.

line: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 f4 d6 f5 Nd4 Bg5 c6 a3 b5 Ba2 Qb6 Nf3 a5 Rf1 a4 Nxd4 Bxd4 Bxf6 gxf6 Qh5 Rf8
en: If 15. Qxh7 then 15... b4 16. axb4 Qxb4 threatening 17... Bxc3+, 17... Qxb2, as well as 17... a3 undermining the protection of the pinned knight.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4 Bh7 Bg3 Nxg3 fxg3 Qc7
en: Black would like to castle queenside next move.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8 Nc4 f6 a4 c6 Nxb6 axb6 Qb3+ Ne6
en: The kinght will eventually move to f4 as part of an attack on the White king.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd4 O-O b3 Rfe8 Bb2 Bf8 Rad1 Qc6 Rd3 Re6
en: Black's plan is to put pressure on White's e pawn and eventually free himself with f5 or d5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Nge7 Ng5 O-O Bd3 Bf5 Bxf5 Nxf5 Ba3 Qg6 Bxf8 Qxg5
en: Now White's kingside has no pieces to defend it.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5 Bd7 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 Bf4 Qg7
en: 14...Qh5 planning Qh3+ might look better in view of White's dangerous looking reply but Black is ready for it. After 14...Qh5 15. Qd4 the position becomes wild.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Nh6 h3 Nc6 dxe5 fxe5 Qd2 Nf7 Nh2 Nd4
en: White notices d4 is weak and he hasn't got Be3 or Nf3 to challenge it.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 e6 Bb3 b5 O-O Be7 Qf3 Qc7 Qg3 O-O Bh6 Ne8 Rad1 Bd7 Nce2 Bf6 Nf3 Nc6
en: Karjakin goes with the tried-and-true answer, develop pieces to fight with.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 e6 Nf3 d5 cxd5 exd5 d4 Bg4 Ne5 cxd4 Nxc6 bxc6 Qxd4 Be7 Bg5 Be6 O-O O-O Qd3 h6 Bf4 Qb6
en: Polgar would rather use a Rd8 to support the pawn than her queen. Also, opposing Qd3 with a Rd8 could enable tactical possibilities.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 e5 Bc4 d6 d3 Be7 Nd2 Bg5 h4 Bxd2+ Bxd2 Nf6 Bg5 Be6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Qd2 Ne7 Bc4 O-O
en: Now Black's ready for ...a7-a6 and ...b7-b5 to squeeze White's queen-side, particularly the bishop, and perhaps to gain control of which files might open for rooks.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 e6 Be3 Nc6 Qd2 Be7 g4 O-O O-O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 b5 a3 Nd7 h4 Rb8 f4 Bb7
en: He sees the weakened Pe4 and attacks it, but has, more or less, wasted 13...Rb8.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nbd2 Bf8 c3 Na5 Ba2 c5 d4 d6 b4 exd4
en: Leave it to Ivanchuk to break all the rules and create something amazing like this. Is it good or just silly horrible? Nobody can know without playing it out.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Ne5 Nd7 Bb5 Bd6 Qg4 Kf8 O-O Nxe5 dxe5 Bxe5 Bg5 Bf6 Rad1 Qc7
en: I'm not sure why he's allowing White to capture at f6 to double his f-file pawns, exposing Kf8 a little. Perhaps he thinks he'll be able to play ...Rh8-g8 to help his own piece development.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5 Ra4 b4 Qh4 O-O Rg8
en: White might like to think his king is safe behind the pawns, but there's room for Black to play on that wing and the g-file is open. It's still anybody's game.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Be2 a6 O-O Qc7 Be3 d6 Kh1 Be7 f4 Na5 Qe1 b5 Bf3 Bb7 a3 Nc4 Bc1 Qc5
en: Perhaps castling was a better move for Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 h5 Nxg5 h4 Nxf7 hxg3 Nxd8 Bg4 Qd2 Nd4 Nc3 Nf3+ gxf3 Bxf3
en: White resigns. Mate in five is inevitable.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 Bc5 Bc4 Nf6 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O O-O Re1 Nf4 Ne4 Ne7 Qd2 Neg6 h3 Nd5
en: Unclear. Again, a better choice would have been 14...Be6 or 14...c6.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 O-O O-O c5 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 dxc5 Na6 a3 Nxc5 b4 Ne6 Bb2 a5 b5 Qd7
en: (!) Now Black, gaining a tempo, can double his forces on the "d" file and create "hidden" threats.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 c5 Rc1 Nc6 O-O Nxe5 dxe5 Ne8 Bf4 f5 Qc2 g5
en: (?) No! Is is impossible! The Great Lasker, with what looks like a "razor shot", thinks he can steal a piece. Schlechter will prove that it is possible to "steal to the thieves"!

line: c4 e6 e3 Nf6 Nf3 b6 Be2 Bb7 O-O d5 d4 Bd6 Nc3 O-O b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Qe7 Nb5 Ne4 Nxd6 cxd6 Nd2 Ndf6 f3 Nxd2 Qxd2 dxc4
en: "Improving the pawn position and trying to open the c-file" (Averbach) "Instead of releasing the pressure in the center, Black could have enhance it with 14...e5" (Tartakower).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc5 f4 b6 f5 Nb3 Qe4 Nxa1 f6 Bc5+ Kh1 Rb8 e6 Rg8
en: (??) the move that such a terrorist as was Bird reached its purpose.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 Bd2 Ne7 Nb5 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O c3 b6 f4 Ba6 Nf3 Qd7 a4 Nbc6 b4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb7 Nd6 f5
en: A big strategical mistake. The eyes and the thoughts of Nimzowitsch are turned on the kingside while the danger is on the queenside.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 d5 a3 Bxc3+ Qxc3 Ne4 Qc2 Nc6 e3 e5 f3 Nf6 cxd5 Qxd5 Bc4 Qd6 dxe5 Nxe5 Bd2 O-O Bb4 c5
en: A malicious trap, but Vidmar sees and avoids it.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Bd6 Nf3 Nge7 Qc2 Bg4 Nbd2 Qd7 O-O f6 Re1 g5 h3 Be6 Nf1 O-O-O b4 Rdg8 a4 Nd8
en: To be able to reply to the possible 15.Bb5 con 15...c6. As Nimzowitsch himself teaches us: "First of all...consolidate your position".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Re1 O-O Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 c6 f3 Ng5 Nc3 Bf5
en: The square e6, if needed, sould be useful to the Knight.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 Be6 Bxe6 fxe6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Ne7 Bg5 Nc6 Bxd8 Nxd4 O-O-O Nb5 Nxb5 axb5 Bxc7 Rxa2
en: Now Black threatens to come out a pawn ahead by ...Ra6.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6 Bxg6+ hxg6 Qd3 Kf7 h4 Qg8
en: This beautiful queen maneuver crosses up White's plan to regain his pawn without losing hold of the center. White intended to protect his king pawn by 15.Bf4 (now that...g6-g5 is prevented) and then capture the queen pawn at his leisure.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Bc5 O-O d6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb6 d5 Na5 Bb2 Ne7 Bd3 O-O Nc3 Ng6 Ne2 c5 Qd2 f6
en: Restricting the range of adverse QB on the long diagonal.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 Bb6 dxe5 Nge7 O-O O-O Ba3 h6 Nbd2 Re8 Nb3 Ng6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ Re6 Nfd4 Nf4
en: Best,as Black had to stop the f-pawn from advancing.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 d6 g4 a6 Be3 Nge7 Nb3 b5 f4 Bb7 Qf3 g5 fxg5 Ne5 Qg2 b4 Ne2 h5 gxh5 Nf5
en: Clearance to allow d8-g5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8 Ng3 Bg6 Ne4 Bc7
