en: I don't understand giving up Pc5 in this situation. What plan does Black follow which demands the bishop be at c7 rather than d6 or f8?

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 Ne7 f4 c5 h4 h5 f5 exf5 g5 Nec6 Bg2 cxd4 Nxd5 Nd7 Nxd4 Ndxe5 Nb5 Rc8
en: It appears Black doesn't want to part with his dark square bishop, but that endangers his king.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Nc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O e5 c3 g5 d4 g4 Nfd2 cxd4 cxd4 exd4 Nc4 c5 Re1 Be6 Nba3 Be7 e5 d5 Nd6+ Kf8
en: This position doesn't look too good for Black, but Na3 is misplaced and Nd6 is far from coordinating with other White pieces.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nb4 Be2 O-O Nc3 Bf5 a3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nc6 Re1 Re8 Bf4 dxc4
en: Black's need to maneuver pieces forces him to allow White's bishop onto the a2-g8 diagonal, controlling d5!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 O-O Kh1 Qc7 a4 Nc6 Be3 Re8 Bf3 Rb8 Qd2 Bd7 Nb3 b6
en: Black's hedgehog position is sturdy. Anand has learned well from Kasparov (and others before him) .

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 e5 h6 Bc1 Nd5 c4 Nb4 d5 d6 a3 N4a6 exd6 Bxd6 Nc3 O-O Bd3 Nc7 Nge2 exd5 cxd5 Nd7 O-O Nf6
en: White has developed quietly, while holding his central pawn. Black got rid of a couple of those White pawns to make it easier for his own pieces to develop. White's advantage is small.

line: d4 e6 c4 Bb4+ Nc3 Nf6 f3 d5 a3 Be7 e4 c5 cxd5 exd5 dxc5 Bxc5 e5 Nfd7 Qxd5 O-O f4 Qb6 Nf3 Bf2+ Ke2 Nc5 b4 Rd8
en: The pawn becomes a piece as black struggles to keep the initiative. However, 14...Rd8 is very dangerous and could have easily won the game against inferior defense.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2 Qxd2 O-O Be2 b6 b4 bxc5 dxc5 Nc6 b5 Ne7
en: The obvious idea is ...e5, but there is another threat that white has so generously helped me to create with his last move...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 Na5 Bc2 c5 d4 Qc7 Nbd2 O-O h3 Nc6 d5 Nd8 a4 b4
en: Weakening c4 and allowing the ensuing play. 14...Bb7 is also nice for white since the bishop has nothing to do there.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb6 O-O Be7 f4 g6 a3 a5 b3 Bd7 g4 Qc7 Bb2 f5
en: Black finds a strong defensive resource. This immediately neutralizes whites kingside play. This is what puts question to whites early g4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 d5 Bg2 Bb4+ Nfd2 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bb2 O-O O-O Nc6 Nc3 Rc8 cxd5 exd5 Na4 Nd4 Nc3 Qe7
en: (14...Bb4, with the idea of destroying the main defender of the e2-pawn, doesn't serve the purpose because of the cool 15. Ndb1! . Black has a combination in store against White's next move which is probably the only move in the position.).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 Bxc3 bxc3 d6 Bg5 Qe7 Qd2 Nd8 Bc4 Be6 Bb3 Bxb3 axb3 Ne6 Bh4 h6 Rfe1 a6
en: (14...Nf4 is still bad because of 15. Nd4 exd4 (Black cannot allow the White knight to occupy f5) 16. Qxf4 dxc3 ( or if 16... g5 17.Bxg5 hxg5 18. Qxg5+ Kh8 19. cxd4 Rfe8 20. Ra5 with attack.) 17. d4 is better for white. ).

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 f5 d4 e4 Ng5 Bb4 Nh3 Nf6 e3 Bxc3+ bxc3 d6 Nf4 O-O h4 Qe7 c5 Nd8 Qb3+ Ne6 Bc4 Re8 Ba3 Kh8
en: Ignoring threats on the b-pawn. After the upcoming exchange, white's only active bishop is gone and black has good counterplay.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7 Qxe7 f4 a6 Nf3 c5 Qd2 Nc6 dxc5 Qxc5 Bd3 b5 a3 Bb7 Qf2 b4 Na4 Qxf2+
en: Now he must make this exchange. 14. Qa5? just gets in the way of his queenside pawns.

line: d4 f5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 d5 e3 c6 Bd3 Bd6 O-O O-O Ne2 Nbd7 Ng5 Bxh2+ Kh1 Ng4 f4 Qe8 g3 Qh5 Kg2 Bg1 Nxg1 Qh2+
en: Driving the King forward -- to his doom!

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Kh1 d5 f4 exf4 Rxf4 Qe7
en: Black ducks the challenge. Now White's plan rolls forward unhindered.

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2 Bb4
en: Black immediately pins the poor Knight.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 a6 e4 b5 e5 Nd5 a4 Nxc3 bxc3 Qd5 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Qd7 Ba3 e6 Bxf8 Kxf8 O-O g6 Nh4 c6
en: Simagin advices the exchange of bishops.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 e3 e6 d4 d5 cxd5 exd5 Be2 Bd6 dxc5 Bxc5 O-O O-O b3 Be6 Bb2 Qe7 a3 Rfd8 Na4 Bd6 b4 Ng4
en: The players fight for their last chance.

line: d4 h6 e4 d6 Nc3 a6 f4 b5 Nf3 Bb7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 dxc5 b3 g5 fxg5 Bg7 Bb2 hxg5 Nxg5 Nd7 Qf3 Bf6 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Qa5+
en: (That came in handy. the game already plays itself in that there is no going back on heavy measures.).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 Bxf7 Nf6 Be6 Qb8 Qd1+ Ke8 O-O g6
en: (With the same intent, White wants to get the Rook available for the d file but even here 14.Bf4 is good.).

line: b3 g6 Bb2 Nf6 e4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Nc3 Nxe4 Bc4 Nxc3 Bxc3 Bxc3 dxc3 O-O O-O e5 Nd2 d5 Be2 f5 c4 d4 Nf3 Nc6 Qc1 e4
en: (The moves play themselves.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Kf2 f6 Be3 fxe5 fxe5 O-O a3 Be7 b4 a6
en: # (The line that I was following continued.

line: Nf3 Nf6 g3 b5 Bg2 Bb7 O-O e6 b3 Bd6 d4 O-O Na3 a6 c4 bxc4 Nxc4 Bb4 Bb2 d5 a3 dxc4 axb4 cxb3 Qxb3 Qd6 Rfc1 Nc6
en: Attacks the isolani on b4.

line: e4 e6 b3 d5 Bb2 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Bxc3 dxc3 Qe7 g4 Qc5 h4 h6 Bg2 Nc6 Bxe4 h5 g5 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qxf2 Nh3 Qc5
en: [If 14. ... Qf5, then 15. Qxf5 exf5 16.Rhe1+ Be6 17.Nf4 Rd8 18.Rxd8+ Kxd8 19.c4 Rg8 20.Nxh5 g6 21.Nf6 Rh8 22.h5 gxh5 23.g6 fxg6 24.Rxe6 h4 25.Nd5 Rg8 26.Kd2 and White's extra piece and greater activity will decide.].

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nxe4 Qh5 Nd6 Bb3 Nc6 Nb5 g6 Qf3 f5 Qd5 Qe7 Nxc7+ Kd8 Nxa8 b6 d3 Bb7 h4 f4 Qf3 Nd4 Qg4 Bh6
en: 14...Bg7!? is Ekebjaerg-Timmerman, corr. 1991 which Black won after extraordinary complications.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6 Ne5 f6 Ng4 g5
en: An aggressive use of pawns in front of the King to keep me from achieving results on the h6 square. It is surprising how well Black does with this.

line: d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O Qc2 c5 d5 exd5 Ng5 h6 Nxd5 Bxd5 cxd5 Bd6 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Re8 O-O Na6
en: A look at the pawn structure suggests the future course of the game. Black has passed pawn Qside and White should push the e and f pawns aiming to obtain a winning attack with e5. Whoever executes his plan first wins.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 f6 exf6 Nxf6 O-O Bd6 Nf3 Qc7 Nc3 a6 Bg5 O-O Bh4 Nh5
en: ... and this is it. It is nearly always dim to stick a Knight on the rim, but here the trusty steed intensifies Black's pressure on the key squares g3 and f4, allowing Black to keep his Black-squared Bishop, his best minor piece.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O Nd5 a5 a3 Bc5 Ng5 g6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Ne4 Qe7 b3 Ba7 Bb2 d6 Ng3 f5 Be2 Be6
en: Is risky and prematured, although white has to play precisely.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3 O-O b4 Be6 Rb1 f6 d3 Qd7 Ne4 Nd5 Qc2 b6 Bb2 a5
en: The strongest answer. Other responses have been tried here also but with less success:.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bc4 Bd6 Qe2+ Kf8 O-O Nbd7 d4 Nb6 Bb3 Nbxd5 c4 Ne3 Bxe3 fxe3 Qxe3 c5 Nc3 Ng4 Qd2 Bf5
en: Black loses the thread here. He could still have fought for advantage in the following line:.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be3 Bg7 f3 Nc6 Qd2 O-O Bc4 Bd7 Bb3 Rc8 O-O-O Ne5 Kb1 Re8 h4 h5 Bg5 Rc5
en: A pawn structure gives White more possibilities for comfortable development - Black should consider every free square to place the pieces more actively but then he has to prove its reliability in rather suspiciously looking complications.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 b5 cxb5 Bxb5 Bg2 c5 O-O Bc6 Ba3 Na6 Nbd2 Be7 dxc5 Bxc5 Bxc5 Nxc5 Rc1 Nb7 e4 O-O
en: Ivanchuk decided to reject this "gift". In case of.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Bd7 b3 Kc8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5 h3 Re8 Rd3 c5
en: Black weakens the d5-square. Maybe he can avoid this and play 14...h5!?

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O Bd7 f4 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Kb1 Qb6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe1 Be7 Bd3 Qc5
en: In exchange for double f-pawns black has two bishops and very solid pawn bastions in the centre.

line: e4 c6 d4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Bg4 h3 Bh5 Bd3 e6 Qe2 d5 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7 Qxe7 g4 Bg6 Bxg6 hxg6 h4 Na6 O-O-O O-O-O Rdg1
en: Both kings have been brought to safety and all pieces developed, so the middlegame begins.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 h5 Bh7 Nf3 Nf6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Be7 O-O-O O-O Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 Bc3
en: Criticised in the tournament bulletin. A possible alternative would be 15 Ne4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Ne5 Qc8 Qd3 b5 Qf3
en: Very surprising! The main idea is 15 ... Be7? 16 Bg5! It is very difficult to find a good move for Black here.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 h6 b3 Ke8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5 a4 h5 Ne2 Be6 c4
en: Fritz wanted to prevent ...Bd5 but this reminded me of when Vishy feasted on 'yoghurt' against Fritz in a Berlin Defence and captured all three pawns with his light squared bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5 Be2 Bb7 Nbd2 Nbd7 Nb3 Bf8 a4 b4 Nfd2 Bd5 f3
en: To play e4 and kick the bishop.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 c5 cxd5 exd5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Nc3 O-O Bg5 cxd4 Nxd4 h6 Bf4 Bg4 h3 Be6 Rc1 Re8 Nxe6 fxe6 e4
en: All theory. With this pawn break, White contests Black's center pawns, aiming to open lines for his two bishops and perhaps an exchange of queens.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 Bb3 cxd4 exd4 Nc6 Nc3 Be7 Re1 O-O Bf4 Na5 d5 Nxb3 Qxb3 exd5 Rad1 Be6 Qxb7
en: Getting the pawn back, but now the queen is exposed on b7.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3 Nc6 Bd2 d5 e5 f6 exf6 Bxf6 Kh1
en: Vacating g1 so that the knight can head for e5.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 Bg5 Be7 Qa4+ Bc6 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 O-O e3 Bb7 Be2 a6 Rc1 Nbd7 O-O b5 Qa2 c5 Rfd1
en: On the surface White's prospects seem quite promising as he has completed his development and centralized his rooks.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Ne2 Qc7 Qe1 d5 Bd4
en: If 15.Bxe4 dxe4, and Black intends a6-a5 and an exchange of dark squared bishops followed by Nd7-c5 and targeting the weak a4-pawn (with Bb7-c6).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 a3 f6 Bd3 Qc7 O-O O-O-O Re1 fxe5 dxe5 c4 Bc2 Bc5 Nbd2 Nh6 b4 Bb6 h3 Nf7 Qe2
en: White has strengthened his outpost on the square e5 and intends to drive the enemy knight from c6, in order to activate his "runner" on the square d4. Black needs to undertake counter-actions quickly.

line: d4 d5 c4 c5 cxd5 Nf6 Nf3 cxd4 Qxd4 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 b4 e5 Qc4 Bxb4 Qxc8+ Ke7 Qxh8 Bxc3+ Bd2 Ne4 Rd1 Nc6 Qxa8 Qb6 e3 Nxd2 Nxd2
en: Now White has no need moves like 15. Bd3.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3 Qg7 Bxf4 Nf6 Ne4 Be7 Bg5 Rg8 Qh5+
en: Planning a brilliant combination.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d3 Nc6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 O-O O-O Nbd2 Rb8 Re1 d6 c3 b6 d4 Qc7 e5 Nd5 exd6 Bxd6 Ne4 c4 Nxd6 Qxd6 Ng5
en: Beginning the kingside attack. Although it weakens his kingside, it turns out that Black should have played 15... h6 here.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6 cxd6 Nd5 Nxd5 Bxe7 Ne3+ Ke1
en: In retrospect, it might have been better to give back the queen with 15. Qxe3 although Black would have ended up a pawn ahead.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Bg5 f6 Bh4 Nh6 Nc3 Be7 O-O O-O Qc4+ Kh8 Nd4 Qd7 Rad1 Rf7 f4 a5 f5
en: Planning to move the knight to e6.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4 Bb2 exd3 Qxd3 a6 h4 axb5 cxb5 Ne7 Qd2 O-O h5
en: To remove the pawn protection from the king and open up the h file. The immediate threat is 16. hxg6 hxg6 17. Nh7 Re8 18. Ne4 and Black is in serious trouble.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4 Bc2 a6 Qf3 b5 Qh3 g6 f5
en: To exchange pawns and open the file for the rook on f1.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5 O-O Bb7 Rc1 Re8 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 cxd4 Rc7
en: Black's days are numbered.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5 Na5 Ne5 Bb7 Ng4

en: Picking up another pawn and making it difficult for White to develop his knight.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5 Bd7 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 Bf4 Qg7 Nb5 Bd6
en: With this clever move Black offers the exchange after 16. Bxd6 cxd6 17. Nc7+ Kd8 18. Nxa8 Nf5 the advantage would be Black's. His pieces are active while White's knight is useless at a8.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nce7 c4 Nxd5 exd5 bxc4 Nxc4 Nf6 Be3 Rb8 Be2 Be7 a4 O-O O-O Bb7
en: The bishop is badly placed on the b-file.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 Nc3 Nxc3 dxc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O Qd2 Nd7 O-O-O Nc5 Be3 Be6 Kb1 Qc8 Nd4 Bd7 h4 Re8 f3 Bf8 g4 Ne6
en: Black has spent five consecutive moves on pieces and hasn't advanced pawns yet. This is unlikely to work. He might be aiming to trade pieces, but that could backfire by bringing White's bishops to even better squares!

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 f6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Nh6 h3 Nc6 dxe5 fxe5 Qd2 Nf7 Nh2 Nd4 Bg4 Nh8
en: I haven't seen this maneuver since a game of Bobby Fischer's. It's maneuvering toward f4 or h4. It takes time for knights to get to their ideal squares, whereas queens, rooks and bishops can often arrive in just a couple of moves.

line: c4 e5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 d6 O-O O-O d4 Nbd7 Qc2 Re8 Rd1 exd4 Nxd4 a5 e4 Nc5 f3 c6 Be3 Qe7 Bf2 Nfd7 b3 Ne5
en: White's pawns are pretty safe, but her pieces will have to be activated and brought into the battle in a more aggressive way, as the game progresses, if she's to win.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O d4 d6 Nf3 Nc6 O-O a6 Re1 Na5 Qa4 b6 Nd5 Bd7 Qc2 c5 Nxf6+ Bxf6 Bh6 Re8 e3 Rc8 d5 b5
en: Black trades one way of attacking Pc4 for another; Bf6 is also more open, though White might soon evacuate the dark square diagonal altogether.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 e4 Bb4 d3 d6 h3 O-O Be2 Ne7 O-O c6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Ng6 Re1 Re8 Bf1 Bd7 Qb3 Qc8 Rb1 b6 Kh2 h6
en: Kasparov is making useful moves, but without committing to a specific plan of offense. Perhaps there isn't one and he's just playing an equal position, in hopes his opponent will allow things to slip a bit.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Ne7 b3 Bg4 Ng5 Ke8 Bb2 Nd5 h3 Bf5 g4 Bd7 Ne2 h5
en: Just when White appears to have his pawns storming up the board Black undermines them, and before Ne2-g3 could secure square h5!

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 c3 Bg7 Bd3 Be6 Qh5 O-O exf5 Bxd5 f6 h6
en: Showing terrific confidence Ivanchuk doesn't try to block Bd3 just yet. He intends, I suppose, to use ...f7-f5 (a standard device in this opening) and leave Bd5 unblocked (by a Pe4) to attack Pa2 & Pg2.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3 bxa3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bb2 Nf4 Bc1 Nxg2 Ng5 Nxe1
en: Black grabs material and White begins an attack...

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nf6 c4 b4 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Nc2 Qg6 Qd5 Bb7 Nxb4 Rc8 Be3 Be7 h4 O-O
en: After this Rc8 is defended, so that ... Nc6xb4 is a real threat. Any move such as ...Nc6-d8 also uncovers a strong threat to Pe4.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 c4 dxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 Nc3 Nd5 Qxc4 Nb6 Qb3 e5 dxe5 Be6 Qc2 Nd4 Qd3 Bc5 e3 Nxf3+ gxf3 Qxd3 Bxd3 O-O-O Be2 Bb4 Bd2 Na4
en: Quickly, before White can castle and bring rooks into play, the Nc3 and it's supporters (Bd2 and Pb2) are threatened.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nbd2 Bf8 c3 Na5 Ba2 c5 d4 d6 b4 exd4 bxa5 dxc3
en: I suppose one of the key ideas is that Nd2 will now have to move and that gives Pe4 to Black. Pa5 might or might not be gathered-in as the game progresses. Anyway, the central Pe4 is much more important as it blocked Black's pieces.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4 b5 Bc2 Bb7 Qe2 Ng6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nh4 Nbd2 Rc8 Bb1 Bd6 a4 bxa4 Rxa4 Nxf3+ Nxf3 Nb4
en: From here the knight defends Pa6 and keeps Ra4 inactive. After an e4-e5 it could go back ...Nb4-d5. However, it's tied to Bd6, so e4-e5 would shove ...Bd6-e7 which isn't a very active square for the bishop.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5 Ra4 b4 Qh4 O-O Rg8 f4 Kd8
en: This ugly-duckling move allows Qh4 to move without Nd5-f6+ picking up Rg8.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 c5 Qg4 Qf6 c3 cxd4 cxd4 b6 O-O Bb7 Be3 h5
en: Karpov really has a nice position - just look how harmoniously placed his pieces are.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 Bd6 Qe2 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qc7 Qg4 Kf8 O-O c5 dxc5 Nxc5 Be3 Nxd3 cxd3 e5
en: Black has to unravel somehow, and this is the best way.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qb3 c5 dxc5 Nc6 Nf3 Ne4 Bd2 Nxd2 Nxd2 Bxc5 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Be2 Bb7 O-O f5 Na4 Be7 Rfd1 Qc7 Rac1 Na5
en: All already seen in the practice.

line: c4 e6 e3 Nf6 Nf3 b6 Be2 Bb7 O-O d5 d4 Bd6 Nc3 O-O b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Qe7 Nb5 Ne4 Nxd6 cxd6 Nd2 Ndf6 f3 Nxd2 Qxd2 dxc4 Bxc4 d5
en: "Clearly to prevent e3-e4". (Tartakower).

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Be7 e3 O-O c5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Qc2 f5 Bc4 Nc6 a3 Bf6 O-O-O Kh8 f3 Qe7 Bg3 f4 Qxe4 fxg3 hxg3 g6
en: Giving up the third pawn Lasker hopes to use the g-file for defence. After the obvious.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 Bd2 Ne7 Nb5 Bxd2+ Qxd2 O-O c3 b6 f4 Ba6 Nf3 Qd7 a4 Nbc6 b4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb7 Nd6 f5 a5 Nc8
en: To eliminate the annoying white Knight in d6.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 d6 Bg5 Bxc3 bxc3 Qe7 Re1 Nd8 d4 Bg4 h3 Bh5 g4 Bg6 d5 c6 Bd3 cxd5 exd5 Rc8
en: Forcing White to a defending move, and preparing a complicate combination.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 d4 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 Qe2 exd4 Nxd4 Bd7 O-O Be7 b3 O-O Bb2 b5 a4 b4 Nd1 c5 Nf3 Bc6
en: And now it is the Black Bishop who seizes his own milky way.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 O-O e3 b6 cxd5 exd5 Bd3 Bb7 O-O c5 Re1 c4 Bb1 a6 Ne5 b5 f4 Re8 Qf3 Nf8
en: Going preventively to further defend the pawn h7 without any resort of castle weakening moves, such as h7-h6 or g7-g6.

line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4 Nf3 Nc6 a3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 gxf3 Nxe5 f4 Nc6 Bg2 Qd7 b4 a6 Bb2 Rd8 Nd2 Nge7 Nb3 Nf5 Qd3 Be7 Be4 Nd6
en: The weakness of Black's QP has prevented him from obtaining a natural development. The result is that his position is already lost.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 d6 g4 a6 Be3 Nge7 Nb3 b5 f4 Bb7 Qf3 g5 fxg5 Ne5 Qg2 b4 Ne2 h5 gxh5 Nf5 Bf2 Qxg5
en: White cannot castle queen side.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bd7 b3 O-O Bb2 g6 Qf3 Nh5 e5 d5 Nd2 a5 c4 c5
en: Black prepares the advance a4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8 Ng3 Bg6 Ne4 Bc7 Nxc5 e5
en: Black threatens to open the position, possibly with ...f7-f5, ...e5-e4, before White can complete his development.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nbd7 Nf3 Be7 Nxf6+ Bxf6 h4 c5 Qd2 cxd4 Nxd4 h6 Bxf6 Nxf6 Qb4 Nd5 Qa3 Qe7 Bb5+ Bd7 Bxd7+ Kxd7
en: Fritz 4 "thinks" this position is equal! That it doesn't "see" any problems for Kd7 is interesting. Topalov certainly saw possibilities.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 Qe2 Bc5 O-O O-O c3 d6 Rd1 Re8 d3 a6 Bxc6 bxc6 Nbd2 a5 Nc4 h6 Nxa5 Rxa5 b4 Bxb4 cxb4 Ra4 a3 Bd7
en: Black clears the way for ...Qa8 to support Ra4, keeping Pa3 backward and threatened. Black holds White's forces in place and hopes to be able to threaten them later-on.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Ng8 f4 f6 Bd4 Qa5 Qd2 fxe5 fxe5 c5 Be3 Bxe5 Bc4 Nf6 O-O Ba6
en: Bc4 is inhibiting ...O-O.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 a6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Qc7 Bd3 Nc6 Be3 Nf6 O-O Nxd4 Bxd4 Bc5 Bxf6 gxf6 Qg4 Kf8 Kh1 h5 Qh4 Be7 f4 b5 f5 Qe5
en: After this it's difficult for White to do any damage on the dark squares.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be3 a6 Bd3 b5 Nxc6 Qxc6 O-O Bb7 a3 Nf6 Qe2 h5 f4 Ng4 Bd2 Bc5+ Kh1 Bd4 Rae1 O-O-O
en: Black has absolutely no weakness White can exploit. This is very nearly winning for Black.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5 d5 e6 O-O O-O Nbc3 Na6 h3 exd5 exd5 Nc4 b3 Nd6 Bf4 b6 Qd2 Re8
en: This fights for control of e4 and eyes Ne2, but it also avoids Bf4-h6xg7, which would weaken Kg8.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Be2 h5 Bxg4 hxg4 Qd2 Qb6 Nb3 a5 Qxg5 Bxc3+ bxc3 a4
en: _By the way, black's idea is ...Ra5-h5, which is realized in the game. However, it turns out to be useless because h2 is extremely solid._.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Bd3 O-O Nge2 Re8 Qc2 c6 h3 Ne4 Bf4 Ndf6 f3 Nxc3 bxc3 Bd6 Bxd6 Qxd6 e4 Nh5
en: Black's N is badly misplaced on h5.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 Ne2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb6 O-O Be7 f4 g6 a3 a5 b3 Bd7 g4 Qc7 Bb2 f5 gxf5 exf5
en: This is a huge decision, and I think that 15...gf5 would have been more natural.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 a3 Bb7 O-O-O Nd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Ngf6 e5 Ng4 Bg1 cxd4 Bxd4 dxe5 fxe5 Bxf3 gxf3 Ngxe5 Qe3 Qc7
en: White has certain compensation here due to pressure on e5 and the ideas of Bh3 and Nd5.

line: Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 c6 d4 Nd7 Bc4 Ngf6 Ng5 e6 N1f3 h6 Nh3 g5 Nhg1 Bd6 Ne2 b6 Qd3 Bb7 Be3 Qc7 O-O-O O-O-O Rhe1 Nd5 Nc3 Nf4
en: This is excellent if followed up right.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Ba6 b3 d5 Bg2 Bb4+ Nfd2 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bb2 O-O O-O Nc6 Nc3 Rc8 cxd5 exd5 Na4 Nd4 Nc3 Qe7 Re1 Nc2
en: "The straw that breaks the camel's back.".

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+ Kf8 Bf4 Nxf2 Qe2 Ng4+ Kh1 Bd7
en: Wollner realizes that he is now on the defensive, and he tries hard to cover the weak e8 square. But Charousek is not to be denied!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Bb7 d3 Nd7 Nbd2 Nc5 Bc2 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nf1 Rad8 Ne3 Qd7
en: The drive begins. From now on, Gligoric's pieces come flooding out with a speed that is truly frightening.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Kh1 d5 f4 exf4 Rxf4 Qe7 d4 Bb6
en: But now we can see clearly the sense in which this piece is more of a target than an asset.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Be3 c5 Qd2 O-O Rc1 Qa5 Nf3 e6 d5 exd5 exd5 Re8 Be2 Bf5 O-O Nd7 h3 Nb6
en: GM Lein thinks White is in deep trouble. GK might play Nb6-a4. Another of GK's ideas might be Qa5-a4.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 Nf3 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 e6 Ndb5 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 e3 Be6 Be2 Be7 Bd2 a6 Nd4 Nxd4 exd4 O-O Qb3 Re8 O-O Bd6
en: Geller has set a trap in an equal position.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Qxd4 d5 exd6 Nxd6 Nc3 Nc6 Qf4 Bf5 Bb5 Qe7+ Kf1 Be4 Bxc6+ Bxc6 Ne5 O-O-O Nxc6 bxc6 Qa4 Nb5 Be3 Qb4
en: Poor Kholmov has to win but suffers in a dangerous position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 c5 Rb1 Bg7 Nf3 O-O Be3 Qa5 Qd2 cxd4 cxd4 Qxd2+ Kxd2 Rd8 d5 Nc6 Bc5 e6 d6 b6
en: (What about 15...e5? A good plan would be then 16.Bc4 with the idea of Ng5 or even Kc2 and Rd1. Black chose a dificult plan.).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 Bxf7 Nf6 Be6 Qb8 Qd1+ Ke8 O-O g6 Ne4 Qd8
en: (Despite the slower than necessary build-up White can now finish off. 15...Bg7 was another try but 16.Bh6 exposes the shortcomings of the Black position. (16. ..Bxh6 17.Nxf6+).).

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 Nf6 e3 Nbd7 f3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Bb3 e6 Nge2 Bb7 a3 a6 e4 Be7 Nf4 Qb6 Bxe6 fxe6 Nxe6 Bf8 Be3 c5 d5 Qa5
en: (Necessary as White was threatening b4.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 c5 exd5 Qxd5 Ngf3 cxd4 Bc4 Qd6 O-O Nf6 Re1 a6 a4 Nc6 Qe2 Be7 Bb3 O-O Nc4 Qc7 g3 Nd5 Bd2 Rd8 Ng5 h6
en: (Of course I could not leave the Ng5 unmolested! White had threats of 16.Qh5, or 16.f4 (the latter strengthens his grip on the e5 square).)#.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Kf2 f6 Be3 fxe5 fxe5 O-O a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bd3 Qc7
en: (Also planning to sacrifice on e5, but to recapture with the queen after d4xe5, but...).

line: Nf3 d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c5 Nxc4 Nc6 b3 Bf5 Bb2 Nf6 Rc1 e6 g3 Be7 Bg2 Qc7 O-O O-O d3 Rad8 Rc2 Rd7 Qa1 Rc8 Nce5 Nb4 Rcc1 Rd6
en: Presumably Black intended to play this Rook to a6, but see note at move 19.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 d5 Nce7 Qe2 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 c4 c5 O-O g6 Bd2 a5 Nc3 h6 Qd1 Nc8 Qa4 Nb6 Qxd7+ Nxd7 b3 Be7
en: Unexpected after preparing to fianchetto on g7. Still the Bishop can support K-side pawn advances better from e7.

line: Nf3 Nf6 g3 b5 Bg2 Bb7 O-O e6 b3 Bd6 d4 O-O Na3 a6 c4 bxc4 Nxc4 Bb4 Bb2 d5 a3 dxc4 axb4 cxb3 Qxb3 Qd6 Rfc1 Nc6 Qc4 Nd5
en: Increasing the pressure on the isolated pawn on b4.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 d4 g3 c5 b4 cxb4 a3 e6 Bg2 Nc6 O-O Nf6 Bb2 bxa3 Nxa3 Bc5 Ne1 e5 Nd3 Bd6 Nb5 e4 Nxd6+ Qxd6 Ba3 Qe6 Nf4 Qe5
en: [15...Qxc4 16.d3 is awkward for Black. Now, my original intention was also 16.d3, but after rejecting that and 16.Rb1, I fortunately settled on a strong move.].

line: d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 e4 d6 Nf3 Bg7 Bc4 O-O Qe2 Nc6 d5 Na5 Bd3 c5 O-O a6 a4 b6 Bd2 Qc7 b3 c4 Bxc4 Nxc4 Qxc4 Qxc4 bxc4 Nd7
en: White's queenside pawn formation has been broken up at the cost of a temporary pawn sacrifice, the Queen's have been exchanged, and I believe that Black now has a slight advantage.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 g3 d5 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 dxc4 Nxc6 Qxd1+ Nxd1 bxc6 Bg2 Nd5 Ne3 e6 Nxc4 Ba6 b3 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nxd2 Nb4 Kd1 Ke7
en: The first original move played in this game. Very typical for modern correspondence play: everybody has a big collection of games and it is nothing unusual to replay known games till late in the endgame.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nf6 Ne5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Qa5+ c3 Qa6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Nd7 Nxd7 Kxd7
en: White has more space for manoeuvring, which defines his advantage. Ponomariov gives a good example how to handle such positions:.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 a6 O-O-O Bd7 f4 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Kb1 Qb6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qe1 Be7 Bd3 Qc5 Qg3 O-O-O
en: It's a novelty: black doesn't worry about his king-side. The previous game runs.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Nxe6 Qe7 O-O fxe6 Bg6+ Kd8 Bf4 b5 a4 Bb7 Re1 Nd5 Bg3 Kc8 axb5 cxb5 Qd3
en: Deep Blue brings his queen into the attack and even gains time by attacking a pawn.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1 Nxd5 cxd5 Ne5 Be2 Re8 h4 c5 f4 Nd7 Bf3
en: Supporting the advance e3-e4. White's plan is to get the pawns e4, f4 and d5 rolling. Black attacks on the queen's side.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Nxc3 bxc3 Nd7 e4 c5 Bf4 Qc8 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Ne5 Qc8 Qd3 b5 Qf3 Bd6 Nxf7
en: Immediately indicating an evaluation of +2, but this is far too optimistic!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 O-O Bg7 Nbd2 O-O Re1 Re8 d4 Bd7 d5 Ne7 Bxd7 Nxd7 a4 h6 a5 a6 b4 f5 c4 Nf6 Bb2
en: This move was criticised by many commentators.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 e6 e3 Nf6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 Bb3 cxd4 exd4 Nc6 Nc3 Be7 Re1 O-O Bf4 Na5 d5 Nxb3 Qxb3 exd5 Rad1 Be6 Qxb7 Bd6 Bg5
en: Keeping the bishop on the board and pinning the knight on f6 against the queen.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Nd2 Bg6 g3 Nc6 e3 a6 b4 b5 cxb5 axb5 Bb2 Na7 h4 h6 d5 exd5 Bg2 c6 O-O
en: White's compensation for his pawn is enormous - a massive lead in development, two raking bishops, and a weakness on g7 that prevents Black catching up in development in a normal manner.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O Kh1 Nbd7 a4 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3 Rc8 Qd2 Qc7 Rac1 h6 Rfd1 Rfe8 Qe1
en: A very useful move preparing pressure on the a-pawn combined with doubling on the d-file.

line: Nf3 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e6 a3 Nxd4 Qxd4 b6 Bf4 Bc5 Qd2 O-O Rd1 Bb7 Bd6 Bxd6 Qxd6 Rc8 e3 Re8 f3 Rc6 Qd4 Ba6 Ne4
en: White is aiming for simplification, but he is in fact helping Black. Correct was 16.Na2!, relieving the pressure on c4. After 16...Rc5 17.Nb4 Bb7 Black has a comfortable game, but no more.

line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5 cxd5 cxd5 e4 dxe4 Bb5+ Bd7 dxe5 Nc6 Qd5 Qe7 Bf4 g5 Bg3 Bg7 Qxe4 Nxe5 Nd5 f5 Qe2 Qd6 Nf3 f4 Nxf4 gxf4 Bxd7+
en: I had thought that 16.Bxf4 would be an error after 16...Bxb5 17.Qxb5+ Qc6! but I didn't have time to analyze 18.Qe2 0-0-0 19.Nxe5 Qxg2 20.Rc1+ which also wins.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3 Nc6 Bd2 d5 e5 f6 exf6 Bxf6 Kh1 a5 a4
en: Precise. On 16.a3 a4 17.Ba2 Qb6! 18.Rb1 Qc5 19.Rc1 Qb6, so you see the problem.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5 Bxb5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qa5+ Nfd2 Qxb5 Nxd6 Qa6 N2c4 Nd7 O-O Nb6 Nxb6
en: Weak is 16.Qd3? when 16...Nxc4 17.Nxc4 Bf5 18.Qe2 Rfe8 gives Black too much activity.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Be7 Qf3 Qc7 O-O-O Nbd7 g4 b5 Bxf6 Nxf6 g5 Nd7 f5 Bxg5+ Kb1 Ne5 Qh5 Qd8 Nxe6
en: After 16.Rg1 I played the novelty 16...h6! in the game Wolff-Browne, World Open 1989, which I managed to win in a very exciting ending.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 a3 Bb7 Nc3 d5 Bg5 Be7 Qa4+ Bc6 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 O-O e3 Bb7 Be2 a6 Rc1 Nbd7 O-O b5 Qa2 c5 Rfd1 Nd5 Bxe7
en: If 16.Bf4 Nxf4 17.exf4 Qb6 18.d5 c4, with an edge for Black.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Ne2 Qc7 Qe1 d5 Bd4 Bc5 Ng3
en: If 16.Bxc5 Qxc5+ followed by Nd7-f6 with a great game for Black.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O b5 Bb3 Bc5 a4 Rb8 c3 d6 d4 Bb6 Na3 Bg4 axb5 axb5 Nxb5 O-O Re1 Bxf3 gxf3 Nh5 Kh1 Qf6 Rg1
en: Winning an important tempo.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Nc3 gxf3 O-O c6 Qxf3 Qf6 e5 Qxe5 Bxf7+ Kxf7 d4 Qxd4+ Be3 Qg7 Bxf4 Nf6 Ne4 Be7 Bg5 Rg8 Qh5+ Qg6 Nd6+
en: If now 16..Bxd6 17. Rxf6+ followed by 18. Rxg6 notice that Black's Queen is pinned, so he cannot play 17...Qxf6.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 d6 d4 Bg4 Qd3 Nc6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Kg6 Qxb7 Nxd4 Qxa8 Nf6 Na3 f3 g3 Bh3+ Ke1 Qg4 Be3 d5 Qxa7 Nc6 Qxc7
en: If 16. Qa4 d4 17. bf4 (If 17. bd2 Qxe4+ and f7 wins or 17. Qxc6 dxe3 wins) 17...Bb4+ 18. c3 dxc3 wins.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4 Qh4+ Kf1 b5 Bxb5 Nf6 Nf3 Qh6 d3 Nh5 Nh4 Qg5 Nf5 c6 Rg1 cxb5 g4 Nf6 h4 Qg6 h5 Qg5 Qf3 Ng8 Bxf4 Qf6 Nc3
en: White now has an enormous lead in development, definitely worth more than a piece.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 d6 Nbd2 Nd7 c3 Nc5 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 Bxa8 Bc2 Bf6 b4 Ne6 Nf1
en: The knight is headed for d5 or f5 via e3.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6 cxd6 Nd5 Nxd5 Bxe7 Ne3+ Ke1 Kxe7 Qd3
en: Breaking the pin on the knight and threatening 17. Qxd6.

line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3 Nc6 fxe4 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nf3 Bd6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O Nd5 Nxf3+ gxf3 Be7 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Qd2 d5 O-O-O dxe4 fxe4 Qxe4 Bxf6
en: If now 16... Qxh1 then 17. Bc4+ wins the queen.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ Nbd7 O-O-O Rd8 Rxd7 Rxd7 Rd1 Qe6 Bxd7+ Nxd7 Qb8+
en: Everything but the king.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4 Bc2 a6 Qf3 b5 Qh3 g6 f5 b4 fxg6
en: If 16... bxc3 then 17. Bxf6 Nxf6 18. Rxf6 fxg6 (Not 18... Bxf6 19. Qxh7#) 19. Bxg6 $1 hxg6 20. Rxg6#. If instead 16... fxg6 then 17. Qe6+ Kh8 18. Nxd7 Nxd7 (If 18... Qxd7 then 19. Bxf6+ wins the queen) 19. Bxe7 wins a piece.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 c3 e5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne7 Bg5 O-O Qxd4 Nc6 Qh4 Qb6 Nc3 Bxe5 Rae1 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxb5 Qh6
en: Threatening 18. Bf6 and 19. Qg7#.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Bg5 Be7 e3 b6 cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5 Bf4 O-O Bd3 c5 O-O Bb7 Rc1 Re8 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 cxd4 Rc7 Bc8 Qh5
en: Threatening 17. Qxh7+ Kf8 18. Qh8#.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5 Na5 Ne5 Bb7 Ng4 Qd8 Ne3
en: If now 16... Qc7 then 17. Nh5 Qd8 18. Nxg7 Kxg7 19. Qg4+ Kh8 20. Qh4 Kg8 21. Bxf6 Bxf6 22. Qxh7#.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4 Bh7 Bg3 Nxg3 fxg3 Qc7 Ne5 Bd6 h4
en: Making 16... 0-0 dangerous. Black still can't play 16... 0-0-0 because17. Nxf7 Qxf7 18. Bxe6+ wins the queen. If 16... Bxe5 17. dxe5 Black cannot play 0-0-0 because of the rook on the open d file.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Bb6 d4 Qe7 O-O d6 h3 Nf6 Re1 O-O Na3 Nd8 Bf1 Ne8 Nc4 f6 a4 c6 Nxb6 axb6 Qb3+ Ne6 Qxb6 g5 Bc4
en: The bishop should stay on f1 to provide the king protection.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O Nge7 Ng5 O-O Bd3 Bf5 Bxf5 Nxf5 Ba3 Qg6 Bxf8 Qxg5 Ba3 dxc3 Bc1
en: Bringing the bishop to the defense of his king and vacating a3 for his knight.

line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 Bc4 g4 Ne5 Qh4+ Kf1 Nh6 d4 d6 Nd3 f3 g3 Qe7 Nc3 Be6 d5 Bd7 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 Bf4 Qg7 Nb5 Bd6 Qe1+
en: Preventing Black from castling and preparing to bring the Queen to the attack.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 d6 c3 g6 Nbd2 Bg7 Nf1 O-O Ba4 Nd7 Ne3 Nc5 Bc2 Ne6 h4 Ne7 h5 d5 hxg6 fxg6 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 Bb3
en: Now we can see the point of White's last two moves. this bishop bears down on Black's weak diagonal.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 d6 Bg5 Bg7 Nc2 O-O Be2 Qa5 Bd2 a6 O-O Bd7 Rc1 Rac8 f4 Rfe8 a3 Qb6+ Kh1 Na5 e5
en: White takes a shot at immediate activity to counter Black's on the c-file. Usually this wouldn't work, but there are instances (exceptions sort of) where it can work. In this case I'm wondering where Nf6 will go.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6 O-O Nf6 Be3 Bb4 Na4 Be7 Nxc6 bxc6 Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Qxc8 Bd4 O-O Qd3 Qc7 b3 a5 Rad1
en: White threatens Bxf6 followed by Qxd7 and seems interested only in simple piece play -- tactical opportunism.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Re8 d4 Bb7 Nbd2 Bf8 d5 Nb8 Nf1 Nbd7 N3h2 Nc5 Bc2 c6 b4
en: This makes Pc3 awkward, but more importantly it pushes Nc5 back, again giving White time to promote his own plan.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6 Nc3 Qc7 Be2 a6 O-O Nf6 Be3 Bb4 Na4 Be7 Nxc6 bxc6 Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Qxc8 Bd4 O-O e5 Nd5 c4 Nf4 Bf3
en: This is a far less desirable square for the bishop than d3, but I suppose it is heading to e4.

line: Nf3 c5 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O Nc6 c3 d5 d4 cxd4 cxd4 e6 Nc3 Nge7 b3 O-O Qd2 b6 Ba3 Ba6 Rac1 Qd7 Rfd1 Rfd8 g4 Rac8 h3 h6 e3
en: If Bg2 can't be useful on the h1-a8 diagonal then perhaps he'll just trade it at f1.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 c3 c5 Be3 Qc7 Ne5 a6 Qa4+ Nd7 O-O-O cxd4 Nxd7 Qxd7 Qc2 Bc5 Bxd4 Bxd4 Rxd4 Qc7 Bd3
en: White's lead in development is significant and his Kc1 isn't terribly weakened by the early c2-c3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Na3 Bxa3 bxa3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bb2 Nf4 Bc1 Nxg2 Ng5 Nxe1 Qh5
en: It's amazing that Black can survive this position for more than a couple of moves.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Qc7 a3 b6 Be3 Bb7 f3 Nc6 Be2 Rb8 b4 Be7 O-O O-O Rc1 Ne5 f4 Ng6 Bd3 Ba8 Qe2
en: I'm not sure why he doesn't commit to the direct e4-e5, but this move allows Rf1 to defend Rc1 and it takes aim at Pa6 as well as getting behind Pe4.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 Be7 Nc3 O-O f4 Re8 Kh1 Nbd7 Qe2 g6 Bd2 Bf8 Rad1 Nh5 Nf3 b6 e5 Bb7 Ng5
en: Now Pd6, Pf7 and Ph7 are all threatened. It's no coincidence.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Qf3 Nbd7 Be2 h5 Bg5 Qa5 Bd2 Qb6 Nb3 Qc7 a4 b6 Bg5 Bb7 Rd1 Be7 Qe3 Nc5 Nd2
en: Why on earth is he avoiding that knight trade? Now Rd1 is blocked and Black can hardly be worse.

line: Nf3 Nc6 d4 d5 e3 Bg4 Be2 e6 c3 Nf6 Qb3 Rb8 Nbd2 Bd6 Nf1 Ne4 Ng3 O-O Bd3 f5 a3 Kh8 Bd2 b5 Qc2 a5 b4 Qf6 Bc1 Qh6 Nf1
en: Forced. 16...Nxg3 was threatened.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 O-O Ne7 Bb3 Na5 d4 exd4 Nxd4 c5 Nf5 Nxf5 exf5 Nxb3 Re1+ Be7 f6 gxf6 axb3 d5 Qh5 Qd6 Nc3 Be6 Nb5
en: (!!) How does it begin the Fifth Simphony of Beethoven? Da-da-da.. .dawn! The "theme of destiny"!

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 d6 Bg5 Ne7 Nh4 c6 Bc4 Ne8 f4 Bxc3 bxc3 d5 Bb3 f6 fxe5 fxg5 Rxf8+ Kxf8 Qf3+ Kg8 Rf1
en: In reality, up to now, an identical game was played a year before in chess club in Berlin and it seems that Emanuel Lasker reported about it on his chess magazine. We may wonder: did Schlechter read that article? We do not know.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 O-O O-O c5 e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 dxc5 Na6 a3 Nxc5 b4 Ne6 Bb2 a5 b5 Qd7 Qe2 Rd8 Nbd2
en: Mikenas again:" A GM with a world reputation should not fall in a trap. I think it is not necessary to point out that white is already in bad shape. It is the effect of the bad omen?".

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bc5 O-O O-O Nxe5 Re8 Nxc6 dxc6 Bc4 b5 Be2 Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 Bf3 Re6 c3 Qd3 b4 Bb6 a4 bxa4 Qxa4 Bd7 Ra2
en: (?) Steinitz:" A silly move".

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 Be7 Nf3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O c5 Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 Nd7 Bf4 Bb7 Qf3 Re8 Qh3 Nf8 Rad1 Ng6 Bg3
en: (!) The beginning of a strategical plan which foresees a powerful attack.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 c5 e3 Nc6 b3 e6 Bb2 Nf6 Nbd2 cxd4 exd4 Bd6 Bd3 O-O O-O Nh5 g3 f5 Ne5 Nf6 f4 Bxe5 fxe5 Ng4 Qe2 Qb6 Nf3 Bd7 a3
en: To prevent Nb4 ... (Capablanca).

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 d4 Bd7 Nc3 Nge7 dxe5 dxe5 Bg5 h6 Bxc6 bxc6 Be3 Ng6 Qd3 Bd6 Nd2 Ne7 Nc4 Nc8 O-O-O Qe7 f4 f6 fxe5 fxe5 Rhf1
en: By means of the foregoing exchange, Lasker has not only opened another file for his pieces, but has induced a new weakness in Black's pawn position. 16...

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6 d4 exd4 Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 c5 Ne2 Bd7 Nbc3 O-O-O Bf4 Bc6 O-O Nf6 f3 Be7 Ng3 g6 Rfe1 Nd7 Nd1 Nb6 Nf1
en: With the idea of controlling his "d2", but all yhis regrouping behind the front demonstrates that all is not well with White. 16...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6 Bxg6+ hxg6 Qd3 Kf7 h4 Qg8 Bd2 Qh7 Bb4
en: So the Bishop tries another tack! It is headed either for Bd6, to bolster the king pawn, or for Bc5, in an attempt to eliminate one of Black's potentially dangerous bishop. 16...

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 a4 Nc6 Qe2 Qc7 Rd1 Bd6 dxc5 Bxc5 b3 O-O Bb2 e5 Nc3 e4 Ng5 Bd6 Nd5 Nxd5 Rxd5
en: With the decisive threat Qh5.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bd7 b3 O-O Bb2 g6 Qf3 Nh5 e5 d5 Nd2 a5 c4 c5 Ne2
en: The knight aims for Nd4-e2-c1-d3.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 Nbd2 Nc5 c3 d4 Ng5 Bd5 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qf3+ Ke6 Qg4+ Kf7 Qf5+ Ke7 e6
en: Theme: Clearance for f5-c5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 d6 Bxc6+ bxc6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bh5 e5 e6 exd6 Bxd6 d3 Ne7 Nbd2 O-O Ne4 Nd5 Re1 Re8 Ng3 Bg6 Ne4 Bc7 Nxc5 e5 a3
en: White, apparently, is not terribly impressed and simply uses Pa3 to oppose Nd5 and possibly to support b2-b4, whereby Nc5 is defended and Bc1-b2 becomes available.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e6 O-O Be7 f4 O-O Kh1 Qc7 a4 Nc6 Be3 Re8 Bf3 Rb8 Qd2 Bd7 Nb3 b6 Rae1 Bc8 e5
en: Ivanchuk bites the bullet and tries to force things to his advantage. But, Black's position is fairly resilient. If the f-file opens Pf7 could be a problem.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Nc3 Qc7 Bd3 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 O-O Nf6 Bg5 Bd6 Kh1 Bf4 Bxf4 Qxf4 Qe2 d5 Rae1 O-O Na4 a5 b3 Rd8 e5
en: At this stage of the game this doesn't seem likely to succeed. Only by really securing c5 could he hold Black down long enough to make any real gains. This is a pretty good indication Black has fully equalized.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 e3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 d4 cxd4 exd4 Be7 Bd3 Nc6 O-O O-O Re1 Nf6 a3 b6 Bc2 Bb7 Qd3 g6 Bh6 Re8 Rad1 Rc8 Bb3
en: This is still completely in line with the classical plan. After ...g6 the white bishop switches to a more active diagonal.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 c5 Ne2 cxd4 exd4 d5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Bxc3 Nxc3 Nxd2 Qxd2 O-O Be2 b6 b4 bxc5 dxc5 Nc6 b5 Ne7 O-O e5 f4
en: After the game white explained that he had been relying on this move, which attempts to break apart my center. Now enormous complications erupt.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 Na5 Bc2 c5 d4 Qc7 Nbd2 O-O h3 Nc6 d5 Nd8 a4 b4 Nc4 a5 Nfxe5
en: This little combination opens up the center so white can exploit his positional advantages, particularly on the light squares. Otherwise black would be fine after 16...Ne8.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6 d5 Ne7 b4 a5 bxa5 Rxa5 a4 Nd7 Ba3 Bh6 Nd2 Bxd2 Qxd2 f5 Nb5 Ra8 f4
en: Very interesting, but I passed up a big chance here. In fact I wanted to play 16.c5 very much as it seems like the thematic move, but I missed the critical follow-up 19.Qb2.

line: e4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 d4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bd3 Nc6 Bf4 f6 Qe2 fxe5 Nxe5 Ndxe5 Bxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 O-O Rf1 g6 O-O-O Bxf2 Kb1 Bd7 Ne4
en: This was my original idea and an interesting one. Unfortunately here I missed a straghtforward chance to beat a GM...

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Re1 Nf8 Rxe6 Nxe6 Bc4 Qd6 Bh6 Bf8 Re1
en: Najdorf tightens the screws mercilessly. How can the Knight be defended? White has a grip on d5 thanks to his Queen's control of the fifth rank, so ...Bd5 is out of the question. That leaves only Bc8.

line: e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nf6 Nf3 Bc5 Nxc3 d6 O-O O-O Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxf7 e5 Ng4 e6 Qh4 exf7+ Kf8 Bf4 Nxf2 Qe2 Ng4+ Kh1 Bd7 Rae1
en: This intensifies the pressure: Charousek now threatens to sacrifice a Queen on e8!

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Bc4 Nc6 d3 Bb4 Bg5 d6 Ne2 Be6 O-O h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Nd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Bc5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Kh1 d5 f4 exf4 Rxf4 Qe7 d4 Bb6 Ng3
en: Mieses consistently prepares for an assault on the King. Now 16...0-0? is poor, since White has 17.Nf5! and 18.Qg4 with decisive threats on g7 and h6.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Bg4 Nf3 Qxd5 Be2 Nc6 c4 Qh5 d5 Ne5 Nbd2 O-O-O O-O e6 Qa4 Bd6 h3 Bxh3 gxh3 Qxh3 Qxa7 Nxf3+ Nxf3 Ne4 Be3 h5 Qa8+
en: Or 16. c5 Rh6 17. Qa8+ Kd7 18. Qxd8+ Kxd8 19. Bxh6 Bxc5 with the double threat of Nxf2! and gxh6. If 20. Be3 then 20... Ng3!

line: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2 Bb4 Bxf6 Rxf6 Rad1
en: Now white deals with the threat of d5-d4.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 Ne7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 Qc7 Nf3 Nd7 O-O Bxc3 bxc3 Nxc5 Ba3 Bd7 Rb1 b6 Re1 Rc8 Bf1 Na4 Qc1 Qxc3 Ba6 Rc5 Bd3
en: This subtlety has great strength.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 f5 c4 Nf6 g3 e6 Bg2 Bb4+ Nc3 Nc6 O-O Bxc3 bxc3 dxc4 Qa4 h6 Ba3 Bd7 Qxc4 Ng4 Rae1 Qf6 e4 O-O-O e5 Qf7 Rb1 a6 Rxb7
en: (The Rook smashes in for the kill. Black cannot accept or refuse the Rook.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Kf2 f6 Be3 fxe5 fxe5 O-O a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bd3 Qc7 Qc2
en: (Pinning the ...Nc6 to the ...Qc7, and also threatening 17.Bxh7+, thus effectively, if Black played 16...Ndxe5 although he is still disolving the White centre, he will have a 2 pawn defecite, not just 1!).

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 cxd5 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qd1 exd5 Qxd5 Bd7 Nf3 Nf6 Qd1 Bc5 e3 Qc7 Be2 O-O-O O-O g5 Nd4 Qe5 Nxc6 Bxc6 Qb3 h5 Qc4
en: Qxf7 seems to give Black more space to attack.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 c6 Nf3 d6 h3 Na6 a3 Nc7 Be3 e6 Qd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 cxd5 Bd3 Qb6 c3 Bd7 Ne5 Bb5 Bxb5+ Qxb5 h4 Nf6 f3
en: Prevents intrusion on e4 & g4.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6 Ne5 f6 Ng4 g5 Bg3 Nc6 Nh2
en: This was prompted by the attractive opening of the d1 h5 diagonal in an attempt to combine Bishop and Queen against h7.

line: Nf3 d5 c4 c6 b3 Nf6 g3 Bf5 Bg2 Nbd7 cxd5 cxd5 Bb2 e6 Nc3 Bb4 O-O O-O Rc1 Rc8 Nh4 Nb6 Nxf5 exf5 e3 Ne4 Qh5 Nxc3 dxc3 g6 Qh6
en: # Now the problem is to deal withcxb4 (move it?) or c4. Time to break all th rules of sensible places for a Queen (ie. get desperate).

line: d4 c6 Nc3 d5 e4 dxe4 f3 exf3 Nxf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd4 Be3 Qf6 Qg3 e5 O-O-O Nd7 Bc4 Nh6 Rhf1 Qg6 Qxg6 fxg6 Bxh6 gxh6 Ne4 O-O-O Be6
en: Followed by Knight to f6 Black will lose the piece or drop the pawns on h7,h6 and g6.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 O-O a3 Bxc3+ Qxc3 b6 Bg5 Ba6 e3 d6 Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 c5 O-O Rc8 Qb3 h6 Bh4 Bb7 Nd2 cxd4 exd4 e5 Bf5
en: Its always very tempting to set up raking Bishops like this. Here Black is coerced into playing his Rook to an awkward square to avoid White breaching the Black Kingside defences by Bxd7 followed by Bxf6.

line: d4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 Be7 Nc3 O-O Qc2 c5 d5 exd5 Ng5 h6 Nxd5 Bxd5 cxd5 Bd6 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Re8 O-O Na6 a3 b5 Be3
en: I think this is wrong. He should go 16.b3! He has to play b3 anyway. The move played just clogs up the e file and delays White's strategic play of e4-e5 etc which never gets going.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 e6 Nge2 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Be3 Nf6 g4 h5 g5 Ng4 Bc1 Qb6 h3 Ne5 Be2 g6 Nb3 Nbc6 f4 Nd7 Rf1 Qc7 Be3 b5 f5
en: A thematic advance, but one which concedes the e5 square, from which a knight can play a major defensive role on the kingside.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3 Qb6 Qd2 Qxb2 Rb1 Qa3 dxc5 Bxc5 Bxc5 Qxc5 Bd3 a6 h4 Nb6 Rh3 Nc4 Bxc4 Qxc4 a3
en: This is a very important move. I need to free the knight from the need to hang around at c3 just to defend the poor pawn.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Bc5 c3 O-O O-O d6 h3 Bb7 Rd1 Re8 a4 b4 a5 Qb8 d4 exd4 cxd4 Ba7 e5 d5 Qd3
en: Now Black must try for complications.

line: c4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3 O-O b4 Be6 Rb1 f6 d3 Qd7 Ne4 Nd5 Qc2 b6 Bb2 a5 b5 Na7 a4
en: The first move deviating from known examples and ... a serious mistake. White is obliged here to sharpen the game by means of 16.d4, although this is pretty risky too, e. g.:.

line: d3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c4 Nf6 a3 d6 Nc3 Be7 g3 O-O Bg2 Be6 O-O Qd7 Ng5 Bf5 e4 Bg4 f3 Bh5 Nh3 Nd4 Nf2 h6 Be3 c5 b4 b6 Rb1 Kh8
en: It's hard to say what this move is about. It might be that Deep Blue envisages a time when the position will open up, in which case the king is best placed tucked away in the corner.

line: e4 c6 d4 d6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Bg4 h3 Bh5 Bd3 e6 Qe2 d5 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7 Qxe7 g4 Bg6 Bxg6 hxg6 h4 Na6 O-O-O O-O-O Rdg1 Nc7 Kb1 f6
en: It is a risky move as it compromises his pawn structure, but it also gives him a chance to counter-attack.

line: d4 d5 c4 Nc6 e3 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 exd4 Nxd5 Nf6 Qb3 Bxf3 gxf3 Rb8 Bd2 Bd6 O-O-O O-O Kb1 Nxd5 cxd5 Ne5 Be2 Re8 h4 c5 f4 Nd7 Bf3 b5
en: There we go. I began to like the Black position more and more. I guess Vishy wanted to have a much more quiet game today!

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O a6 dxc5 Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5 Kf1 b5 Be2 Bb7 Nbd2 Nbd7 Nb3 Bf8 a4 b4 Nfd2 Bd5 f3 Bd6 g3 e5
en: Its vital to keep the bishop shadowing the Nb3 and limit those white knights which are poised to invade.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O e3 Ne4 Bxe7 Qxe7 cxd5 Nxc3 bxc3 exd5 Qb3 Rd8 c4 dxc4 Bxc4 Nc6 Be2 b6 O-O Bb7 Rfc1 Rac8
en: Preparing for an eventual ...c5 pawn break to butt heads with White's rock-solid d-pawn.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4 e5 h6 Be3 Ne4 Qg4 Kf8 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nxc3 Bd3 b6 h4 Ba6 Rh3 h5 Qf4 Qe7 Rf3 Kg8 Nh3 Bxd3 cxd3 Na6
en: 16...Nd7 fails to 17.Rc1.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 d6 f4 Nc6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Bg7 O-O e6 d3 Nge7 Qe1 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Ne2 O-O Bb3 Nc6 Bd2 d5 e5 f6 exf6 Bxf6 Kh1 a5 a4 Qd6
en: The latent dangers for Black are revealed in a line like 16...Qb6 (a bit further away from the king) 17.f5! when either 17...gxf5 18.Nf4 or 17...exf5 18.Qg3 exposes him to a powerful White initiative. Boris sensibly stays more central.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Bd3 O-O Nf3 e6 h3 exd5 cxd5 b5 Bxb5 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qa5+ Nfd2 Qxb5 Nxd6 Qa6 N2c4 Nd7 O-O Nb6 Nxb6 axb6
en: Tal played 16...Qxb6 and after 17.Nxc8 Rfxc8 Black has good pressure for the pawn.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 Nbd7 Be3 e6 a4 b6 f4 Bb7 Bf3 Rc8 O-O Rxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Ne2 Qc7 Qe1 d5 Bd4 Bc5 Ng3 f5
en: Of course not 16...Qxf4?? 17.Bxe4 losing a piece for Black.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 c6 e3 Nf6 Nf3 Nbd7 Qc2 Bd6 g4 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 b6 Rg1 Bb7 Nd2 c5 cxd5 exd5 g5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Bb2 cxd4 cxd4 O-O
en: If I had imagined what the next move would be I would have preferred 16...Bd5, safely blocking the pawn d.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 a3 f6 Bd3 Qc7 O-O O-O-O Re1 fxe5 dxe5 c4 Bc2 Bc5 Nbd2 Nh6 b4 Bb6 h3 Nf7 Qe2 Rdf8 Kh1 g5
en: After the white king has moved to the square h1, a pawn attack becomes more effective.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5 e6 Qd2 Be7 O-O-O O-O f4 Nxd4 Qxd4 a6 Bc4 Qc7 Bb3 Rd8 e5 dxe5 Qxe5 Qb6 Qe2 Bd7 f5 Qc5
en: An important resource, which allows Black to keep the position.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 O-O O-O Bxd2 Qxd2 d6 b3 Nbd7 Bb2 Rb8 Rad1 Ne4 Qe3 f5 d5 exd5 cxd5 Ndf6 Nh4 Qd7 Bh3 g6
en: Black has been forced to weaken his dark squares and thus enhance the effectiveness of White's bishop on b2.

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nd7 Nc3 Ngf6 Bg5 Bb4 cxd5 exd5 Qa4 Bxc3+ bxc3 O-O e3 c5 Bd3 c4 Bc2 Qe7 O-O a6 Rfe1 Qe6 Nd2 b5 Qa5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4
en: Black has successfully prevented e4, but at a cost. White is ahead in development and Black is left with weak queenside pawns that White can use his advantave in development to attack.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Be7 Bg5 Nbd7 e3 O-O Rc1 c6 Qc2 a6 a3 h6 Bh4 Re8 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4 b5 Ba2 c5 Rd1 cxd4 Nxd4 Qb6 Bb1 Bb7
en: It looks as if White could now play 17. Ndxb5 axb5 18. Rxd7 Nxd7 19. Qh7+ Kf8 20. Qh8#. However, Black would answer 17. Ndxb5 with 17... Qc6 18. Nd4 Qxg2 with a very good game.

line: d4 d5 c4 dxc4 e4 e5 d5 f5 Nc3 Nf6 Bxc4 Bc5 Nf3 Qe7 Bg5 Bxf2+ Kf1 Bb6 Qe2 f4 Rd1 Bg4 d6 cxd6 Nd5 Nxd5 Bxe7 Ne3+ Ke1 Kxe7 Qd3 Rd8
en: Guarding the d pawn. Black has no desire to trade his wonderful knight on e3 for the rook on d1.

line: c4 e5 g3 Nc6 Bg2 d6 Nc3 Be6 d3 g6 b4 Qd7 b5 Nd8 Nf3 Bg7 Ng5 e4 Bb2 exd3 Qxd3 a6 h4 axb5 cxb5 Ne7 Qd2 O-O h5 gxh5 Rxh5 Bf5
en: Guarding the pawn on h7.

line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 b6 Bd3 Bb7 cxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nbd7 f4 c5 O-O c4 Bc2 a6 Qf3 b5 Qh3 g6 f5 b4 fxg6 hxg6
en: If now 17. Ne2 then 17... Ne4 and Black has counterplay.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Ng3 e6 Nf3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 dxc5 Bxc5 a3 O-O O-O b6 b4 Be7 Bb2 Qc7 b5 Na5 Ne5 Bb7 Ng4 Qd8 Ne3 Nd5
en: A mistake. The knight is needed on the kingside to defend the king.

line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bc4 Bf5 Qe2 e6 Bg5 Be7 O-O-O h6 Bh4 Ne4 g4 Bh7 Bg3 Nxg3 fxg3 Qc7 Ne5 Bd6 h4 f6
en: Once the knight is chased away Black will finally be able to castle.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 N1c3 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Nce7 c4 Nxd5 exd5 bxc4 Nxc4 Nf6 Be3 Rb8 Be2 Be7 a4 O-O O-O Bb7 Nb6 Nd7
en: There it is! But, does it really work?

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 c5 e3 Nc6 d4 d5 cxd5 exd5 Bb5 Bd6 O-O O-O dxc5 Bxc5 h3 Bf5 b3 Qd7 Ne2 a6 Bxc6 bxc6 Ng3 Ne4 Nxf5 Qxf5 Bb2 Bd6
en: Black's formation looks well-coordinated and safe, but I don't see any easy offensive.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Bd3 Nf6 O-O d6 c4 b6 Nc3 Bb7 f4 g6 Be3 Bg7 Qf3 O-O Rad1 Nbd7 Bf2 Qc7 Rfe1 Rfe8 Nb3 Nc5 Nxc5 bxc5
en: Black controls more central squares and probably plans ...Nf6-d7, where it's more centrally located and can move to e5 or f8 and it controls e5.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Nc6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb6 O-O Be7 a3 O-O b4 Be6 Rb1 f6 d3 Nd4 Nd2 c6 e3 Nb5 Nxb5 cxb5 Nb3 Na4 Bb2 Bd5
en: There were a number of interesting possibilities for Black. I don't know whether trading light square bishops is particularly useful for Black. Was Bg2 really that much of a problem?

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3 Re4 g5 Qe2 Nf6
en: Black has no reason to give his Bc8 for Re4 when the knight can do the job.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O a4 Bb7 d3 Re8 Nbd2 Bf8 c3 Na5 Ba2 c5 d4 d6 b4 exd4 bxa5 dxc3 Nf1 Nxe4
en: I'd generally want to put the "biggest, most dangerous" piece in front. In this case he may have felt it was simply unsafe to capture with the rook or bishop. But, if safe, either would be preferable to the knight.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 c3 a6 Ba4 b5 Bc2 Bb7 Qe2 Ng6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nh4 Nbd2 Rc8 Bb1 Bd6 a4 bxa4 Rxa4 Nxf3+ Nxf3 Nb4 Bd2 a5
en: This secures Nb4, but it also forces Nb4 to remain because it defends Pa5 from Ra4 & Bd2. It also sneakily (perhaps by accident) threatens ...Bb7-a6!

line: d4 d5 Nf3 e6 g3 Nf6 Bg2 Be7 c4 O-O Qc2 c5 dxc5 Qa5+ Nc3 dxc4 O-O Nc6 Bg5 Qxc5 Bxf6 Bxf6 Ne4 Qe7 Rfd1 b5 a4 Ba6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Rd6 Rac8
en: Black is steadfastly holding onto the pawn. White doesn't want to capture axb5 because he likes the alignment of Rd6 with Ba6; though opening the a-file at some point might be useful.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 e6 Bb3 Be7 O-O O-O c3 Nc6 Re1 b5 Nbd2 d5 e5 Nd7 d4 Ba6 Nf1 b4 Ba4 Rc8 Bxc6 Rxc6 cxb4 Bxf1 Rxf1 cxb4
en: This certainly solves a lot of Black's problems. Kg8 is a lot safer and Black already has control of the only open file (Rc8) . By trading a couple of minor pieces it should also be easier for Black to maneuver comfortably.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O h3 Bb7 d3 h6 Nc3 Bc5 a4 b4 Ne2 Na5 Ba2 d5 Nxe5 dxe4 d4 Ba7 Be3 Bd5
en: Common sense, really. Leko has to do something about the knight on a5, and his move (challenging the Shirov's strong, white-squared bishop) makes way for the knight to come back into the game via b7 or c6.

line: c4 c5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nc7 b3 e5 Bb2 Be7 Rc1 O-O Na4 Nd7 Nf3 f6 Qc2 Ne6 Nh4 Nb6 Nf5 Nxa4 bxa4 Rb8 f4 exf4 gxf4 Re8
en: Of course the Pf4 is at present one of the "untouchables": 16... Nxf4 17. Qc4+ Ne6 18. Bd5 Qd7 19. Bxe6+ Qxe6 20. Nxe7+.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 Bb7 Nf3 Qc8 Bg2 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6 O-O Ne7 Qc2 c5 Bg5 cxd4 Bxf6 gxf6 Ne4 Ng8 Nxd4 f5 Nd2 Bg7 Qd3 Nf6 Rfe1 f4
en: Uncertain. Probably 16.. .0-0 was better. With the Pawn sacrifice Black tries to exploit the opening of the g-file.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 d5 a3 Bxc3+ Qxc3 Ne4 Qc2 Nc6 e3 e5 f3 Nf6 cxd5 Qxd5 Bc4 Qd6 dxe5 Nxe5 Bd2 O-O Bb4 c5 Rd1 Qc6 Bd2 Bf5
en: For Alekhine, just one of the many ways to get some advantages. An immagination and spontaneous nature with no equal.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bb4 O-O O-O d3 d6 Bg5 Bxc3 bxc3 Qe7 Re1 Nd8 d4 Bg4 h3 Bh5 g4 Bg6 d5 c6 Bd3 cxd5 exd5 Rc8 c4 e4
en: Looks risky, since the Re1 and Bg5 are looking at the Qe7 straight into the eyes.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 b5 Bb3 d5 dxe5 Be6 c3 Be7 Re1 O-O Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 c6 f3 Ng5 Nc3 Bf5 g4 Bc8 f4 b4
en: Pong! The opponents hit each other to control the e4 square.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O Bc5 a3 Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Bd7 g3 f6 Bxg6+ hxg6 Qd3 Kf7 h4 Qg8 Bd2 Qh7 Bb4 g5
en: Now we begin to see the depth pf Botvinnik's strategy. He will force the removal of White's annoying king pawn, and then build up a strong pawn center of his own, even though it costs him a pawn.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 g3 g6 Bg2 Bg7 O-O O-O Nc3 Bb7 d4 Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 d5 e5 Be3 f5 Ne1 Bxg2 Nxg2 d6 Qd2 Nd7 f3 a5 Rab1 Nc5 b3 Rf7
en: And prophylaxis! Observe the way in which Nimzowitsch guards the c7 point before it is attacked.

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 b6 d4 e6 g3 Ba6 Qb3 Nc6 Bd2 Bb7 Bc3 Ne4 a3 Nxc3 Qxc3 Be7 Qd3 d5 cxd5 Qxd5 e4 Qa5+ Nbd2 O-O-O Rc1 f5 b4 fxe4 Qc3 Qd5
en: The pressure on the isolated pawn grows.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 d4 d5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Be7 c4 Nf6 h3 O-O Nc3 Nb4 Be2 dxc4 Bxc4 c6 Bg5 Nbd5 Re1 Be6 Qb3 Qb6 Nxd5 cxd5
en: Now neither side has perfect pawns, but Pd5 might possibly be the weakest. At least Black has kept the e-file closed, so Re1 isn't terribly useful (yet) .

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bd3 Be6 O-O Bxd5 exd5 Ne7 c3 Bg7 Qh5 e4 Bc2 O-O
en: Black secures his king and eyes White's queen-side pawns while considering the ways White might try to attack at h7.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e6 Be2 Be7 a4 Nc6 O-O O-O f4 Qc7 Kh1 Re8 Bf3 Bf8 Nb3 b6 a5 bxa5 e5 dxe5 fxe5 Rd8
en: Black takes this moment to transfer the rook to a more active square.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nb6 Ne2 c5 d5 e6 O-O O-O Nbc3 Na6 h3 exd5 exd5 Nc4 b3 Nd6 Bf4 b6 Qd2 Re8 Rad1 Bb7
en: Black develops modestly to catch up on piece activity, before embarking on any offensive measures.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 c5 e5 h6 Bc1 Nd5 c4 Nb4 d5 d6 a3 N4a6 exd6 Bxd6 Nc3 O-O Bd3 Nc7 Nge2 exd5 cxd5 Nd7 O-O Nf6 Bc4 b6 Ng3 Be5
en: Black threatens simply Bxc3 and then to capture Pd5.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 h6 Bh4 g5 fxg5 Nd5 Ne4 Qb6 Bd3 hxg5 Bxg5 Qxb2 c4 Qxe5 cxd5 Bg7
en: Very strong. If I move the rook then black has simply 17...cxd5. So eventually I realized that my next move, bizarre as it looks, is forced.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 O-O Nc6 d5 Ne7 b4 a5 bxa5 Rxa5 a4 Nd7 Ba3 Bh6 Nd2 Bxd2 Qxd2 f5 Nb5 Ra8 f4 b6
en: Very calm. Black is apparently under a lot of pressure but he still wants to let me release the central tension. I think I justified his choice in the game.

line: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 a3 Bb7 O-O-O Nd7 f4 c5 Nf3 Ngf6 e5 Ng4 Bg1 cxd4 Bxd4 dxe5 fxe5 Bxf3 gxf3 Ngxe5 Qe3 Qc7 Bh3 Nc4
en: _?? Andy sort of implies that this is a fatal blunder, but I don't want to leave any doubt!_.

line: e4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 d4 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bd3 Nc6 Bf4 f6 Qe2 fxe5 Nxe5 Ndxe5 Bxe5 Nxe5 Qxe5 O-O Rf1 g6 O-O-O Bxf2 Kb1 Bd7 Ne4 dxe4
en: He played this quickly, presumably happy because in the ending he is not likely to lose, i.e. the old "playing for two results"... yet Fritz found another spoiler.

line: c4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 f5 d4 e4 Ng5 Bb4 Nh3 Nf6 e3 Bxc3+ bxc3 d6 Nf4 O-O h4 Qe7 c5 Nd8 Qb3+ Ne6 Bc4 Re8 Ba3 Kh8 Bxe6 Bxe6 Qxb7 d5
en: The only move, but it still deserves an exclamation mark. This ignores the threat on the c7 pawn as well. Positionally speaking, this move is very effective at closing in the a3 bishop.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e5 Nfd7 Bxe7 Qxe7 f4 a6 Nf3 c5 Qd2 Nc6 dxc5 Qxc5 Bd3 b5 a3 Bb7 Qf2 b4 Na4 Qxf2+ Kxf2 a5 Bb5 Ke7
en: The best move. After the queens are exchange black rightly sees there's no need to castle.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 Be7 O-O b6 Ne5 Bb7 Nxf6+ gxf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Re1 Nf8 Rxe6 Nxe6 Bc4 Qd6 Bh6 Bf8 Re1 Bc8
en: Now Black's pieces are so awkwardly pinned and stuck together that it's almost a miracle he's not mated already. Najdorf gleefully adds another pin to the mix.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3 Bb7 d3 Nd7 Nbd2 Nc5 Bc2 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nf1 Rad8 Ne3 Qd7 d4 exd4
en: Black would love to bypass the exchange, but because of the attack on his N/c5, he cannot: 16...e4 17.Nd2 ... and Black must move the Knight, allowing the e-pawn to fall.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Be3 c5 Qd2 O-O Rc1 Qa5 Nf3 e6 d5 exd5 exd5 Re8 Be2 Bf5 O-O Nd7 h3 Nb6 g4 Bd7
en: Time: AK: 1:31 GK: 0:49. GM-elects Watson and Gallagher say Karpov is still under pressure, but improving. Mephisto "thinks" it's slightly better for Black. And the Russians say that Kasparov should have played h7-h5, not Nd7-b6.

line: c4 c5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 g3 b6 Bg2 Bb7 O-O Be7 d4 cxd4 Qxd4 O-O e4 Nc6 Qe3 d6 Rd1 Qc7 Qe2 Ne5 b3 Nxf3+ Bxf3 a6 Bb2 Rfd8 Rac1 Rab8
en: Black remains passive. The rook can go to c8 in one move.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Qa5 Rc1 Rd8 Qa4 Qxc5 b4 Qc6 Qxc6 bxc6 Bc7 Rd7 Ba5 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Ng5 c5 Nxe4 cxb4
en: Black offers a pawn for counteraction.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Qxd4 d5 exd6 Nxd6 Nc3 Nc6 Qf4 Bf5 Bb5 Qe7+ Be3 Nxb5 Nxb5 Qb4+ Qxb4 Bxb4+ c3 Ba5 b4 Bd3 a4 a6 O-O-O Be2
en: The highlight of a theoretical duel has been reached.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Be2 O-O Bg5 c5 d5 e6 Nf3 h6 Be3 exd5 exd5 Bf5 O-O Ne4 Nxe4 Bxe4 Bd3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Nd7 Qh3 Ne5 Rad1 Qd7
en: Draw is a useful result for Stein. Exchange of the queens brings him toward his goal.

line: d4 h6 e4 d6 Nc3 a6 f4 b5 Nf3 Bb7 Bd3 c5 dxc5 dxc5 b3 g5 fxg5 Bg7 Bb2 hxg5 Nxg5 Nd7 Qf3 Bf6 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Qa5+ Kf1 Rh6 d6 Rb8
en: #(Now how on earth will White save the Ng5 or Bb2?).

line: Nf3 d5 d4 Nc6 c4 Bg4 Nc3 Bxf3 exf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd4 Qb3 Nd8 Be3 Qd7 Rd1 Qc8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 Bxf7 Nf6 Be6 Qb8 Qd1+ Ke8 O-O g6 Ne4 Qd8 Qb3 Qb8
en: (Again 16...Bg7 prolongs matters.).

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 f4 c5 c3 Nc6 Ndf3 Qb6 h4 cxd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Kf2 f6 Be3 fxe5 fxe5 O-O a3 Be7 b4 a6 Bd3 Qc7 Qc2 h6
en: ("Chickening out" of liquidating the centre under my terms.).

line: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 d4 Bg7 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 Nxc3 bxc3 e6 e3 O-O Bd3 b6 cxd5 exd5 O-O Bg4 h3 Be6 Ne5 f6 Ng4 g5 Bg3 Nc6 Nh2 Ne7
en: Bringing more defensive forces into the arena.

line: e4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ng5 d6 d4 h6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Bc4+ Kg7 Bxf4 Be7 O-O Bxh4 Qd2 a6 g3 Be7 Rf2 Nf6 Raf1 b5 Bd5 Bd7
en: [This move blocks the Black queen's power down the d-file. The influence of the Black Queen had been preventing White pushing onto e5. If 16...Nxd5 17.Nxd5 Be6 18.Nxe7 Qxe7 19.d5+= or 16...Bb7 17.Bg5! Nxd5 18.Rf7+ Kg8 19.Bxh6+-].

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 Bf5 f3 Nd6 Nc3 e6 Qe2 Be7 O-O-O Bg6 e4 c6 h4 h5 Re1 Nc4 Qf2 Bb4 Bxc4 dxc4 Nge2 Nd7 Qg3 Nf6 Rd1 O-O
en: I had expected 16...Qd7 followed by Queenside castling. With oposite side castling White will engage the Black h pawn first.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4 Qb6 Nb3 Nbd7 Qf3 Qc7 Bd3 b5 O-O-O Bb7 Bxf6 Nxf6 Kb1 Be7 g4 Rc8 g5 Nd7 Qh3 b4
en: At this point my opponent took a month off to avoid distraction from the Sydney Olympics.

line: c4 c6 e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 cxd5 d4 e6 Nf3 Bb4 cxd5 Nxd5 Qc2 Qc7 Bd2 Nd7 Bd3 Bxc3 bxc3 N5f6 a4 b6 O-O Bb7 Nh4 O-O f4 Bd5 Nf3 Bc4
en: Now light squares in White's camp are weak, while his dark-squared bishop is an unfortunate piece.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nc3 Bd7 b3 Kc8 Bb2 Be7 Rad1 a5 h3 Re8 Rd3 c5 Rfd1 Bc6 Nd5 Bxd5
en: Black can't bear such a strong knight and has to part with his main plus - a pair of bishops.
